title: Chronicon Omnimodae Historiae
author: Flavius Lucius Dexter
source: Translated by Claude from tmp582.tmp582.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Sed ut semel ejus potestas, et officii celsitudo palam fiat, placet in Dextri gratiam hic inserere formulam, quae praefec- tis praetorio ab imperatoribus dabatur, cum ad hu- jusmodi dignitatem jubebantur ascendere, prout a Cassiodoro ponitur lib. VI Variarum cap. 3, qui eam scribit, quo tempore erat eadem profectura insignitus, ut ex prologo ipsarum lectionum Varia- rum constat, et ex lib. XI et XII, per multas epistolas.
passages.english: But so that his power and the loftiness of his office may once and for all be made plain, I have decided, as a courtesy to Dexter, to insert here the formula that was given by the emperors to praetorian prefects when they were ordered to ascend to a dignity of this kind, as it is set out by Cassiodorus in book VI of the Variae, chapter 3. He wrote it at the time when he himself was distinguished with that same prefecture, as is clear from the prologue of those Variae and from books XI and XII, through many letters.
passages.notes: "profectura" is read as "praefectura" (prefecture).

passages.original: Quid vero in causa fuerit, ut nihil gestorum addiderit anno 430, ad quem primum historiam protraxerat, et locupletatio non in annis, sed in rebus facta fue- rit, explicatum a nobis est in Apologia § 2. Porro Lalaetanum vocat Orosium, quod Tarraco ad vete- rem Lalaetaniam spectaret; Orosius vero esset Tar- raconensis : quamquam nonnihil inter se differre Lalaetuniam et agros Tarraconenses, ex veteribus scia- mus, nam Plinius lib.
passages.english: As for the reason why he added nothing of events to the year 430, to which he had first carried the history, and why the enlargement was made not in years but in matter, we have explained this in the Apology, § 2. Further, he calls Orosius a Lalaetanian because Tarraco belonged to ancient Lalaetania, and Orosius was from Tarraco; although we know from the ancients that Lalaetania and the territory of Tarraco differ somewhat from each other, for Pliny, in book
passages.notes: "Lalaetuniam" is read as "Lalaetaniam". The sentence breaks off; the reference continues in the following passage (Natural History XIV).

passages.original: A. C. 37. Multos etiam discipulos, praecipuos autem numero duodecim, more apostolico in Hispa- A. R. 788. niam secum portat. Scilicet episcopos Basilium, Pium, Athanasium : Maximum, Chrysogonum, presbyteros : Theodorum, Caecilium, Thesiphontem, Iscium, Calo- cerum, lectores : Torquatum, exorcistam; et Secundum, Indalecium, Euphrasium ostiarios.
passages.english: Year of Christ 37; year of Rome 788. He also brings many disciples with him into Spain, but chief among them twelve in number, after the apostolic pattern: namely the bishops Basilius, Pius and Athanasius; Maximus and Chrysogonus, priests; Theodorus, Caecilius, Thesiphon, Iscius and Calocerus, lectors; Torquatus, exorcist; and Secundus, Indalecius and Euphrasius, doorkeepers.
passages.notes: The subject (presumably the apostle James) is not named in the passage. The marginal year notes, which the edition splits into the text, have been gathered at the start.

passages.original: A. C. 116. Rutilius ad Hispaniam missus fit martyr. Meminit ejus Tertullianus praeclaro quidem A. R. 867. elogio.
passages.english: Year of Christ 116; year of Rome 867. Rutilius, sent to Spain, becomes a martyr. Tertullian mentions him with a splendid tribute indeed.

passages.original: 143. Justinus philosophus librum pro religione tradidit Antonino. 894.
passages.english: [Year of Christ] 143; [year of Rome] 894. Justin the philosopher delivered a book on behalf of the religion to Antoninus.

passages.original: Felix presbyter Vallatae urbicuae in Vaccaeis, scribit ad Cyprianum Carthaginen- sem episcopum, in causa Basilidis Asturicensis episcopi, illumque de maximis accusat criminibus.
passages.english: Felix, a priest of the city of Vallata among the Vaccaei, writes to Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, in the case of Basilides, bishop of Astorga, and accuses him of the gravest crimes.
passages.notes: "urbicuae" is apparently a scanning error for "urbis" or similar. Vallata is not securely identified.

passages.original: 352. Natali pontifici Toletano succedit Olympius, vir pius, et doctissimus, ad quem ali- 1103. quotiens scripsit Gregorius Nazianzenus. Hic fuerat prius in Thracia episcopus :
passages.english: [Year of Christ] 352; [year of Rome] 1103. Natalis, bishop of Toledo, is succeeded by Olympius, a pious and most learned man, to whom Gregory of Nazianzus wrote several times. He had previously been a bishop in Thrace:
passages.notes: The passage ends with a colon; what follows is missing.

passages.original: Carthagine Spartaria, durante impiissima Juliani persecutione, Donatus martyr Hi- spanus (ad quem scripsit Lactantius librum de Ira Dei) sub judice Verano.
passages.english: At Cartagena (Carthago Spartaria), during the most impious persecution of Julian, Donatus, a Spanish martyr (to whom Lactantius wrote the book On the Anger of God), [suffered] under the judge Veranus.
passages.notes: The sentence has no main verb; "[suffered]" is supplied from the sense.

passages.original: Justo... episcopo Vicensi scribit sanctus Ambrosius.
passages.english: Saint Ambrose writes to Justus..., bishop of Vic.
passages.notes: The edition's ellipsis after "Justo" is kept.

passages.original: A. C. 388. Higinio Cordubensi succedit Gregorius Junior : scripsit ad Orosium super ann. 380. A. R. 1139.
passages.english: Year of Christ 388; year of Rome 1139. Higinius of Córdoba is succeeded by Gregory the Younger. He wrote to Orosius about the year 380.
passages.notes: "super ann. 380" is unclear: it may mean that he wrote about [events of] the year 380, or it may be a cross-reference to the entry for the year 380.

passages.original: A. C. 388. Hic Barcinonensem vitiat Ecclesiam, ubi presbyter fuit, et Ecclesias alias Hi- A. R. 1139. spaniae : contra quem scripsit sanctus Hieronymus.
passages.english: A.D. 388. This man corrupts the Church of Barcelona, where he was a priest, and other Churches of Spain; against him St Jerome wrote. A.R. 1139.
passages.notes: 'A. R. 1139' is a marginal date (year of the Roman or Spanish era) printed in the middle of 'Hispaniae'; moved here. The subject 'hic' is not identified in the passage (probably Vigilantius, against whom Jerome wrote).

passages.original: Haeresis Priscillianistarum multum in Hispania repullulat. Paulo Concordiensi Lusitano scribit Hieronymus. Constantius imperator in regionibus Hispaniae praedatur.
passages.english: The heresy of the Priscillianists sprouts up again greatly in Spain. Jerome writes to Paul of Concordia, a Lusitanian. The emperor Constantius plunders in the regions of Spain.
passages.notes: 'Constantius imperator' is as printed; the historical figure meant is uncertain (perhaps Constantine III or the general Constantius).

passages.original: III Christus Dominus venerit ad baptisma anno XV im- perii Tiberii Caesaris, existens annorum XXX, qui videlicet Tiberii annus consules habuit duos ge- minos, Rubelium et Rufium. Si autem ab his coss. et anno Caesaris sursum ascendendo XXX consulatus enumeres in Fastis, qui apud Cassiodorum et Onu- phrium re periuntur, pervenies ad consulatum Cor- nelii Lentuli et Valerii Messalae; atque in eo acci- disse Christi nativitate certum erit : totidem siquidem consulatus, nec plus, nec minus, inter hos et illos Coss.
passages.english: 3, Christ the Lord came to baptism in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, being thirty years old; and that year of Tiberius had two consuls who were twins, Rubellius and Rufius. Now if, starting from these consuls and that year of Caesar and going back, you count thirty consulships in the Fasti found in Cassiodorus and Onuphrius, you will arrive at the consulship of Cornelius Lentulus and Valerius Messala; and it will be certain that Christ's nativity took place in it, since exactly that many consulships, neither more nor less, are found between these consuls and those.
passages.notes: 'III' continues 'cap.' from the preceding context (Luke ch. 3). 'Rubelium et Rufium' are presumably the two Gemini (Rubellius and Fufius Geminus); 'duos geminos' is a play on their cognomen. 'Rufium' may be an error for Fufium. The sentence runs on into the context after ('reperiuntur').

passages.original: Hoc etiam ex olympiadum supputatione, quae po- tissima inter Graecos erat, deducitur, annus siquidem XV Tiberii, Eusebio teste lib. II de Praepar. Evang. cap. 3, fuit quartus et ultimus Olympiadis CCI; ab hoc vero usque ad secundum Olympiadis CXCIV quo Len- tulus et Messala consulatum inierunt, indusive in- tersunt septem integrae olympiades, quae cum quae- libel sit quadriennia, viginti octo annos conficiunt;
passages.english: This is also deduced from the reckoning by Olympiads, which was the chief one among the Greeks. For the fifteenth year of Tiberius, as Eusebius attests in book II of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 3, was the fourth and last of the 201st Olympiad. From this back to the second year of the 194th Olympiad, in which Lentulus and Messala entered the consulship, there lie, inclusively, seven whole Olympiads. Since each of them is four years long, they make twenty-eight years;
passages.notes: 'indusive' read as 'inclusive', 'quaelibel' as 'quaelibet'.

passages.original: Sic etiam docuit Dionysius Halicarnasseus : et Messala Corvinus lib. de sua progenie ad Augus- tum, Ferunt, ait, undecimo kalendas Maias, Romu· lum Urbis fundamenta jecisse. Pro eadem sententia auctor Chronologiae in Historiam LIVII in principio, refert Tullium, Plutarchum, et Solinum; et idem asserit Marlianus lib. de Origine urbis Romae, et Velcurio in Comment. ad lib. II Titi LIVII : Dies, in- quit, Romae natalitius, quo condi capta est, habetur adIIkal Maias. Denique Propertius lib. IV haec ait :
passages.english: Dionysius of Halicarnassus also taught this; and Messala Corvinus, in his book on his own lineage addressed to Augustus, says: "They report that Romulus laid the foundations of the City on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May." For the same opinion the author of the Chronology on the History of Livy, at the beginning, cites Tully, Plutarch and Solinus; and Marlianus asserts the same in his book On the Origin of the City of Rome, as does Velcurio in his Commentary on Book II of Titus Livy: "The birthday of Rome," he says, "on which its founding was begun, is held to be the eleventh day before the Kalends of May." Finally Propertius, in Book IV, says this:
passages.notes: "adIIkal Maias" is evidently a misprint for "ad XI kal. Maias" (21 April), consistent with the earlier statement; translated accordingly. The Propertius quotation follows outside the passage.

passages.original: Antonium Reipublicae constituendae. Contigit vero quadraginta annis ante Christi Domini natalem, et Urbis conditae 712, ut in Comment. Fastorum probat Onuphrius lib. II. Sed quorsum haec? scilicet ut discas, Plinium eo loro minime egisse de illa trini solis comparitione, quae Christo recens nato in Hispaniis facta est; quandoquidem quaedam ex recensitis ab co longe simi anteriores, cum ca quae sub Plancio et Lepido coss.
passages.english: Antony, for settling the Republic. This happened forty years before the birth of Christ the Lord, and in the 712th year from the founding of the City, as Onuphrius proves in his Commentary on the Fasti, book II. But to what end is this? Namely so that you may learn that Pliny in that passage was not at all treating of that appearance of a triple sun which took place in Spain when Christ was newly born. For some of those he lists are far earlier, while the one that happened in the consulship of Plancius and Lepidus
passages.notes: 'loro' read as 'loco'; 'co' as 'eo'; 'longe simi' probably for 'longissime' or 'longe sunt'; 'ca' as 'ea'. The sentence continues in the following context.

passages.original: Praecesserat quidem Romae fons olei, qui in Transtiberina taberna meritoria repente eru- pit. et unius diei spatio finxisse dicitur, anno tertio Triumviratus, et ante Christi nativitatem 37, ut Orosius noster testatur lib. VI cap. 19, quem Baro- nius sequitur; tres autem soles in Hispania visi, Deum in carne recens natum demonstrabant, utpote qui altero ab ejus Nativitate anno, testimonio Dextri apparuerint : cui in hac re fides adhibenda est, eo vel maxime quod robus Hispanicis annotandis ante omnes incubuit, et illi in hac parte nemo reluctetur.
passages.english: There had indeed earlier been at Rome a spring of oil, which suddenly burst forth in an inn for veterans across the Tiber and is said to have flowed for the space of one day, in the third year of the Triumvirate and 37 years before the birth of Christ, as our Orosius attests in book VI, chapter 19, and Baronius follows him. But the three suns seen in Spain pointed to God newly born in the flesh, since they appeared in the second year after his Nativity, on the testimony of Dexter. He is to be trusted in this matter, especially because he devoted himself before all others to recording Spanish affairs, and no one opposes him on this point.
passages.notes: 'finxisse' read as 'fluxisse'; 'robus' as 'rebus'. 'Taberna meritoria' is the inn or hostel for veteran soldiers.

passages.original: Siquidem (ait) non solum ex auro, argentove, aut certe ex aere in Bibliothecis dicantur illi, quorum immor· tales animas in iisdem locis ibi loquuntur; quinimmo etiam quae non sunt finguntur, pariuntque desideria non traditi vultus, sicut in Homero evenit. Incidit consu- latus Asinii in annum Urbis 747 ut placet Cassio- doro, sexennio ante Christi natalem, sociumque ha- buit C. Martium. Sed quoniam sua aetate Cicero flumen novum eloquentiae floruerat, et Asinius ab ejus nitore et jucunditate tantum aberat, ul videri posset saculo prior; effectum est, ut ejus filius Asi- nius Gallus, vir etiam consularis, librum scripserit de comparatione patris cum Cicerone, ubi Pollio- nem Ciceroni praetulit; contra quem in defensio- nem Ciceronis Cl. Caesar defensorium edidit, ut Suetonius in Claudio refert, de quo etiam Caelius Rhodiginius in suis lect. antiqu. De Asinio haec ha- bet Eusebius in chronico : Anno Domini 6, Asinius Pollio orator, et consularis, qui de Dalmatis trium- phaverat, octogesimo aetatis suae anno, in villa Tuscu- lana moritur.
passages.english: "For indeed," he says, "not only are those whose immortal souls speak in these same places dedicated in libraries in gold or silver, or at least in bronze; nay, even those likenesses that do not exist are invented, and faces not handed down give rise to longing, as happens in the case of Homer." Asinius's consulship fell in the 747th year of the City, as Cassiodorus holds, six years before the birth of Christ, and he had C. Marcius as colleague. But since Cicero in his time had flourished as a new river of eloquence, and Asinius was so far from his brilliance and charm that he could seem a generation earlier, it came about that his son Asinius Gallus, also a man of consular rank, wrote a book on the comparison of his father with Cicero, in which he preferred Pollio to Cicero; against which Claudius Caesar published a defence of Cicero, as Suetonius reports in his Claudius; on which see also Caelius Rhodiginius in his Ancient Readings. Eusebius in his Chronicle has this about Asinius: "In the year of the Lord 6, Asinius Pollio, orator and consular, who had triumphed over the Dalmatians, dies in his Tusculan villa in the eightieth year of his age."
passages.notes: The Pliny quotation is garbled in the text ('ibi loquuntur'); translated as it stands. 'ul' read 'ut', 'saculo' as 'saeculo'. The stated consular year (747, six years before Christ) is the author's claim; it does not match Pollio's actual consulship.

passages.original: A. C. 9. Tiberius, etc. Eisdem fere verbis uti- tur Eusebius in Chronico : Anno Domini 9, Tibe- rius Caesar Dalmatas, Sarmatasque in Romanam re- digit potestatem. Dalmatae inter caeteras gentes pos- tremae fuerunt, quas Octavianus Augustus Romano subjecit imperio.
passages.english: A.D. 9. "Tiberius," etc. Eusebius uses almost the same words in his Chronicle: "In the year of the Lord 9, Tiberius Caesar brought the Dalmatians and Sarmatians under Roman power." The Dalmatians were the last, among the other peoples, whom Octavian Augustus brought under the Roman empire.

passages.original: Sarmatarum regio latissime patebat, ab ipsis ni- mirum Germaniae finibus, et amne Vistula, in Hirca- niam usque protensa : nunc Croatia dicitur. Ab efferatissimis incolebatur hominibus, qui partim in montibus et saltibus degebant, partim palustribus domibus utebantur. Scribit Plinius lib. XXII, cap. 1, eosdem formae gratia, ritusque perpetui, corpora sua quarumdam herbarum succis pingere solitos (quod aevo quoque nostro Americis in usu fuit), et quod, ut plurimum, alebantur pulte confecto ex cruda milii farina, equino lacte, vel sanguine ad- misto.
passages.english: The region of the Sarmatians extended very widely, stretching namely from the very borders of Germany and the river Vistula as far as Hyrcania; it is now called Croatia. It was inhabited by very savage men, who lived partly in mountains and forests and partly in marsh dwellings. Pliny writes in book XXII, chapter 1, that for the sake of beauty and by a perpetual custom they were accustomed to paint their bodies with the juices of certain herbs (which was also in use among the Americans in our own age), and that for the most part they fed on a porridge made of raw millet flour mixed with mare's milk or blood.
passages.notes: The identification of Sarmatia with Croatia is the author's.

passages.original: Ita Eusebius in Chro- nico : Anno Domini 14 Augustus cum Tiberio filio censum Romae agitans, invenit hominum nonagies tre- centa, et septuaginta millia. Mos fuit Romanis quoli- bet lustro censum agere; immo, ut Varro auctor est, lustrum a luendo, id est, solvendo, dictum fuit spa- tium quinque annorum, quod quinto quoque anno vectigalia per censores locata persolvebantur, et a civibus tributa conferebantur.
passages.english: So Eusebius in the Chronicle: "In the year of the Lord 14 Augustus, conducting a census at Rome with his son Tiberius, found nine million three hundred and seventy thousand people." It was the custom of the Romans to hold a census every lustrum; indeed, as Varro is the authority, a period of five years was called a lustrum from luere, that is, "to pay", because every fifth year the revenues farmed out by the censors were paid in full, and taxes were contributed by the citizens.
passages.notes: "nonagies trecenta et septuaginta millia" literally "ninety times three hundred and seventy thousand"; the intended figure (9,370,000) is ambiguous in the Latin.

passages.original: A. C. 15. — 1. Defectio, etc. Utrumque hoc anno accidisse, praeter Dextrum, Eusebius in Chro- nico affirmat : et quod Augustus obierit aetatis suae anno 76. Obiit autem Attellae (nunc Nolae) in Cam- pania, inde in Campum Martium urbis translatus. Sunt qui asserant, quod supremum agens diem, ja- ctaverit se urbem relinquere marmoream, quam lateritiam invenerat.
passages.english: A.D. 15. — 1. "The eclipse," etc. Besides Dexter, Eusebius in his Chronicle affirms that both these things happened in this year, and that Augustus died in the seventy-sixth year of his age. He died at Atella (now Nola) in Campania, and from there was carried to the Campus Martius of the City. Some assert that on his last day he boasted that he was leaving a city of marble, which he had found of brick.
passages.notes: 'Defectio' may mean 'eclipse' or 'revolt'; the lemma is truncated. The identification of Atella with Nola is the author's.

passages.original: Sub amphi- theatro erat cavea 40 millia hominum capax. In ornamentum autem ipsius mirabiles Pompeius po- suit effigies, magnorum artificum ingeniis diligen- tissime elaboratas, inter quas Plinio auctore, lib. VII, cap. 3, erat Eutyche a 20 liberis rogo illata Tral- libus, enixa 30 partus. Hoc igitur anno Domini 23 magno Romanorum dolore flamma corripiente vasta- tum est Aliud ab eo fuit Theatrum a M.
passages.english: Beneath the amphitheatre was the seating area, holding 40,000 people. To adorn it Pompey set up wonderful statues, worked with the greatest care by the talents of great artists. Among them, on the authority of Pliny, book VII, chapter 3, was Eutyche, who was carried to her pyre at Tralles by twenty of her children, having given birth thirty times. In this year of the Lord 23, then, to the great grief of the Romans, it was laid waste when fire seized it. Another theatre, distinct from this one, was built by M.
passages.notes: The sentence breaks off at 'M.'; the context continues 'Scaurus'. 'Sub amphitheatro' is as printed; the building described is Pompey's theatre.

passages.original: Sane duxisse secum uxorem suam in Syriam Pi- latum, cum Praeses ejus provinciae factus fuit, non solum ex Evaugelio, sed ex Ethnicorum libris ha- bemus; nam tametsi ante quinque annos (ut scribit Cornelius Tacitus lib. annal. 3, sub quarto nomi- rum Tiberii Caesaris Consulatu, qui incidit in an- num Christi vigesimum secundum, ut ex Fastis Onu- phrii liquet) Severus Cecinna gravissima Oratione censuisset, ne uxores maritos in provinciam profi- ciscentes comitarentur;
passages.english: Certainly, that Pilate took his wife with him into Syria when he was made governor of that province we know not only from the Gospel but also from the books of the pagans. For although five years earlier (as Cornelius Tacitus writes in book 3 of the Annals, in the fourth consulship of Tiberius Caesar, which falls in the twenty-second year of Christ, as is clear from the Fasti of Onuphrius) Severus Caecina had proposed, in a very weighty speech, that wives should not accompany husbands setting out to a province;
passages.notes: 'Evaugelio' read as 'Evangelio'. 'quarto nomirum' is evidently a scanning error; read as 'in the fourth consulship'.

passages.original: et inde nihilominus Hieronymo in Oriente degenti munera ac litteras mittentis : subdit, ejus mirandam fidem jam olim Cornelium centurionem cohortis Italicae praefigu- rasse, qui scilicet in eadem provincia ortus, ad fidem pariter perductus est : atque in utroque im- pletum esse sermonem Dominicum : Multi ab Oriente et Occidente venient, et recumbent cum Abraham, etc. Addit hoc ipsum desiderio desiderasse Apostolum, dum ad Romanos scriberet illud : Cum in Hispaniam proficisci coepero, etc., a vobis deducar illuc : tantis fluctibus approbans, quid de illa provincia quaereret, fidem scilicet Hispanorum, qualis in Cornelio, et Lucinio Baeticis micabat. En verba Hieronymi : Vere nunc in te (o Lucini Baetice) sermo Dominicus com- pletus est : Multi ab Oriente et Occidente venient, et recumbent in sinu Abrahae. Cornelius centurio cohortis Italicae, jam tunc Lucinii mei praefigurabat fidem. Apostolus Paulus scribens ad Romanos : Cum, inquit, in Hispaniam proficisci coepero, spero quod praeteriens videam vos, et a vobis deducar illuc. Tantis fluctibus approbavit, quid de illa provincia quaereret. Haec ille. Utrumque igitur ad eamdem rem facere sensit Hie- ronymus : et Cornelii fidem, et Pauli desiderium. In quo, quaeso, praefigurabat fidem Lucinii Cornelius, nisi quia ex illis oriundus erat, ex quibus postea ortus est Lucinius, et quos Paulus ad fidem perdu- cere cupiebat?
passages.english: and who nonetheless sent gifts and letters from there to Jerome, who was living in the East. He adds that Cornelius, centurion of the Italian cohort, had long ago prefigured his wonderful faith, since Cornelius was born in the same province and was likewise brought to the faith; and that in both the Lord's saying was fulfilled: 'Many will come from the East and the West, and will recline with Abraham,' etc. He adds that the Apostle had longed for this very thing with desire when he wrote to the Romans: 'When I begin to set out for Spain,' etc., 'may I be escorted there by you,' showing, through such great waves, what he was seeking from that province, namely the faith of the Spaniards, such as shone in Cornelius and Lucinius, men of Baetica. Here are Jerome's words: 'Truly now in you (O Lucinius of Baetica) the Lord's saying is fulfilled: Many will come from the East and the West, and will recline in the bosom of Abraham. Cornelius, centurion of the Italian cohort, even then prefigured the faith of my Lucinius. The Apostle Paul, writing to the Romans, says: When I begin to set out for Spain, I hope that I may see you in passing, and be escorted there by you. Through such great waves he showed what he was seeking from that province.' So far Jerome. Jerome therefore held that both bear on the same point: the faith of Cornelius and the desire of Paul. In what, I ask, did Cornelius prefigure the faith of Lucinius, unless in this, that he came from the same people from whom Lucinius later came, and whom Paul longed to bring to the faith?
passages.notes: 'tantis fluctibus approbans/approbavit' is obscure: perhaps 'proving by the dangers of so many seas'. The author assumes Cornelius came from Italica in Baetica, reading 'Italian cohort' that way.

passages.original: Oppii spectat (ne quis eo moveri contingat) Romanum est, et nobilissimis ci- vibus in usu exstitit, quales fuere Sp. Oppius Cor- nicen cognomine, et M. Oppius, ambo Decemviri, et L. Oppius dictus Salinator, quorum meminit Livius lib. III et lib. XXXV, et celeberrimus ille C. Oppius qui, sub Q· Fabio, et Tito Sempronio coss. anno Ur- bis 544, legem Oppiam de cultu matronarum tule- rat, ab ejus nomine dictam, qua cavebatur : Ne qua mulier plus semiuncia auri haberet, neu vestimento ver- sicolori uteretur, neu juncto vehiculo in urbe oppidove, aut propius inde mille passus, nisi sacrorum publico- rum causa veheretur.
passages.english: As for the name of C. Oppius (lest anyone happen to be troubled by it), it is Roman, and was in use among very noble citizens, such as Sp. Oppius, surnamed Cornicen, and M. Oppius, both decemvirs, and L. Oppius called Salinator, whom Livy mentions in book III and book XXXV; and that very famous C. Oppius who, in the consulship of Q. Fabius and Titus Sempronius, in the year of the City 544, had carried the Oppian law on the adornment of matrons, named after him, by which it was provided: 'That no woman should have more than half an ounce of gold, nor wear a garment of varied colour, nor ride in a yoked carriage in the city or a town, or within a mile of it, unless she were riding for the sake of public rites.'

passages.original: 6. Sancta Petronilla, etc. D. apostolum Petrum, cum a captura piscium ad piscationem hominum jussu Domini transiit, uxorem habuisse, nemo est qui abnuat : id quod (ut Hieronymum et Tertullia- num missos faciam) perspicue docuit vetustissimus Martyr Ignatius ad Philadelphios scribens : Non de- traho, ait. Beatis, qui nuptiis copulati fuerunt. Opto enim Deo dignos ad vestigia eorum in regno ipsius inveniri, sicut Petrus et aliqui Apostoli qui nuptiis fuerunt sociali.
passages.english: 6. Saint Petronilla, etc. That the blessed apostle Peter had a wife when, at the Lord's command, he passed from catching fish to fishing for men, there is no one who denies. This (to leave aside Jerome and Tertullian) the most ancient martyr Ignatius taught plainly, writing to the Philadelphians: 'I do not disparage,' he says, 'the blessed who have been joined in marriage. For I pray that, worthy of God, I may be found in his kingdom at their footsteps, like Peter and some apostles who were partners in marriage.'
passages.notes: 'sociali' presumably for 'sociati'.

passages.original: Sed et M. Marcellus Eugenius ejusdem Apostoli discipulus hoc ipsum, luco statim citando, profitetur. Petri autem uxorem martyrio coram ipso coronatam, ex majorum relatione traditum sibi re- fert Clemens Alexandrinus VII suorum Stromatum libro : Aiunt certe B. Petrum (verba sunt Clementis) cum videret uxorem suam duci ad mortem, laetatum quidem esse propter vocationem, et quod domum re- verteretur (hoc est quod ad patriam pergeret coe- lestem, quae domus nostra est, et a qua peregrina- mur).
passages.english: Moreover M. Marcellus Eugenius, a disciple of the same Apostle, professes this very thing in the passage to be cited presently. And Clement of Alexandria, in the seventh book of his Stromata, reports that it was handed down to him by the account of the elders that Peter's wife was crowned with martyrdom in his presence: 'They say indeed that blessed Peter (these are Clement's words), when he saw his wife being led to death, rejoiced on account of her calling, and because she was returning home' (that is, because she was going to the heavenly fatherland, which is our home and from which we are exiles).
passages.notes: 'luco' read as 'loco'. Marcellus Eugenius is not identified with certainty.

passages.original: Unde ad Caium, qui eam absolverat, dixit : Tu quidem imperator, ut tua maje- state dignum est, loqueris : sed mihi conjugalis amor im- pedimento est, quominus fruar hac indulgentia : non enim aequum censeo, ut cui secundae fortunae fui socia, eum nunc in adversa deseram. At ille indigne ferens (ait Josephus) tam excelsum animum in femina, ipsam quoque cum Herode expulit, et bona ejus Agrippae lar- gitus est. Atque ita effectum est, ut ambo extra Ju- daeam ad Occidentem ortus partem concesserint, exsilio perpetuo damnati.
passages.english: Hence she said to Gaius, who had acquitted her: 'You, emperor, speak as befits your majesty; but conjugal love prevents me from enjoying this indulgence; for I do not think it right that, having been the partner of one in good fortune, I should now desert him in adversity.' But he, resenting (says Josephus) so lofty a spirit in a woman, banished her too along with Herod, and gave her property to Agrippa. And so it came about that both withdrew from Judaea to the western part, condemned to perpetual exile.
passages.notes: 'ad Occidentem ortus partem' seems garbled; rendered as 'to the western part'.

passages.original: Atqui in re dubia Dextrum libentius amplec- tor, sive de mortis genere, sive de persona mortem perpessa sermo sit : tum quia multis saeculis Nice- pboro fuit anterior, tum quoniam ipse Hispanus erat, et Barcinonensis, et ea retulit quae Herdae in provin- cia sua, non longe n Barcinone contigerant : ille vero recentior multo, et in Grecia natus, et educatus fuit. Neque vero lego apud Josephum saltatricem fi- tam in exsilium quoque actam, seu ipsam comita- tam fuisse matrem, ut submergi, vel detruncari Her- dae potuisset. Quis scit si in matrimonium data cum conjuge in Galilaea, Judaeave manserit?
passages.english: Yet in a doubtful matter I more willingly follow Dexter, whether the question is the manner of death or the person who suffered it: both because he was many centuries earlier than Nicephorus, and because he was himself a Spaniard, and from Barcelona, and reported things that had happened at Ilerda in his own province, not far from Barcelona; whereas the other was much more recent, and was born and raised in Greece. Nor do I read in Josephus that the dancing daughter was also driven into exile, or accompanied her mother, so that she could have been drowned or beheaded at Ilerda. Who knows whether, given in marriage, she remained with her husband in Galilee or Judaea?
passages.notes: 'Herdae' taken as Ilerda (Lleida). 'fitam' read as 'filiam'; 'n Barcinone' as 'a Barcinone'.

passages.original: 6 de verbis Domini in monte) : Dicendo autem se indignum, praestitit dignum, non in cujus parietes, sed in cujus cor Verbum Dei Christus intraret. Neque hoc diceret cum tanta fide, et humilitate, nisi illum, quem timebat intrare in do- mum suam, corde gestaret. Ubi ait Ambrosius, quod ad mysterium specta, vidit in pectora adhuc gentilium, non esse penetrabile n Christum. Prudentia autem centurionis (ait Hieronymus) apparet in hoc, quod ultra corporis tegumentum, latentem vidit Divinita- tem : et ideo tam reverenter erga Illum se exhi- buit. Adde prudentiae opus fuisse quoi prius misit ad illum seniores Judaeorum;
passages.english: (Sermon 6 on the Lord's words on the mount): 'By calling himself unworthy he showed himself worthy, worthy that Christ the Word of God should enter not his walls but his heart. Nor would he have said this with such faith and humility unless he bore in his heart the one whom he feared to have enter his house.' Here Ambrose says, as regards the mystery, that he saw that the hearts of the gentiles were not yet open to Christ. 'The prudence of the centurion,' says Jerome, 'appears in this, that beyond the covering of the body he saw the hidden Divinity, and therefore showed himself so reverent toward him.' Add that it was a work of prudence that he first sent elders of the Jews to him;
passages.notes: Opening citation is incomplete (begins mid-reference to Augustine, Sermon 6). 'penetrabile n Christum' read as 'penetrabile Christo'; 'quoi' as 'quod'.

passages.original: deinde amicos, cum jam non longe esset a domo, ut Lucas refert : De- mum vero et ipse accessit rogans, ne intraret in de- mum suam; quod Matthaeus scripsit. Haec mihi ex Chrysostomo accepta facilior videtur conciliatio Evangelistarum : Quod enim Matthaeus non ait per amicos (Chrysostomus loquitur), sed per se ipsum, hoc eumdem dixisse, nihil contrarium est : conveniens autem est opinari, et ipsum postquam misit amicos ad- venientem, per se haec dicere. Si autem hoc non dixit Lucas, neque illud Matthaeus, non sibi contradicunt, sed complent quae ab invicem derelinquebantur.
passages.english: then [he sent] friends, when he was now not far from the house, as Luke reports; but at last he himself also came, asking him not to enter his house, which is what Matthew wrote. This reconciliation of the Evangelists, taken from Chrysostom, seems to me the easier: "For that Matthew says not 'through friends' (Chrysostom is speaking) but 'through himself', that is, that the same man said this, there is nothing contradictory: and it is fitting to suppose that he himself too, after sending the friends, came and said these things in person. And if Luke did not say this, nor Matthew that, they do not contradict each other, but complete what was left out by one another."
passages.notes: "demum suam" read as "domum suam" (scanning error).

passages.original: Hoc demum gloriae nostro Capharnaunensi ascribi opor- tet, quod toti Ecclesiae formam dederit recipiendi Christum in suorum corporum domibus. Antiquissi- ma siquidem consuetudine receptum est, ut qui sa- cram Eucharistiam recipiunt, verba centurionis promant, Domine, non sum dignus, etc., quod tanta gaudet antiquitate, ut id Origenes summopere com- mendaverit, dicens : Quando corpus, et sanguinem Domini manducas, et bibis, tunc Dominus sub tectum tuum ingreditur; et tu ergo humilians teipsum di- cas : Domine, non sum dignus, etc.
passages.english: Finally, this must be ascribed to the glory of our man of Capernaum, that he gave the whole Church the pattern for receiving Christ into the houses of their bodies. For by most ancient custom it is established that those who receive the holy Eucharist utter the centurion's words, 'Lord, I am not worthy,' etc.; and this enjoys such antiquity that Origen commended it highly, saying: 'When you eat and drink the body and blood of the Lord, then the Lord enters under your roof; and so you too, humbling yourself, should say: Lord, I am not worthy,' etc.

passages.original: et id non obscure videtur innuere D. Clemens Rom. in epist. 1 ad Jacobum fratrem Domini. Alii ad aliud extremum declinantes contendunt, anno 12 ab eadem passione perfectam; id quod inter vetu- stissimos docuit Apollonius apud Eusebium lib. V Hist. c. 17, cujus ea sunt verba : Se traditione acce- pisse, Servatorem mandatum suis dedisse Apostolis, ne ad annos 12 Hierosolymis discederent. Clemens Ale- xandrinus refert in hanc sententiam praecepti formam lib.
passages.english: And St Clement of Rome seems to hint at this not obscurely in his first letter to James the brother of the Lord. Others, leaning to the other extreme, contend that it was carried out in the twelfth year from that same Passion; this is what Apollonius taught among the most ancient [writers], as reported by Eusebius, book V of the History, chapter 17, whose words are these: that he had received by tradition that the Saviour gave His Apostles a command not to depart from Jerusalem for twelve years. Clement of Alexandria reports the form of the precept to this effect, in book
passages.notes: The sentence runs on into the text after the passage ("VI Stromat."), i.e. book VI of the Stromata.

passages.original: Joan- nis discipulus in ejus historia affirmat, inter caetera quae in hac divisione facta sunt, primam fuisse Ja- cobi Minoris electionem, et consecrationem in epi- scopum Hierosolymorum. Nec mirum, cum haec illius Apostoli sors fuerit : auctore autem Eusebio in Chron. ann. 34, constat S. Jacobum consecratum esse die 37 Decembris (quem sequitur Rabanus in suo Marty- rologio apud Canisium Antiq. Lect. tomo 6) : unde relinquitur, ut ipsa Apostolorum divisio eadem die peracta sit.
passages.english: [Prochorus], disciple of St John, affirms in his history that among the other things done at this division, the first was the election of James the Less and his consecration as bishop of Jerusalem. Nor is this surprising, since this was that Apostle's lot; and on the authority of Eusebius in the Chronicle, year 34, it is established that St James was consecrated on the 37th day of December (Rabanus follows him in his Martyrology, in Canisius, Antiquae Lectiones, volume 6); from which it follows that the division of the Apostles itself was carried out on the same day.
passages.notes: "die 37 Decembris" is impossible; probably a misprint (perhaps 27 December). The name Prochorus begins in the text before the passage.

passages.original: Multa sunt quae doc- tores sancti scripserunt elogia in hujus centurionis laudem; Hieronymus Arium, alias Christianum, hujus gentilis confessione confundit : Ex hoc con- sid randum quod centurio in ipso scandalo passionis vere Dei Filium confiteatur, et Arius in Ecclesia prae- dicat creaturam; additque : novissimi autem, nunc primi efficiuntur, gentilis confitetur populus; Judaea excaecata negat, ne fiat ultimus error pejor priore. Ubi Theopbylactus : Sic ordo convertitur, dum Judaei occidunt, discipuli fugiunt, et gentilis confitetur.
passages.english: Many are the eulogies the holy doctors have written in praise of this centurion. Jerome confounds Arius, otherwise a Christian, by this Gentile's confession: "From this it must be considered that the centurion, in the very scandal of the passion, truly confesses the Son of God, while Arius in the Church preaches [him] a creature"; and he adds: "But the last are now made first; the Gentile people confesses; blinded Judaea denies, lest the last error be worse than the first." Where Theophylact [says]: "Thus the order is reversed: while the Jews kill, the disciples flee, and the Gentile confesses."

passages.original: in qua praedicationi Petri inter- fuerunt Parthi, et Medi, et Elamitae qui habitabant Mesopotamiam, Cappadociam, Pontum, et Asiam Minorem (quae omnes regiones sub Asia Majori con- tinentur), et praeter hos etiam adfuerunt advenae Ro- mani; quo nomine Italos omnes, et eos qui Romana utebantur lingua, praesertim Hispanos appellabant, ut Josephus ipse testis est, cujus verba refert Baro- nius tom. I ad ann. D. 72, videlicet : Romanorum clementia cunctis, non parvulum donum appellationis suae concessit; non solum viris singulis, sed etiam maximis gentibus in communi; Hispani denique anti- qui et Tyrrheni, et Sabini, Romani vocantur. Idemque habet Augustinus in ps. LVIII : Omnes Romani facti sunt, et omnes Romani dicuntur. Quod vero nonnulli ad Europam venisse dicantur, non leve argumentum praebet Maria illa Salome uxor Zebedaei, quae hac ipsa persecutione fugata, in Italiam concessit, et Ve- rulis apud Hernicos itinere fatigata, in pacc quievit, ut produnt vetera monumenta Ecclesiae Verulanae, ubi ejus venerandum corpus religiose asservatur.
passages.english: at which Parthians, Medes and Elamites were present at Peter's preaching, who dwelt in Mesopotamia, Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia Minor (all of which regions are contained under Greater Asia), and besides these there were also present visitors from Rome; by which name they called all Italians, and those who used the Roman language, especially Spaniards, as Josephus himself testifies, whose words Baronius quotes in volume I at the year of the Lord 72, namely: "The clemency of the Romans granted to all no small gift, that of their own name, not only to individual men but also to the greatest nations in common; indeed the ancient Spaniards, and Etruscans, and Sabines are called Romans." Augustine says the same on Psalm 58: "All have been made Romans, and all are called Romans." That some, indeed, are said to have come to Europe, no slight argument is offered by that Mary Salome, wife of Zebedee, who, driven out by this very persecution, withdrew to Italy, and, worn out by the journey at Veroli among the Hernici, rested in peace, as the ancient records of the Church of Veroli relate, where her venerable body is devoutly preserved.
passages.notes: "pacc" read as "pace".

passages.original: Huc accedit, in gratiam peregrinationis, quam ad ipsam Hispani fecisse dicuntur, ipsos rerum magna- rum videndi avidissimos semper fuisse, et ea de causa in remotissimas orbis plagas, si opus esset, peregrinandi. Qua do re multa nobis suppeditant exempla antiquorum historiae, ubi pro levioribus rebus id ipsos fecisse legimus. Et ut aliquod affera- mus : Ad Titum Livium (ait D. Hieronymus ad Pau- linum scribens) lacteo eloquentiae fonte manantem, de ultimis Hispaniae finibus, quosdam venisse nobiles, le- gimus : et quos ad contemplationem sui Roma non traxerat, unius hominis fama perduxit. Audita magni Antonii fama, multos etiam cum Hispanorum visu- ros, remotissimas solitudines penetrasse auctor est D. Athanasius iu ejus Vita : Hominem alio pene crbe celatum, et inter tantas positum solitudines Africae et Hispaniae demonstravit.
passages.english: Add to this, in support of the pilgrimage that the Spaniards are said to have made to it, that they have always been most eager to see great things, and for that reason to travel, if need be, to the remotest regions of the world. On this matter the histories of the ancients supply us with many examples, where we read that they did this for lesser things. And to adduce one: "We read" (says St Jerome, writing to Paulinus) "that certain noblemen came from the furthest bounds of Spain to Titus Livy, flowing with a milky fountain of eloquence; and those whom Rome had not drawn to contemplate her, the fame of one man brought." St Athanasius, in his Life, is the authority that, having heard the fame of the great Antony, many, among them Spaniards, penetrated the remotest wildernesses to see him: "It revealed a man hidden almost in another world, and set amid such great wildernesses, to Africa and Spain."
passages.notes: "crbe" read as "orbe"; "cum Hispanorum" is awkward, probably for "cum Hispanis" or similar, rendered as 'among them Spaniards'.

passages.original: vel quia (ut Chrysosto- mus putavit) audierat, In viam Gentium ne abieritis : propterea cum condiscipulo communicans, Magistro refert : Andreas rursus et Philippus dixerunt Jesu; Jesus autem respondit dicens : Venit hora ut clarifi- cetur Filius hominis. Ubi Augustinus ait : Videbat Gentiles post passionem et resurrectionem suam in omnibus Gentibus credituros. Ex occasione igitur isto- rum Gentilium, qui eum videre cupiebant, annuntiat futuram plenitudinem Gentium, et promittit jam edesse horam glorificationis suae. Chrysostomus vero : Quia igitur de reliquo debebat mittere Discipulos ad Gentes. Videt autem Gentiles praesilientes ad fidem, ostendit quod tempus erat, ut ad crucem veniret.
passages.english: or because (as Chrysostom thought) he had heard, "Do not go into the way of the Gentiles"; therefore, sharing it with his fellow disciple, he reports it to the Master: "Andrew and Philip in turn told Jesus; and Jesus answered, saying: The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified." Where Augustine says: "He saw that the Gentiles would believe in all nations after His passion and resurrection. On the occasion, then, of these Gentiles who desired to see Him, He announces the future fullness of the Gentiles, and promises that the hour of His glorification is now at hand." And Chrysostom: "Since, then, He was henceforth to send the Disciples to the Gentiles, and He saw the Gentiles leaping forward to faith, He shows that it was time for Him to come to the cross."
passages.notes: "edesse" read as "adesse".

passages.original: Danieli : Confirmabit, inquit, testamentum multis hebdomada una; tempore scilicet ante crucem et eo quo sancti apostoli post Salvatoris resurrectionem, Hierosolymis docuerunt, simul collecto. Hactenus Theodoretus : quibus conformia scribunt Eusebius, lib. VIII de Praeparatione Evangelica, et Hieronymus in Com- mentariis ad hunc locum Danielis. Liquido igitur constat, non amplius quam duos annos cum dimi- dio apostolos cum Judaeis Testamenti novi stabi- liendi gratia moratos fuisse.
passages.english: to Daniel: "He will confirm the covenant with many for one week," he says; that is, the time before the cross and that in which the holy apostles taught at Jerusalem after the Saviour's resurrection, taken together. Thus far Theodoret; and in agreement with this write Eusebius, book VIII of the Preparation for the Gospel, and Jerome in his Commentaries on this passage of Daniel. It is therefore clearly established that the apostles stayed with the Jews for no more than two and a half years for the sake of establishing the New Testament.
passages.notes: The opening is truncated; the preceding sentence (about the archangel [Gabriel] speaking to Daniel) is in the text before the passage.

passages.original: Cui sane multam fidem adhibendam esse convincit Vita ipsius S. Petri ante 1350 annos scripta B. Caledonio episcopo pari- ter Bracarensi, qui obiit anno Domini 260, übi re- fert quidquid hic S. Athanasius dixit : uti ea de re perhibet Irrefragabile testimonium Hugo Portugal- lensis episcopus, in epistola a nobis superius inter elogia auctoris allata, quam tu consulas. Et certe S. Anastasius Synaita ob ejusmodi forsan S. Petri suscitationem, in lib.
passages.english: That much credence should indeed be given to him is proved by the Life of St Peter himself, written more than 1350 years ago by Blessed Caledonius, likewise bishop of Braga, who died in the year of the Lord 260, where he relates whatever St Athanasius said here; as Hugo, bishop of Porto, bears irrefutable witness on this matter in the letter quoted by us above among the testimonies to the author, which you may consult. And certainly St Anastasius of Sinai, perhaps on account of this raising of St Peter [from the dead], in the book
passages.notes: "ante 1350 annos" taken as 'about 1350 years ago'. These attributions (Caledonius, the Athanasius fragment) belong to the forged Spanish chronicles and are not historical.

passages.original: Ejus itineris facti ia Nabuchodonosor in Hispaniam auctores sunt Megasthenes lib. IV Rerum Indicarum; Josephus lib. X. Antiq. Jud. cap. 11 et lib. contra Apionem; et Strabo lib. XV Geographiae, secuti Megasthenem, qui contendit (apud Josephum) subjugasse eum bonam partem Hispaniae, et ( apud Strabonem) usque ad columnas Herculis pervenisse; quousque etiam Tearconem (lego Tarraconem): illum tamen exercitum ex Hispania in Thraciam Pontumque deduxisse. In co exercitu multos Judaeorum deduxisse Nabuchodonosorem nemo negat.
passages.english: For that expedition made by Nebuchadnezzar into Spain the authorities are Megasthenes, book IV of the Indica; Josephus, book X of the Jewish Antiquities, chapter 11, and the book Against Apion; and Strabo, book XV of the Geography, following Megasthenes, who maintains (in Josephus) that he subdued a good part of Spain, and (in Strabo) that he reached the Pillars of Hercules, as far as which Tearco (I read Tarraco) [also reached]; yet that he led that army from Spain into Thrace and Pontus. No one denies that Nebuchadnezzar brought many Jews in that army.
passages.notes: The Tearco/Tarraco clause is elliptical. "ia" read as "a".

passages.original: et hi decem Mar- tyrium passi sunt sub Neronis principatu, anno Christi 60, apud Penniscolam regni Valentini urbem, ut eo anno dicemus cum Dextro. Quod autem hi omnes discipuli S. Jacobi fuerint, deducitur aperto ex testimonio Pelagii Ovetensis, qui inter Apostoli discipulos refert Basilium et Pium : Caledonius Bra- carensis refert Pium et Elpidium, cum aliis. Item Ecclesia Asturicensis, traditione per majorum ma- nus accepta, habet S. Ephraem B. Jacobi discipulum fuisse suum primum Antistitem.
passages.english: and these ten suffered martyrdom under the reign of Nero, in the year of Christ 60, at Peñíscola, a city of the kingdom of Valencia, as we shall say under that year with Dexter. That all these were disciples of St James is plainly deduced from the testimony of Pelagius of Oviedo, who lists Basilius and Pius among the Apostle's disciples; Caledonius of Braga lists Pius and Elpidius, with others. Likewise the Church of Astorga, by a tradition received through the hands of its forebears, holds that St Ephraem, disciple of Blessed James, was its first bishop.

passages.original: Vocarunt Romani Carpeta- niam eam Hispaniae partem quam nunc Toletanum regnum nuncupamus; et juga Carpentana quae modo dicimus Puerto de Somo Sierra, de Guadarrama, Fonfrida, et Palomera, quibus una ab altera Castella secernitur. Sic vocatam ab antiquis videre est apud Plinium, et Strabonem, Moralem, Marianam, et cae- teros; nonnulli Carpentaniam nuncupant, quod apud veteres minus receptum est.
passages.english: The Romans called Carpetania that part of Spain which we now call the kingdom of Toledo, and [called] the Carpetanian ranges those we now call the Puerto de Somosierra, de Guadarrama, Fonfría and Palomera, by which the one Castile is separated from the other. That it was so called by the ancients can be seen in Pliny and Strabo, Morales, Mariana and the others; some call it Carpentania, which was less accepted among the ancients.
passages.notes: The text has "juga Carpentana" here, though it then says the form "Carpentania" is less accepted.

passages.original: 41 Viennae Galliarum, ubi relegatus exsulem agebat, propria se manu interfecerit, cum prius justo Dei judicio in multas incidisset calamitates; agit Eusebius in Chro- nico, citans Romanos historicos; et idem referunt Orosius lib. VII cap. 5, Cassiodorus in Chronico, et Ado etiam in Chronico (et ipse Viennensis episcopus), cujus sunt haec verba : Pilatus qui sententiam dam- nationis in Christum dixerat, perpetuo exsilio Viennae recluditur, tantisque ibi, irrogante Caio (imperatore), angoribus coarctatus est, ut sua se transverberans manu multorum malorum compendium mortis celeri- tate quaesiverit.
passages.english: 41, at Vienne in Gaul, where he was living in banishment as an exile, he killed himself with his own hand, having first, by the just judgement of God, fallen into many calamities. Eusebius treats this in the Chronicle, citing Roman historians; and the same is reported by Orosius, book VII chapter 5, Cassiodorus in the Chronicle, and Ado too in the Chronicle (himself bishop of Vienne), whose words are these: "Pilate, who had pronounced the sentence of condemnation on Christ, is shut up in perpetual exile at Vienne, and there, at the instigation of Gaius (the emperor), he was so hemmed in by anguish that, piercing himself with his own hand, he sought by the swiftness of death a short way out of many evils."
passages.notes: The sentence begins in the text before the passage ("how, in the year of the Lord 41").

passages.original: exponerent Blasto petitionem suam; et rex tandem condiceret diem allocutionis publicae; et illo transacto tempore, percussus ab angelo, et consumptus a vermibus cruciatu per continuos quinque dies nihil se remitente confectus (ut ait Josephus lib. XIX Antiq. cap. 7) expirasset? Aliunde ergo supputatio petenda est, quam inquirimus.
passages.english: set out their petition to Blastus; and the king at length appointed a day for a public address; and, once that time had passed, struck by an angel and consumed by worms, worn out by an agony that gave him no respite for five continuous days (as Josephus says, Antiquities book XIX, chapter 7), he expired? The reckoning we are seeking must therefore be sought elsewhere.
passages.notes: The passage completes a rhetorical question begun in the preceding context ("Who does not see that more time must be allowed ..."). "remitente" read as "remittente".

passages.original: Nec anno 36, ut Eusebius docuit, quia ejus epacta fuit XII, correspondens dici 19 Martii, et luna 14 in- cidit in 1 diem Aprilis.
passages.english: Nor in the year 36, as Eusebius taught, because its epact was XII, corresponding to 19 March, and the fourteenth day of the moon fell on 1 April.
passages.notes: "dici" read as "diei".

passages.original: Apostolorum inde aucto- ritas ad posteros valuit : caeter aeque, deinde aetates certatim caelestis Reginae incunabula, Deique con- cepit vestigia celebrarunt, qua dignum erat Religione, cultu. Refert pro eadem sententia Annales Flu- menses apud Hieronymum Angelitam exstantes. Caetera quae ad Deificam domunculam spectant, lege in eodem Tursellino.
passages.english: From then on the authority of the Apostles prevailed with posterity: other ages likewise thereafter vied with one another in celebrating the cradle of the heavenly Queen and the traces of God conceived [there], with the devotion and worship that were fitting. For the same opinion he cites the Annals of Fiume, extant in Hieronymus Angelita. For the rest that concerns the divine little house, read the same Torsellino.
passages.notes: Text corrupt: "caeter aeque" read as "caeterae quoque"; "Deique concepit vestigia" is ungrammatical, perhaps "Deique concepti vestigia"; "qua dignum erat Religione, cultu" taken as "with the religion and worship that were fitting". The subject of "Refert" is presumably Torsellino (the Holy House of Loreto).

passages.original: Primum quia tot tantaque negotia intercesserunt usque ad concilium, quod ipsum usque ad annum 48 minime celebrari potuerit : namque in Actib. apost. cap. XII, post liberationem Petri a vin- culis, et Herodem consumptum a vermibus, ponitur fames celebris ab Agabo prophetata, quae facta est sub Claudio (Act. II). Contigit vero teste Eusebio et aliis anno 4 Claudii, qui fuit Christi 46; nam Clau- dius successit Augusto ad finem anni 42, quo tem- pore Paulus et Barnabas missi sunt ab Ecclesia An- tiochiae Hierosolymam, collectam et subsidium allaturi habitantibus in Judaea fratribus : quo mu- nere expleto (ait Lucas cap. XII), reversi sunt ab Hie- rosolymis Antiochiam. Haec igitur anno 46 acta sunt. Narrat deinde evangelista, cap. XIII, quod dum morarentur Antiochae, segregati sunt in opus aposto- latus gentium, jubente Spiritu sancto; et quod sta- tim abierunt Seleuciam, et inde navigaverunt Cy- prum, ubi praedicaverunt Salaminae : et cum peram- bulassent universam insulam usque Paphum, Paulus excaecavit Elymam magum, et convertit ad fidem Sergium Paulum proconsulem. Inde navigarunt Per- gem Pamphiliae, et venerunt Antiochiam Pisidiae : ubi multis gentilium conversis, ad Judaeos dixerunt : Vobis oportebat primum loqui verbum Dei;
passages.english: First, because so many and such great affairs intervened before the council that it could not possibly have been held before the year 48: for in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter XII, after Peter's release from his chains and Herod's consumption by worms, there is placed the famous famine prophesied by Agabus, which took place under Claudius (Acts 11). And according to Eusebius and others it happened in the fourth year of Claudius, which was the year 46 of Christ; for Claudius succeeded Augustus at the end of the year 42, at which time Paul and Barnabas were sent by the Church of Antioch to Jerusalem to bring a collection and relief to the brethren living in Judaea: and when this service was completed (says Luke, chapter XII), they returned from Jerusalem to Antioch. These things therefore were done in the year 46. The evangelist then relates, in chapter XIII, that while they were staying at Antioch they were set apart for the work of the apostolate to the Gentiles, at the command of the Holy Spirit; and that they immediately went off to Seleucia and from there sailed to Cyprus, where they preached at Salamis; and when they had travelled through the whole island as far as Paphos, Paul struck the magician Elymas blind and converted the proconsul Sergius Paulus to the faith. From there they sailed to Perga in Pamphylia and came to Antioch in Pisidia, where, after many of the Gentiles had been converted, they said to the Jews: "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you;
passages.notes: "Act. II" should be Acts 11. "Claudius succeeded Augustus" is as the text reads; Claudius actually succeeded Caligula ("Augustus" may mean "the emperor"), and the date 42 is the author's.

passages.original: Vultus Domini quem sanguine proprio sudario Veronicae impressit ser- vatur Romae apud S. Petrum, ubi saepius ipsum ve neratus sum : alter vero ( nam linteum duplicatum erat) servatur in Hispania in urbe Gienensi, vulgo Jaen, cum summa reverentia. Equilinus. lib. VI, cap. 151, refert ex Ambrosio, mulierem (??)aemor- rhoissam de qua Marcus V et Lucas VIII, fuisse Mar- tham. Versimile autem id nou videtur; non enim taceret Evangelista nomen ejus, si esset Martha. Celebrius est illud Eusebii, mulierem haemorrhoissam civem fuisse Caesareae Philippi, et in gratitudinem ac memoriam accepti a Christo beneficii, statuam ejus in viridario suo posuisse ad cujus pedes ipsamet fimbriam ejus tangere videbatur : factumque esset ut herbae quae sub statua subortae fimbriam Domini contingebant, ea potirentur virtute, ut haemorrhois- sae ad ipsarum contactum mederentur : caeterum hanc imaginem, Julianum apostatam sustulisse ejusque loco substituisse suam : quam tamen ictu fulminis fuisse idem Equilinus testatur.
passages.english: The face of the Lord, which he impressed with his own blood on Veronica's cloth, is kept at Rome at St Peter's, where I have often venerated it; the other (for the linen was folded double) is kept with the greatest reverence in Spain, in the city of Gienna, commonly Jaén. Equilinus, book VI, chapter 151, reports from Ambrose that the woman with the issue of blood, of whom Mark 5 and Luke 8 speak, was Martha. But this does not seem likely; for the Evangelist would not keep silent about her name if she were Martha. Better known is the account of Eusebius, that the woman with the issue of blood was a citizen of Caesarea Philippi, and in gratitude for and memory of the benefit received from Christ set up a statue of him in her garden, at whose feet she herself appeared to touch the hem of his garment; and it came about that the plants that sprang up beneath the statue and touched the Lord's hem acquired such power that women with an issue of blood were healed by touching them; moreover, that Julian the Apostate removed this image and put his own in its place; which, however, the same Equilinus testifies was [destroyed] by a stroke of lightning.
passages.notes: The last clause lacks a verb ("fuisse" with no participle); probably a word such as "dejectam" or "consumptam" has dropped out. "Equilinus" is Petrus de Natalibus, bishop of Equilium.

passages.original: Quod ad genus mor- tis quo obiit, attinet, Galesinus credidit esse con- fessorem ad 15 Maii in suo Martyrologio : nec mi- rum cura sola M. Maximi auctoritate (cujus scripta nondum cum Galesinus scripsit comparuerant) mar- tyrium ejus constet : is vero in quodam hymno do tribus primis episcopis Caesaraugustanis, haec canit inter alia : Nimirum Athanasium et Epitectum : ait vero vidisse utrumque fortiter passum Iberum flumen, quia prope Caesaraugustam ad ejus ripam martyrio sublati sunt. Caeterum tametsi illic obierit, corpus tamen Com- postellam translatum est a discipulis, sicut ipse primo testamento caverat, sepulcrum sibi eligens ex latere S.
passages.english: As for the kind of death by which he died, Galesini believed him to be a confessor, under 15 May in his Martyrology: and no wonder, since his martyrdom is established solely on the authority of M. Maximus (whose writings had not yet come to light when Galesini wrote). Maximus, in a certain hymn on the first three bishops of Zaragoza, sings among other things: "Namely Athanasius and Epitectus"; and he says that the river Ebro saw both of them suffer bravely, because they were put to death by martyrdom near Zaragoza on its bank. However, although he died there, his body was nonetheless carried to Compostela by his disciples, as he himself had first provided in his testament, choosing for himself a tomb beside St
passages.notes: "cura" read as "cum"; "do" as "de". The verse quotation appears truncated. Ends mid-phrase ("beside St [James] the Apostle").

passages.original: Sane ut haec aliquatenus in concordiam deduci queant, necessario cum Dextro dicendum est, non unam solum Carteiam in oris Baeticis olim fuisse, sed duas, alteram quam Titus Livius collocat ad oram Oceani a parte exteriori freti, ubi primum e faucibus angustis panditur Oceanus; et in hoc dissentimus a Ptolomaeo : atteram quam modo Cartayam nuncu- pamus, non longe a Nova Carthagine. Priorem voca- verunt antiqui Tartessum, uti referunt Plinius lib. III cap. 1 (qui etiam locat eam in mari Atlantico, videlicet Oceano, Ex Atlantico mari Carteia, ait, Tartessus a Graecis dicta) et D. Hieronymus lib. II Commentariorum in Epist. ad Galatas, in prooemio.
passages.english: Indeed, so that these things may to some extent be brought into agreement, one must necessarily say with Dexter that there was formerly not just one Carteia on the coasts of Baetica but two: one, which Titus Livius places on the shore of the Ocean on the outer side of the strait, where the Ocean first opens out from the narrow straits (and in this we disagree with Ptolemy); the other, which we now call Cartaya, not far from New Carthage. The ancients called the former Tartessus, as Pliny reports, book III, chapter 1 (who also places it on the Atlantic sea, that is, the Ocean: "From the Atlantic sea, Carteia, called Tartessus by the Greeks," he says), and St Jerome, book II of the Commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians, in the preface.
passages.notes: "atteram" read as "alteram".

passages.original: Sedes specialis ipsius fuit Ili- turgi urbs praeclara, cujus ruinae adhuc videntur super Andujar ad unam leucam in confluenti Baetis, seu Guadalquivir, vocaturque nunc Andujar el viejo : nam ejus loco successit Andujar el nuevo. Ita Am- brosius de Morales in suis Antiquit. verbo Iliturgi fol. 57, idque probat egregie ex Plinio : idem habet lib. VI, C. 1. Quare fallitur Carolus Clusius citatus ab Hortelio, dum vult, quod Iliturgi sil Aldea del Rio. Et quod Ptolemaeus illam vocaverit Ilurgi in Turdulis, quandoquidem Iliturgi non fuit nisi in Contestanis, ubi et Carthagena est, ut etiam ex Plutarcho dedu- cimus in vita Scipionis. Erravit etiam Villanova, volens, ut sit Lora, et quod eam vocarit Plinius Fo- rum Julium. Terminus praedicationis S. Euphrasii notatur ab Iliturgi usque ad Assotum quam Ptolo- maeus et Plinius vocant Asso.
passages.english: His particular see was the famous city of Iliturgi, whose ruins are still seen above Andújar at a distance of one league, at the confluence of the Baetis, or Guadalquivir, and it is now called Andújar el Viejo; for Andújar el Nuevo took its place. So Ambrosio de Morales in his Antiquities, under the word Iliturgi, fol. 57, and he proves it excellently from Pliny; he says the same in book VI, chapter 1. Therefore Carolus Clusius, cited by Ortelius, is mistaken in holding that Iliturgi is Aldea del Río, and that Ptolemy called it Ilurgi among the Turduli, since Iliturgi was only among the Contestani, where Cartagena also is, as we also infer from Plutarch in the Life of Scipio. Villanova also erred in holding that it is Lora, and that Pliny called it Forum Julium. The limit of St Euphrasius's preaching is marked as from Iliturgi to Assotum, which Ptolemy and Pliny call Asso.
passages.notes: "sil" read as "sit". The construction "Et quod Ptolemaeus..." is loose; taken as a further claim of Clusius being rejected.

passages.original: agens enim de victoriis Jacobi regis sic ait : Plura alia eo tractu oppida et arces vitam to- lerabant, quae necessario regi ditiontm fecerunt, im- primis Penniscola Ptolomaeo Cherronesus. Diceret po- tius Straboni, nam Ptolomaeus ejus non meminit. Idem auctor lib. XX, cap. ultimo, Peninsulam dicit. De eodem Jacobo agebat Hieronymus Zurita lib. I Indicarum rerum ab Aragoniae regibus gestarum, cum dixit : Anno 1225 kalen. Octobr. rex hostilem re- gionem incurrens, Peniscolam Itergaonum oppidum obsidet : is situs est, ut scopulo impositum pene mari cinctum sit : e re vulgatum nomen invenit.
passages.english: For, treating of the victories of King James, he says this: "Many other towns and fortresses in that region held out, which of necessity came under the king's dominion, above all Peñíscola, Ptolemy's Cherronesus." He should rather have said Strabo's, for Ptolemy does not mention it. The same author, book XX, last chapter, calls it Peninsula. Jerónimo Zurita was dealing with the same James in book I of the Indices of the deeds of the kings of Aragon, when he said: "In the year 1225, on the Kalends of October, the king, invading enemy territory, besieges Peñíscola, a town of the Ilercavones: it is so situated, set on a rock, that it is almost surrounded by the sea; from this fact it got its popular name."
passages.notes: "vitam tolerabant" (lit. 'sustained life') rendered 'held out'; "ditiontm" read as "ditionem". "Itergaonum" read as Ilercavones.

passages.original: In Martyrologio Romano deficil nomen S. Pii episcopi et martyris Hispalensis, cujus nihilominus cum caeteris sociis meminit Pelagius Ovetensis, et Hugo Portugallensis, quorum mentionem fecimus in superioribus, et ante eos S. Caledonius Braca- rensis in Vita S. Petri Ratensis.
passages.english: In the Roman Martyrology the name of St Pius, bishop and martyr of Seville, is missing; yet Pelagius of Oviedo and Hugo of Porto, whom we have mentioned above, record him with his other companions, and before them St Caledonius of Braga in the Life of St Peter of Rates.
passages.notes: "deficil" read as "deficit".

passages.original: Josephus in Vita sua agit de Alituro, qui fuit Neroni charus, sed hic erat Judaeus genere, et Mimorum auctor, non quaestor aut judex, nec ostendi potest Hispanias adiisse. Attamen procul dubio fuit A lotus (sive Halotus) alter ex spadonibus Claudii Caesaris, qui ei, monente Agrippina, venenum, ut Nero im- peritaret, propinavit; cujus meminit Tacitus lib. XIII Annalium. Ejus rei meritis missus est Aloltus in Hispanias, et quaestorinstitutus initio imperii Neronis.
passages.english: Josephus in his Life deals with Aliturus, who was dear to Nero, but he was a Jew by birth and an author of mimes, not a quaestor or judge, nor can it be shown that he went to Spain. However, beyond doubt it was Alotus (or Halotus), one of the eunuchs of Claudius Caesar, who at Agrippina's prompting gave him poison so that Nero might rule; Tacitus mentions him in book XIII of the Annals. As a reward for this he was sent to Spain and appointed quaestor at the beginning of Nero's reign.
passages.notes: Josephus actually calls Aliturus an actor of mimes; "Mimorum auctor" may mean 'performer'.

passages.original: Creditur a poetis Laureolus sceleratissi- mus latro, eoque nomine in crucem actus, et ab urso dilaceratus. Quae fabula aliquoties Romae in spectaculis repraesentata est, semel quidem a Len- tulo, de quo Dexter inferius anno 86, cujus etiam meminit Juvenalis inquiens : Quod ergo in Scena figurate dumtaxat repraesenta- batur, Domitianus in martyribus expressit ad vi- vum : idemque ante ipsum Nero, ut jam videbi- mus. Hos igitur deridet Martialis, ut ethnicis arri- deat, epigrammate 9 ante lib.
passages.english: Laureolus is believed by the poets [to have been] a most wicked bandit, and on that account to have been put on a cross and torn apart by a bear. This story was several times represented in the shows at Rome, once indeed by Lentulus, of whom Dexter [speaks] below at the year 86, and whom Juvenal also mentions, saying: What, then, was represented on the stage only figuratively, Domitian enacted to the life in the martyrs; and the same [was done] before him by Nero, as we shall soon see. Martial, therefore, mocks these [martyrs], in order to please the pagans, in epigram 9 before book
passages.notes: The quotations from Juvenal and Martial are omitted in the text as held (colons followed by nothing). The passage ends mid-reference; context continues 'I', i.e. book I (the Liber spectaculorum epigram on Laureolus).

passages.original: Subinfert Martialis : Nunc supponit martyri crimina : Caeterum nihil horum commisisse constat, cui nullum certum crimen objicitur, sed hoc vel illud : videlicet vel parricidium, vel domini sui necis, vel templi spolium, vel denique Romanae urbis incen- dium.
passages.english: Martial adds: Now he imputes crimes to the martyr: but it is evident that he committed none of them, since no definite crime is laid against him, but this or that: namely either parricide, or the murder of his master, or the plundering of a temple, or finally the burning of the city of Rome.
passages.notes: The quoted lines of Martial are missing after 'adds:'.

passages.original: A. C. 61. Nero, etc. Utriusque mortem violen- tam hoc quoquo anno designat Eusebius in Chroni- co, dicens; Nero Agrippinam matrem suam et sororem patris interficit. De quibus Suetonium, Dionemve le- gito.
passages.english: A.D. 61. Nero, etc. Eusebius in his Chronicle also places the violent death of both in this year, saying: Nero kills his mother Agrippina and his father's sister. On these, read Suetonius or Dio.
passages.notes: 'quoquo' read as 'quoque'.

passages.original: 2. Epaenetus, etc. Egimus iterum de eodem, cum Auctore ad annum Domini 30, numero 5, ubi docui- mus ex Metaphraste, episcopum fuisse Sexifirmi, cujus Plinius meminit in Baetica lib. III, cap. 1, fuit- que urbs insignis olim in monte Fregiliana, altero ex Granatensibus Alpuxarris aut quod aliis forsan magis arrideat, Motril, aut Velezmalaga. Nunc illud addendum putamus, Dorotheum abbatem, quem re- fert et sequitur Petrus Equilinus lib.
passages.english: 2. Epaenetus, etc. We have treated the same man again with the Author at the year of the Lord 30, number 5, where we showed from Metaphrastes that he was bishop of Sexifirmum, which Pliny mentions in Baetica, book III, chapter 1; and it was once a notable city on the mountain Fregiliana, one of the Alpujarras of Granada, or, as may perhaps please others more, Motril or Vélez-Málaga. Now we think this should be added: that the abbot Dorotheus, whom Petrus Equilinus cites and follows in book
passages.notes: Sentence breaks off; continues in following context ('VI, cap. 100...'). Petrus Equilinus = Petrus de Natalibus, bishop of Equilium.

passages.original: (ejus opus esse, et non Hervaei alibi in meo Anselmo Vindicato in causa Conceptionis Virginis ostendi). Sic enim ait : Nec falsum loquitur, qui se in Hispaniam profec- turum pollicetur; profectus est enim, sicut Hieronymus, et Beda, caeterique Doctores testantur. Unde et Narbo- nam praeteriens quemdam discipulum suum nomine Paulum, fertur ibi reliquisse episcopum. Pervenit igi- tur usque ad Hispanias, et a mari Rubro usque ad Oceanum praedicando cucurrit, imitans solis cursum ab oriente usque ad occasum, ut ante ei terra defice- ret, quam studium praedicandi;
passages.english: (that it is his work, and not Hervaeus's, I have shown elsewhere in my Anselm Vindicated, in the matter of the Conception of the Virgin). For he says thus: Nor does he speak falsely who promises that he will set out for Spain; for he did set out, as Jerome and Bede and the other Doctors testify. Hence also, passing by Narbonne, he is said to have left there a certain disciple of his named Paul as bishop. He came, then, as far as the Spains, and ran preaching from the Red Sea to the Ocean, imitating the course of the sun from east to west, so that the earth would fail him before his zeal for preaching [did];

passages.original: Constabit ex ibi dicendis, S. Timotheum Paulum euntem ad Hispanias comitatum esse. Quod vero addit Dexter de Philemone, inde elici potest, quod cum scribit Apostolus ad ipsum, et ei Onesimum in vinculis fidei a se genitum, olim vero Philemonis servum commendat, asserit, voluisse illum secum detinere, quia erat illi proficuus, noluit tamen quid- quam agere eo inconsulto.
passages.english: It will be established from what is to be said there that St Timothy accompanied Paul as he went to Spain. What Dexter adds about Philemon can be drawn from this: when the Apostle writes to him and commends to him Onesimus, whom he had begotten in the bonds of faith, formerly Philemon's slave, he asserts that he had wished to keep him with himself, because he was useful to him, yet he was unwilling to do anything without consulting him.

passages.original: Magis hac in re Dextro assentimur, qui ejus- dem fuit cum ipsis provinciae, videlicet Tarraconen- sis, et idcirco multo magis erat illi patria Sanctarum istarum comperta. Setabis fuit nobilis urbs, non longe a Valentia, quam nunc Satiba seu Xatiba di- cimus, et Romanis dicta est Augusta Valeria apud Plinium, ut notarunt Taraffa lib. de Regibus Hisp., Michael Villanonanus in Notis ad Ptolomaeum, et Nonnius in sua Hispania cap. 68, qui omnes conve- niunt esse Xativam, cisque astipulatur Ambrosius Morales lib.
passages.english: In this matter we agree rather with Dexter, who was of the same province as they, namely Tarraconensis, and therefore the homeland of these saints was much better known to him. Setabis was a noble city not far from Valencia, which we now call Satiba or Xátiva, and it was called Augusta Valeria by the Romans in Pliny, as Tarafa noted in his book On the Kings of Spain, Michael Villanovanus in his Notes on Ptolemy, and Nonius in his Hispania, chapter 68, who all agree that it is Xátiva; and Ambrosio de Morales supports them in book
passages.notes: 'cisque' read as 'eisque'; 'Villanonanus' as 'Villanovanus' (Michael Servetus). Reference continues in context (X, ch. 32).

passages.original: Fuit alia Hispaniae Baetulo, non longe a Barcinone, de qua Morales lib. IX, cap. 33, ait hodie nuncupari Badalonam, sed ea non erat ad propositum Livio. De nobilitate Castulonis alibi (id est, lib. XXIV) agens idem Livius ait : Castulo urbs Hispaniae valida ac nobilis, et adeo conjuncta societate Poenis, ut uxor inde Annibali esset, ad Romanos defe- cit, etc.
passages.english: There was another Baetulo in Spain, not far from Barcelona, which Morales, book IX, chapter 33, says is today called Badalona; but that was not relevant to Livy's purpose. Treating elsewhere (that is, in book XXIV) of the nobility of Castulo, the same Livy says: Castulo, a strong and noble city of Spain, and so closely joined in alliance with the Carthaginians that Hannibal's wife came from there, defected to the Romans, etc.

passages.original: 8. Persius, etc. Haec ex Eusebii Chronico de- sumpta sunt ad verbum, nisi quod ille narrat Persii mortem anno Domini 65. Dexter vero anno 66.
passages.english: 8. Persius, etc. These things are taken word for word from Eusebius's Chronicle, except that he records the death of Persius in the year of the Lord 65, but Dexter in the year 66.

passages.original: 10. Nero, etc. Eusebius anno 65 sic ait : Nero Romae in citharistarum agone contendens, omnes su- perat. Et anno 67 iterum agit de simili Neronis cer- tamine, quo, cunctis musicis et poetis devictis, in Olympicis coronatus est; et rursus de eodem anno 68.
passages.english: 10. Nero, etc. Eusebius at the year 65 says thus: Nero, competing at Rome in the contest of lyre-players, defeats everyone. And at the year 67 he again treats of a similar contest of Nero's, in which, having beaten all the musicians and poets, he was crowned at the Olympic games; and again of the same at the year 68.

passages.original: Annaeum Lucanum facun- dissimum oratorem, sive, ut quidam malunt, histori- cum : quod lepidis carminum numeris veritatem historicam, non fabulas poetarum cecinerit. Sunt qui dicant natum Luque, oppido 9 leucas a Corduba distanti. Sed, ut Ambrosius Morales advertit lib. IX hist. cap. 10, non est quo probari queat. Natus fuit die 2 Novembris anno Domini 39. Romae degens uxorem accepit Pollam Argentariam, non minus poesi, quam opibus ac genere illustrem. Comprehen- sus in Pisoniana conjuratione, qua, Nerone e medio sublato, imperium Calpurnio Pisoni (vel ut aliis placet quos Corn. Tacitus refert lib. XVI, agente tri- buno militum Suberio Flavio, ipsi Senecae) paraba- tur, damnatus ad mortem, et genus eligere valens, incisa vena, ac sanguine effuso obiit, annos natus 27 et anno Domini 66, ut Eusebio et Morali placet, cum Dextro; die vero Aprilis ultimo Petrus Crinitus auctor est, Neronem amici memorem, et facti poe- nitentem, Lucano erexisse statuam cum hac inscrip- tione : Polla uxor mariti amantissimi natalem diem ce- lebrem fecit, in cujus gratiam Statius Papinius lib. II Sylvarum versus finem Genethliacon Lucano cecinit, cujus initium est : ubi inter alia haec ait de Corduba; Fratrem scilicet Senecae et Annaei Melae patris Lu- cani, ac nobilem Oratorem. Cecinit et Martialis ter de natali Lucani epigrammata, quae exstant lib. VII num. 21, 22 et 23; in priore sic alloquitur Pollam : In alio vero de die natalis ejus loquens, inquit : Ac tandem in ultimo epigrammate : De eodem, ejusque patria Corduba egerat lib.
passages.english: [fathered] Marcus Annaeus Lucanus, a most eloquent orator or, as some prefer, historian, because in charming metres of verse he sang historical truth, not the fables of the poets. There are those who say he was born at Luque, a town 9 leagues distant from Córdoba. But, as Ambrosio de Morales points out in book IX of his History, chapter 10, there is nothing by which this can be proved. He was born on 2 November in the year of the Lord 39. Living at Rome, he took as wife Polla Argentaria, illustrious no less for poetry than for wealth and birth. Caught in the Pisonian conspiracy, by which, once Nero had been removed, the empire was being prepared for Calpurnius Piso (or, as others prefer, whom Cornelius Tacitus reports in book XVI, at the instigation of the military tribune Subrius Flavus, for Seneca himself), he was condemned to death and, being allowed to choose the manner, died with a vein cut and his blood poured out, aged 27, in the year of the Lord 66, as Eusebius and Morales hold, together with Dexter; and on the last day of April.
