Petrus Crinitus is the authority that Nero, mindful of his friend and repenting of the deed, erected a statue to Lucan with this inscription: Polla, his wife, made the birthday of her most loving husband a festival; in whose honour Statius Papinius, towards the end of book II of the Silvae, sang a Birthday Poem for Lucan, whose beginning is: where among other things he says this of Córdoba; that is, the brother of Seneca and of Annaeus Mela, Lucan's father, and a noble orator. Martial also sang three epigrams on Lucan's birthday, which survive in book VII, nos. 21, 22 and 23; in the first he addresses Polla thus: And in another, speaking of his birthday, he says: And finally in the last epigram: He had treated of the same man and his homeland Córdoba in book
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence (subject Annaeus Mela in context). Punctuation around 'die vero Aprilis ultimo Petrus Crinitus' is ambiguous; the date may belong with Crinitus's report. 'Suberio Flavio' read as Subrius Flavus. The inscription as given seems to conflate statue and birthday texts. Quoted verses of Statius and Martial are omitted in the source; 'Fratrem scilicet Senecae...' glosses a missing quotation.

passages.original: Duosque Senecas, unicumque Lucanum Facunda loquitur Corduba.
passages.english: And eloquent Cordoba speaks of two Senecas and its one and only Lucan.
passages.notes: A verse quotation (Martial 1.61).

passages.original: 14. Florebat, etc. Nobilitatis ac divitiarum C. Caeso- nii Maximi non semel meminit Martialis lib. VII, epi- gram. 73 ad Maximum, ubi tria ejus narrat palatia : In libro autem II, duo illi dat epigrammata, docens monensque ne Caesaris auram captet, quasi servus, quia domi suae princeps est.
passages.english: 14. Florebat, etc. Martial mentions the nobility and wealth of C. Caesonius Maximus more than once, in book VII, epigram 73, addressed to Maximus, where he tells of his three palaces. In book II, moreover, he gives him two epigrams, teaching and warning him not to court Caesar's favour like a slave, since he is a prince in his own house.
passages.notes: The quoted verses are omitted in the edition; the colon after 'palatia' introduces a quotation not printed.

passages.original: quod de Senecae morte agebat, cui unice amicus Caesonius fuit, utpote qui in exsilium Corsicam amandatum a Caligula Sene- cam, sponte exsul factus, comitatus sit, et post ejusdem Senecae mortem, amicitia Senecae ipsi in crimen data, exsilium agere in Sicilia a Nerone coac- tus est. Hoc posterius docet Cornel. Tacitus lib. XVI, illud autem Martialis lib. VII, duobus quae ad quem- dam Ovidium dedit, epigrammatibus; erat hie Cae- sonio familiaris, ipsumque, sicut ille Senecam, se- cutus fuerat. Primum sic habet, sub num. 44 : Et post pauca : Altero epigrammate iterum alloquens Ovidium Caeso- nii Maximi familiarem, ait (sub numero 45) : Quis vero furens is dominus sit, subdens declarat,
passages.english: that he was dealing with the death of Seneca, to whom Caesonius was a singular friend, inasmuch as he accompanied Seneca, when he had been sent into exile in Corsica by Caligula, having become an exile of his own accord; and after the death of that same Seneca, when his friendship with Seneca was charged against him as a crime, he was compelled by Nero to live in exile in Sicily. The latter point is taught by Cornelius Tacitus in book XVI; the former by Martial in book VII, in two epigrams which he addressed to a certain Ovidius; this man was an intimate of Caesonius and had followed him, just as Caesonius had followed Seneca. The first runs thus, under number 44: And shortly after: In the other epigram, again addressing Ovidius, the intimate of Caesonius Maximus, he says (under number 45): Who this raging master is, he declares in what follows,
passages.notes: The Martial quotations are not printed in the text, so the colons lead to nothing. Ascribing the Corsican exile to Caligula follows the source (historically it was Claudius).

passages.original: Erat Caesonius sanguine conjunctus imperatrici Caesoniae uxori Caii Caligulae, de qua agit Suetonius in Caio, cap. 59, et in cujus natali epigramma cecinit Martialis lib. IX cujus mitium est, Prima Palatino lux est, etc. De alio Frontone agit S. Ignatius in epistola ad Ephesios, qui eum in vinculis visitavit, cum aliis viris Ephesiis.
passages.english: Caesonius was related by blood to the empress Caesonia, wife of Gaius Caligula, of whom Suetonius treats in his Gaius, chapter 59, and on whose birthday Martial sang an epigram in book IX, whose beginning is, 'The first day is to the Palatine,' etc. Of another Fronto St Ignatius treats in his letter to the Ephesians; he visited him in chains, together with other Ephesian men.
passages.notes: 'mitium' read as 'initium' (scanning error). The Martial epigram is in fact on Caesonius's birthday; the author's attribution is translated as given.

passages.original: nam alias antequam de adventu Pauli in Hispanias meminisset, referen- dum erat, sub annum Domini 60 vel circa, uti ex dicendis constabit; quare notanter hoc loco usus est auctor verbo praeteriti temporis, cum ait, S. Paulus scripsit epistolam, etc., cum tamen verbo praesentis in caeteris, quae propriis annis acciderunt, pro more utatur inquiens : Persius moritur. Nero omnes supe- rat. Lucanus perit, etc.
passages.english: for otherwise it would have had to be reported before he mentioned Paul's coming to Spain, under about the year of the Lord 60, as will be clear from what is to be said. Therefore the author has pointedly used a verb in the past tense at this place, when he says, 'St Paul wrote the letter,' etc., whereas in the other [entries], which happened in their own years, he uses the present tense as is his custom, saying: 'Persius dies. Nero surpasses all. Lucan perishes,' etc.

passages.original: 17. Lucius Annaeus, etc. Cum eodem relectae con- jurationis Pisonianae tempore tam Seneca quam Lu- canus necatus sit, nescio quomodo Eusebio in men- tem venit mortem Senecae in annum Domini 67 reji- cere, cum tamen, ipso referente, anno Domini 66, Lu- canus mortem oppetierit. Quare multo consonantius Dexter Senecam quoque eodem anno absumptum tradit. Assentitur his etiam Ambrosius Morales li- br. IX, cap. 9, in eo leviter emendandus, quod mense Martio dicat Senecam mortuum, cum deberet dicere mense Maio; siquidem Lucanus qui, Eusebio et Dex- tro auctoribus, prius cecidit, ultima Aprilis obiit : quapropter Senecam mense Maio sequenti mortuum esse, congruum est ut dicamus.
passages.english: 17. Lucius Annaeus, etc. Since both Seneca and Lucan were put to death at the same time, when the Pisonian conspiracy was uncovered, I do not know how it came into Eusebius's mind to put Seneca's death off to the year of the Lord 67, when nevertheless, by his own report, Lucan met his death in the year of the Lord 66. Hence Dexter, much more consistently, records that Seneca too was carried off in the same year. Ambrosio de Morales also agrees with these, book IX, chapter 9, though he must be slightly corrected in that he says Seneca died in the month of March, when he ought to have said the month of May; for since Lucan, who on the authority of Eusebius and Dexter fell first, died on the last day of April, it is fitting for us to say that Seneca died in the following month of May.
passages.notes: 'relectae' read as 'detectae' (uncovered).

passages.original: Caeterum quod Dexter addit, occisum fuisse apud Ratem in regione Ophirina, a nepotibus Ophir illuc appulsis nomen hoc obtinente, cogit nos ut de Ophirinae regionis loco proprio disseramus : et quia ejus disputatio af- finis est ei quae de vero situ Tharsis edisserit, de utroque simul agere visum mihi necessarium est : Sic enim et D. Hieronymus ad Marcellam scribens fecit epistola 133 et quotquot de Ophir vel Tharsis hactenus scripserunt.
passages.english: But what Dexter adds, that he was killed at Ratis in the Ophirine region, which got this name from the descendants of Ophir who landed there, compels us to discuss the proper location of the Ophirine region. And since that inquiry is closely related to the one that examines the true site of Tarshish, it has seemed necessary to me to treat both together; for so did St Jerome too, writing to Marcella in letter 133, and all who have so far written about Ophir or Tarshish.
passages.notes: 'Ratem' (Ratis) is an unidentified place.

passages.original: Mirabile sane est quantum torserit hominum in- genia ejusmodi disceptatio. Josephus contendit Thar- sis idem esse quod Tarsus Urbs Ciliciae maritima, unde Paulus traxit originem : atque adeo ubique in Scriptura sacra pro Tharsis reddendum esso Tar- sum. A quo non dissentit Rethicius Augustodinensis in Cantica Cant. V, quem D. Hieronymus refert epist. 133, et auctor Hebraei dictionarii Arca Noe nuncu- pati, dum inquit : Verbum fortasse praestat hanc si- gnificationem non ita facile admittere, sed urbem Tar- sum hic et semper interpretari.
passages.english: It is truly remarkable how much this sort of dispute has tormented men's minds. Josephus contends that Tarshish is the same as Tarsus, the coastal city of Cilicia from which Paul took his origin, and so that everywhere in sacred Scripture 'Tarsus' should be rendered for 'Tarshish'. From him Rethicius of Autun does not dissent, on the Song of Songs V, whom St Jerome cites in letter 133, nor the author of the Hebrew dictionary called Arca Noe, when he says: 'Perhaps it is better not to admit this meaning of the word so easily, but to interpret [it] here and always as the city of Tarsus.'
passages.notes: 'esso' read as 'esse'. 'Rethicius' is presumably Reticius of Autun.

passages.original: Enimvero tres Noe filii, tres orbis principales partes sic occuparunt, ut Japhet cum filiis suis Europam acceperit (constat ex Thubal qui Hispaniam et Ita- liam, et ex Gomer qui Galliam incoluit) : at vero Cham cum filiis et nepotibus suis Palaestinam, AEgy- pturo, et Africam (nam teste Hieronymo Phuth nepos Chami Africam, Chanaam vero frater ipsius, et Chus utriusque pater, Chananaeorum provinciam seu Palaestinam possederunt); ac demum Sem natu major cum filiis et successoribus suis Orientalem Asiae partem occupavit, uti ipsamet ejusdem capitis verba demonstrant : Et facta est habitatio eorum de Messa pergentibus usque Sephar montem Orientalem.
passages.english: Indeed the three sons of Noah occupied the three principal parts of the world in such a way that Japheth with his sons received Europe (this is clear from Tubal, who settled Spain and Italy, and from Gomer, who settled Gaul); while Ham with his sons and grandsons [received] Palestine, Egypt and Africa (for, as Jerome attests, Put, the grandson of Ham, possessed Africa, and Canaan his brother, and Cush the father of both, the province of the Canaanites, that is Palestine); and finally Shem, the eldest, with his sons and successors occupied the eastern part of Asia, as the very words of the same chapter show: 'And their dwelling was from Mesha as you go toward Sephar, the mountain of the east.'
passages.notes: The genealogy (Put as grandson, Cush as father of Put and Canaan) follows the author, not Genesis, where all are sons of Ham.

passages.original: addimus tamen, ejus nepotes inde sedem mutantes, Lusitaniam ap- pulisse, et avi sui nomen regioni Bracarensi indi- disse. Neque novum judicari id debet, cum Africae Mauros ex India advectos multi affirment, ut Strabo notatum reliquit lib. XVII inquiens : Sunt qui dicant Mauros Indos esse, qui cum Hercule in hunc locum descenderunt. Et de ipso Ophiro lego doctos viros, alibi quoque praeterquam in India colonias insti- tuisse.
passages.english: we add, however, that his descendants, changing their seat from there, landed in Lusitania and gave their ancestor's name to the region of Braga. Nor should this be judged a novelty, since many affirm that the Moors of Africa were brought over from India, as Strabo left noted in book XVII, saying: 'There are those who say that the Moors are Indians who came down to this place with Hercules.' And concerning Ophir himself I read that learned men [say he] founded colonies elsewhere too, besides in India.

passages.original: 8) a Chananaeis, et Jebusaeis, quo tempore suis pulsi sedibus sunt a Jesu filio Nave, populum Israeliticum in terram re- promissam inducente. Non solum autem Gadem, sed et Cartheiam, Abderam, Malacam, et nonnullas alias Hispaniae littorales urbes a Tyriis scu Phoeni- cibus conditas referunt Strabo libr. III Geogr., Mela ipse lib. III, cap. 6, Solinus lib. de Mirabilibus mundi cap. 34, Dionysius Aphrodisaeus lib. de Situ Orbis; quos afferunt Alderete libr. II Antiq. Hisp., cap 3 se 4, Tarapha lib.
passages.english: 8) by the Canaanites and Jebusites, at the time when they were driven from their homes by Joshua the son of Nun, as he led the Israelite people into the promised land. And not only Gades, but also Carteia, Abdera, Malaca, and some other coastal cities of Spain were founded by the Tyrians or Phoenicians, as Strabo reports in Book III of the Geography, Mela himself in Book III, chapter 6, Solinus in the book On the Wonders of the World, chapter 34, and Dionysius Aphrodisaeus in the book On the Situation of the World; these are cited by Alderete in Book II of the Antiquities of Spain, chapters 3 and 4, [and] Tarapha in the book
passages.notes: The passage opens mid-reference: '8)' closes a chapter citation begun in the preceding context ('cap.'). 'scu' read as 'seu'; 'se 4' taken as 'et 4' (chapters 3 and 4). 'Dionysius Aphrodisaeus' is as printed; probably Dionysius Periegetes is meant, but the identification is uncertain.

passages.original: Igitur longitudinem pro- missae terrae definit ab Ortu scilicet in Occasum, cum ait : Ponam terminos tuos a mari Rubro usque ad mare Palaestinorum. Et cum in confesso sit apud omnes, Pa- laestinorum mare esse Mediterraneum, utpote cujus ipsi habitabant littora, ut apud Strabonem, Jose- phum, et alios videre est, restat ut nomine maris Rubri, quod illi ab Oriente opponitur, mare Mor- tuum Deus velit significare; ipsum enim Mediter- raneo opponitur ab Oriente, et est promissionis terrae certus limes.
passages.english: Therefore he defines the length of the promised land, namely from East to West, when he says: "I will set your borders from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines." And since it is admitted by all that the sea of the Philistines is the Mediterranean, inasmuch as they inhabited its shores, as can be seen in Strabo, Josephus, and others, it remains that by the name of the Red Sea, which is set opposite to it on the east, God means the Dead Sea; for it lies opposite the Mediterranean on the east, and is a sure boundary of the land of promise.
passages.notes: 'Palaestinorum' is rendered 'Philistines', following the biblical sense of Exodus 23:31.

passages.original: Quod autem in ejus definitione terrae additur, et a deserto usque ad fluvium, latitudinis terminatio est; nimirum a Meridie, ubi est desertum Gazae, usque nd fluvium, hoc est fluvii Jordanis geminos fontes, qui, uti apud Hieronymum tegimus in com- ment. cap. XVI Matthaei, Jor et Dan nuncupamur, Jordanisque simul nomen efficientes ad radices Li- bani exstant : Libanum vero ipsum additionem Tyrii regis spectasse ex III Reg., cap.
passages.english: And what is added in his definition of the land, "and from the desert to the river," is the boundary of the breadth; that is, from the South, where the desert of Gaza is, to the river, that is, to the twin sources of the river Jordan, which, as we read in Jerome in his commentary on chapter XVI of Matthew, are called Jor and Dan, and which, together making the name Jordan, are found at the foot of Lebanon. Lebanon itself, however, we learn from III Kings, chapter
passages.notes: 'tegimus' read as 'legimus', 'nuncupamur' as 'nuncupantur', 'nd' as 'ad'. The final clause is broken off: 'Libanum vero ipsum additionem Tyrii regis spectasse' seems to mean that Lebanon belonged to the domain of the king of Tyre. 'additionem' is probably a misreading of 'ditionem' (dominion); the rest of the sentence continues in the next passage.

passages.original: Vidimus hactenus non in India Orientali, sed in Occidente orbis parte exstare Tharsis et Ophir : sed unde habemus esse in Hispania potius quam in Ci- licia ad Tarsum Pauli Apostoli urbem, aut juxta Septuaginta in Africa ad Carthaginem? Nam idem Theodoretus (ubi supra) inquit de Tharsis loquens, Carthaginem civitatem Libyae principem, et B. Isaias, et admirabilis Ezechiel nuncupant. Sane quod Tharsis Tarsus non sil, D. Hieronymus sufficienter refellit ad Marcellam scribens; et constat tum ex eo quod magnopere vicina est Palaestinae; Scriptura autem sacra navigationem magnam fieri significat in Thar- sist : tum etiam quoniam Tarsus numquam lanio auro, argentove abundavit, quantum de Tharsis et Ophir afferebatur Salomoni, et Hiramo : ut sileam pavos, simias, et elephantos de Tharsis et Ophir allatos, minime Tarsi nec in universa Cilicia re- periri.
passages.english: We have seen so far that Tarshish and Ophir are not in the East Indies but in the western part of the world. But from what do we learn that [it] is in Spain rather than in Cilicia at Tarsus, the city of the Apostle Paul, or, according to the Septuagint, in Africa at Carthage? For the same Theodoret (in the place cited above), speaking of Tarshish, says: "Both blessed Isaiah and the admirable Ezekiel call [it] Carthage, the chief city of Libya." Indeed, that Tarshish is not Tarsus St Jerome sufficiently shows, writing to Marcella. It is also clear from two facts. First, [Tarsus] is very near to Palestine, whereas sacred Scripture indicates that a great voyage was made to Tarshish. Second, Tarsus never abounded in as much gold or silver as was brought to Solomon and Hiram from Tarshish and Ophir; not to mention that the peacocks, apes, and elephants brought from Tarshish and Ophir are not found at all at Tarsus, nor in all Cilicia.
passages.notes: 'sil' read as 'sit', 'Tharsist' as 'Tharsis', 'lanio' as 'tanto'.

passages.original: atque eamdem ob causam Gades ipsae aliquando Thartessus dictae reperiuntur : Cum tamen ab ejus nominis urbe, in ostio Baetis olim exstante, provincia tota, eamdem nuncuparetur nomenclatura : quo pacto lo- cutus videtur Ovidius, Metamorph. XV, cum dixit, Et Ausonius : Auri deinde tanta Thartesiaci copia fuit, ut Homerus (Strabone auctore) ct Suidas illuc Plutonis regnum, Avernum lacum, atque campos Elysios constitue- rint; nam inibi Elisam fuisse non difficulter ex Eze- ch(??)e(??)e, cap. XXVII, elicimus, cum Tyro Thartesi do- mino ait : Hyacinthus et purpura de insulis Elisa, facta sunt operimentum tuum;
passages.english: and for the same reason Gades itself is found to have been sometimes called Tartessus. Yet the whole province was called by the same name, after the city of that name which once stood at the mouth of the Baetis. In this way Ovid seems to have spoken in Metamorphoses XV, when he said, And Ausonius: Then there was so great an abundance of Tartessian gold that Homer (on Strabo's authority) and the Suda placed there the kingdom of Pluto, Lake Avernus, and the Elysian Fields. For that Elisha was there we readily gather from Ezekiel, chapter XXVII, when he says to Tyre, lady of Tartessus: "Blue and purple from the isles of Elisha became your covering";
passages.notes: The verse quotations from Ovid and Ausonius are missing from the text after 'dixit,' and 'Et Ausonius :'. 'Ezech(??)e(??)e' read as 'Ezechiele'. 'Suidas' is taken as the Suda. 'domino' is rendered 'lady' because it refers to Tyre; it literally means 'master'.

passages.original: etenim Elisam et Thar- sis fratres, in Occidente simul urbes condidisse, et totam Japheticam populationem Occidentalem in- sulas gentium fuisse nominatas ex cap. X Genes. liquet : eo praesertim quod nullibi tam exquisita purpura fuit, quam Thartesi; unde Martialis de Toga Partheniana dixit lib. VIII epigr. 27 : Nunc vero Granatensis celebris est. Baderianus auctor est, voci Hebraeae Tharsis re- spondere Cheman Jama, quae aliquando (ait) ponitur pro colore cramesino, et multoties pro hyacinthino, ut verum sit de Hispanae Thartesi domino, Hyacin- thus et purpura operimentum tuum, Cordubam quoque unam esse ex Thartesiacis ditissimis urbibus, idem Martialis lib.
passages.english: for it is clear from chapter X of Genesis that Elisha and Tarshish, brothers, founded cities together in the West, and that the whole western Japhethite settlement was called "the isles of the nations"; especially since nowhere was there such exquisite purple as at Tartessus. Hence Martial, on the Parthenian toga, said in Book VIII, epigram 27: Now, however, that of Granada is famous. Boderianus states that to the Hebrew word Tarshish corresponds Cheman Jama, which (he says) is sometimes used for crimson colour and often for blue, so that it is true of the lord of Spanish Tartessus: "Blue and purple [are] your covering." That Córdoba too was one of the richest Tartessian cities, the same Martial reports in Book
passages.notes: Martial's verses are missing after the citation. 'Baderianus' is taken as Boderianus, as printed in the next passage. 'Cheman Jama' is uncertain and probably garbled.

passages.original: 61 refert : Longum esset, ne dicam impossibile, regionis His- panae divitias enumerare, quae passim apud aucto- res leguntur. Plinius dixit : Metallis, plumbi, aeris, argenti, auri tota ferme Hispania scatet. Quod in causa fuit ut Catullus cuidam dixerit, Cuniculosae Celtiberiae fili, vocans Celtiberiam Hispaniae provinciam cuni- culosam, quod auri fodinis scateret, ut Textor in sua Cornucopia commentatur. Papinius autem lib. III Sylv. : Alibi Plinius : Vicena millia pondo auri annis singulis Asturiam atque Gallaeciam et Lusitaniam praestare : Et Silius Hispanus quidem, et Thartesiacus : Sed quid peregrinamur ad gentes, cum canonicum sacrumqne testimonium praebeat nobis Machabaeorum liber I, cap.
passages.english: 61: It would be long, not to say impossible, to enumerate the riches of the Spanish region that are read here and there in the authors. Pliny said: "Almost all Spain teems with mines of lead, copper, silver, and gold." This was the reason why Catullus said to someone, "Son of rabbity Celtiberia," calling Celtiberia, a province of Spain, burrowed [cuniculosa], because it teemed with gold mines, as Textor comments in his Cornucopia. And Papinius in Book III of the Silvae: Elsewhere Pliny [says] that Asturia, Gallaecia, and Lusitania furnish twenty thousand pounds of gold each year. And Silius, himself a Spaniard and a Tartessian: But why do we wander off to foreign peoples, when the first book of Maccabees, chapter
passages.notes: '61' completes 'Book IX, epigram 61', begun in the preceding context. The verse quotations from Statius (Papinius) and Silius are missing. 'cuniculosa' means both 'full of rabbits' and 'full of burrows or mines'; the pun is kept by keeping the Latin word.

passages.original: constat nihilominus damnatos in concilio Romano sub Damaso ubi haec legimus : Pau- lus non diverso, sicut falso haeretici garriunt, sed uno eodemque die cum Petro, in urbe Roma sub Caesare Nerone coronatus est. Crediderim eos asseruisse alia ejusdem vel sequentis mensis die Paulum quam Pe- trum occisum, non autem eodem dio sequentis anni, ut vult Augustinus. Sed quidquid dc illis sit, concors est jam in Ecclesia a Patribus per manus accepta sententia, eodem prorsus anno, et die pariter ex hac vita sublatos : eam que docuit Epiphanius haeresi 27, Maximus sermone de SS.
passages.english: it is nevertheless established that they were condemned in the Roman council under Damasus, where we read this: "Paul was crowned [with martyrdom] together with Peter in the city of Rome under Caesar Nero, not on a different day, as the heretics falsely chatter, but on one and the same day." I would suppose that they asserted that Paul was killed on another day of the same or the following month than Peter, but not on the same day of the following year, as Augustine holds. But whatever be the case with them, there is now agreement in the Church on the view handed down from the Fathers, that they were taken from this life in exactly the same year and likewise on the same day. This Epiphanius taught in heresy 27, Maximus in the sermon on Saints
passages.notes: 'dio' read as 'die', 'dc' as 'de'.

passages.original: alteram in Macedonia, quam Sinticam vocat : prope Paludem Maeotidem, unam in Taurica Chersoneso; apud Pontum et Bithyniam aliam, ac demum unam In Asia Minore. Ejus vero de qua Dex- ter agit, meminit Strabo lib. III, asseritque sitam juxta fretum Gaditanum in ea continentis parte, quae ab Oriente proxime adjacet ipsi Gaditanae In- sulae. Consonat aliis locis Dexter, nam ad annum 296 ait : Heracleae in Hispania, prope fretum Hercu- leum, etc.;
passages.english: another in Macedonia, which he calls Sintica; near Lake Maeotis, one in the Tauric Chersonese; another in Pontus and Bithynia; and finally one in Asia Minor. The one of which Dexter speaks is mentioned by Strabo in Book III, who says that it lies near the Strait of Gades, in that part of the mainland which lies closest on the east to the island of Gades itself. Dexter agrees with this in other places, for under the year 296 he says: "At Heraclea in Spain, near the Strait of Hercules," etc.;

passages.original: Ex Arabia Felice ortos, indeque in Bethleem adoraturos Dominum in stabulo, ivisse Magos illos Evangelicos, docent Justinus in Tryphone; Tertullianus contra Judaeos, et lib. III contra Marcionem; Cyprianus serm. de Stella et Magis, Epiphanius in Epitome, reges vero fuisse (regulos intelligo) scribunt Tertullianus, et Cyprianus relatis locis, Chrysostomus hom. 6 in Matth., Hilarius lib. IV de Trinit., Basilius homil. de humana Christi Generatione, Idacius ad Varimundum. Addit vero Chrysostomus, quem Equilinus refert lib. II, cap. 48, Magos istos (id est, sapientes) et in astrorum cogni- tione peritos, a Balaam originem duxisse, et ex illa phophetia ipsius, Orietur stella ex Jacobo, etc., in co- gnitionem tandem novae stellae Christi ortum publi- cantis venisse.
passages.english: That those Magi of the Gospel arose from Arabia Felix and went from there to Bethlehem to adore the Lord in the stable is taught by Justin in the Trypho; Tertullian Against the Jews and in Book III Against Marcion; Cyprian in the sermon On the Star and the Magi; Epiphanius in the Epitome. That they were kings (petty kings, I understand) is written by Tertullian and Cyprian in the places cited, Chrysostom in Homily 6 on Matthew, Hilary in Book IV On the Trinity, Basil in the homily On the Human Generation of Christ, and Idacius to Varimundus. Chrysostom, whom Equilinus cites in Book II, chapter 48, adds that these Magi (that is, wise men), skilled in the knowledge of the stars, drew their origin from Balaam, and from that prophecy of his, "A star shall rise out of Jacob", etc., came at length to recognise the new star announcing the birth of Christ.
passages.notes: "Equilinus" presumably Petrus de Natalibus, bishop of Equilio (Jesolo); "phophetia" read as "prophetia".

passages.original: Fuerat is a Nerone Hierosolymam missus, et in totam Judaeam, quae Festi Flori avari- tiam non ferens rebellarat contra Romanos. Re- greditur autem Romam, ut imperium invaderet, Tito filio cum exercitu in Judaea relicto, ut cum Josepho caeteri auctores rerum Romanarum enarrant. De annis imperii Vespasiani conveniunt omnes exegisse 9, sed non complevisse 10. Eusebius in Chronico putat imperasse ann. 9, mens. 11, dies 22, nimirum per 8 dies non complevisse annos 10; Ba- ronius vult ei tantum dies 6 defuisse. Dexter solum illi dat menses 6, supra annos 9, nisi mendum sit in codice.
passages.english: He had been sent by Nero to Jerusalem and to all Judaea, which, unable to bear the greed of Gessius Florus, had rebelled against the Romans. He returned to Rome to seize the empire, leaving his son Titus with the army in Judaea, as Josephus and the other writers of Roman history relate. As to Vespasian's years of rule, all agree that he passed 9 but did not complete 10. Eusebius in the Chronicle thinks he ruled 9 years, 11 months, 22 days, that is, he fell 8 days short of completing 10 years; Baronius holds that he lacked only 6 days. Dexter gives him only 6 months beyond 9 years, unless there is an error in the manuscript.
passages.notes: 'Festi Flori' is apparently a confusion of the procurators Festus and Gessius Florus; Florus is meant, and the translation gives Gessius Florus.

passages.original: Barnabae apostoli, qui SS. Ger- vasium et Protasium baptizavit, et multa in persecu- tione Neronis passus, in pace quievit. Agitur de eo in Vita eorumdem sanctorum quam Philippus Philo- theus scripsit, et est apud Ambrosium, et apud Su- rium tomo III, et Mombricium tom. I : Semper nova parit Caius. En quanta pro Christi nomine in Neronis persecutione sustulit, et quos filios baptismate ge- nuerit. Sane unius hominis difficile tanta et tam magnifica facinora reperies, quanta de Caio elocuti sumus.
passages.english: [the feast] of Barnabas the apostle, who baptized Saints Gervasius and Protasius, and, having suffered much in the persecution of Nero, rested in peace. He is treated in the Life of those same saints which Philip Philotheus wrote, and which is found in Ambrose, and in Surius, volume III, and in Mombritius, volume I. Caius always brings forth new things. See how much he endured for the name of Christ in the persecution of Nero, and what sons he begot through baptism. Truly you will hardly find in one man such great and such magnificent deeds as we have recounted of Caius.
passages.notes: The passage opens mid-sentence, continuing the Martyrology entry in the preceding context ('disciple of St Barnabas the apostle'). 'Semper nova parit Caius' is terse; it may be meant as a heading or exclamation.

passages.original: Cui objectioni sic satisfacit. Jam vero si ille omnia theologica ordine deinceps disposito (hoc est, non ita in communi et abstracte, ad singularia mi- nime descendens, quod altissimae sapientiae pro- prium esse Aristoteles docet), digerere voluisset; particularibusque explicationibus unumquodque totius theologiae caput disposuisset, numquam nos in tantum furoris vel ruditatis incidissemus, ut perspicatius vel divinius quam ille theologica penetrare mysteria confi- deremus;
passages.english: He answers this objection thus: "Now if he had wished to arrange all theological matters in order, set out in sequence (that is, not so generally and abstractly, descending very little to particulars, which Aristotle teaches is proper to the highest wisdom), and had set out each chief point of the whole of theology with particular explanations, we would never have fallen into such madness or ignorance as to trust that we could penetrate theological mysteries more clearly or more divinely than he;
passages.notes: The parenthesis is awkward: it seems to describe the master's actual general method, which is proper to the highest wisdom, rather than the ordered method he did not adopt.

passages.original: Quod ad historiam vitae ejus spectat, communi Hispanicorum auctorum calculo receptum est id quod Dexter ait, in Hispania ortum fuisse; unde philoso- phandi gratia Athenas petiit, non aliter quam Sene- ca, aut Quintilianus Romam, seu uti quidam nobiles (ut Hieronymus loquitur) qui ad Titum Livium lacteo eloquentiae fonte manantem ex ultimis Hispaniae provinciis venerunt; postmodum a D. Paulo ad fidem adductus episcopus Atheniensis factus est : inde Dionysio in ejus locum suffecto in patriam migravit commissurus concivibus suis divinum scientiae the- saurum.
passages.english: As for the history of his life, what Dexter says has been accepted by the common reckoning of Spanish authors: that he was born in Spain; from there he went to Athens to study philosophy, just as Seneca or Quintilian went to Rome, or as certain nobles (as Jerome puts it) came from the farthest provinces of Spain to Titus Livy, flowing with a milky fountain of eloquence. Afterwards, brought to the faith by St Paul, he was made bishop of Athens; then, when Dionysius had been appointed in his place, he moved to his homeland, to entrust to his fellow citizens the divine treasure of knowledge.
passages.notes: The subject is evidently Hierotheus, Dionysius's teacher.

passages.original: et haec est illa gravior causa, quae S. Crescentem compulit ut ferret ipsum inde, et ad latus Jacohi apostoli collo- caret. Habemus ejus rei irrefregabile testimonium S. Leonis Papae IV in epistola de Translatione S Jacobi, ubi de SS. Athanasio et Theodoro haec ait : Illi duo discipuli p(??)dissequi pro reverentia sui Magistri, jusserunt se post obitum suum a Christia- nis juxta magistrum suum, unus ad dexteram illius, alius ad sinistram sepeliri. Idemque ait Callixtus Papa II, quem refert Vincentius Belvacensis in Spe- culo historiali, quibus assentiuntur recentiores, Morales, Marieta, Alderete, et caeteri. Et in antiquo Cordubensi Breviario haec lego : Alii vero discipuli Athanasius, et Theodorus, ut in B. Leonis epistola le- gitur, juxta Apostoli corpus, unus ad dexteram et alter ad laevam sepultus est. Et hoc ipsum traditione re- ceptum est in Ecclesia Compostellana.
passages.english: and this is the weightier reason which compelled St Crescens to carry him from there and place him beside James the apostle. We have an irrefutable testimony of this matter from St Leo IV, Pope, in his letter on the Translation of St James, where he says this of Saints Athanasius and Theodore: "Those two disciples, followers, out of reverence for their Master, ordered that after their death they be buried by the Christians beside their master, one at his right, the other at his left." Pope Callixtus II says the same, as Vincent of Beauvais reports in the Speculum historiale; and the more recent writers agree with them, Morales, Marieta, Alderete and the rest. And in the ancient Breviary of Córdoba I read this: "But the other disciples, Athanasius and Theodore, as is read in the letter of Blessed Leo, were buried beside the Apostle's body, one at the right and the other at the left." And this very thing has been received by tradition in the Church of Compostela.
passages.notes: 'p(??)dissequi' read as 'pedissequi' (followers, attendants). 'Jacohi' read as 'Jacobi'.

passages.original: Is vitam finierat anno Do- mini 81, cum gubernasset imperium annos 10. ha- buitque successores duos filios, primo quidem Titum annis duobus, et co veneno sublato Domitianum anno Domini 83, qui secundam in Ecclesia persecu- tionem commovit, uti Eusebius lib. III, cap. 13, testatur. Ejus fructus nonnullos mox refert Dexter, egerat de prima sub Nerone ad an. 60.
passages.english: He had ended his life in the year of the Lord 81, having governed the empire for 10 years; and he had two sons as successors: first Titus for two years, and, when he had been removed by poison, Domitian in the year of the Lord 83, who stirred up the second persecution against the Church, as Eusebius testifies in book III, chapter 13. Dexter shortly reports some of its fruits; he had dealt with the first, under Nero, at the year 60.
passages.notes: 'co veneno' read as 'eo veneno'.

passages.original: Ptolomaeus in Vettonibus ( seu Vergonibus ) Lusitaniae Caparam constituit, quo loci olim inter C(??)eum Pompeium, et Aulum Trebonium acriter certatum est, et hodieque ejus belli plura exstant lapidum monumenta, militum scilicet ibidem occisorum, quae apud Ambrosium Moralem videre licet lib. VIII, cap. 18. Nunc Capara nomen relinet; estque in limine Extrematurae, non longe a Civita- tensi urbe, vulgo Cividad Rodrigo : felicior sane sanctorum Carilippi et sociorum martyrio, quam incolarum numero aut divitiis.
passages.english: Ptolemy places Capara among the Vettones (or Vergones) of Lusitania, where formerly there was fierce fighting between Gnaeus Pompey and Aulus Trebonius; and even today several stone monuments of that war survive, namely of soldiers killed there, which can be seen in Ambrosio de Morales, book VIII, chapter 18. Now it keeps the name Capara, and it lies on the border of Extremadura, not far from the city of Civitas, commonly Ciudad Rodrigo: more fortunate, truly, in the martyrdom of Saints Carilippus and his companions than in the number or wealth of its inhabitants.
passages.notes: 'C(??)eum' read as 'Cnaeum' (Gnaeus); 'relinet' read as 'retinet'.

passages.original: Caralippi et sociorum festus dies 28 Aprilis in Martyrologiis Redae, Adonis, Usuardi, et Romano, ubi tamen pro Carilippo corrupte legitur Caralippum, cum in cae- teris et in Equilino, lib. XII, cap. ult., num. 131, sicut in Dextro Carilippus scribatur. Sociorum no- mina sunt Aphrodisius, Agapius (Usuardo Agapatus, Equilino Agapitus) et Eusebius : ita enim a prae- dictis auctoribus nominantur; sed nullus acta eorum- dem recenset.
passages.english: [The feast] day of Caralippus and his companions is kept on 28 April in the Martyrologies of Bede, Ado, Usuard, and the Roman, where, however, instead of Carilippus, Caralippus is read in corrupt form, whereas in the others and in Equilinus, book XII, last chapter, no. 131, as in Dexter, Carilippus is written. The names of the companions are Aphrodisius, Agapius (in Usuard Agapatus, in Equilinus Agapitus) and Eusebius: for so they are named by the aforesaid authors; but none records their acts.
passages.notes: 'Redae' read as 'Bedae' (Bede). 'Equilinus' is Petrus de Natalibus, bishop of Equilio.

passages.original: 60 praesertim ex Juvenale aiente : et Martiale, cujus etiam dedimus epigramma 9 : quo Martyris cujusdam Christiani passionem veram, simulatam agentis Laureoli Latronis fabulam, re- fert. Consuevisse etenim Domitianum prae nimia crudelitate, casus Tragicos in miserorum corpora ad Theatrum ex vero repraesentare, narrant multi : et Tacitus in Vita Agricolae addit : Nero subtraxit ocu- los; jussitque scelera, non spectavit, praecipua sub Do- mitiano miseriarum pars erat, videre, et aspici; cum suspiria nostra subscriberentur, cum denotandis tot ho- minum palloribus, sufficeret saevus ille vultus, et rubor, a quo se contra pudorem muniebat.
passages.english: 60, especially from Juvenal, who says: and from Martial, whose epigram 9 we have also given, in which he relates the true passion of a certain Christian martyr who was acting the play of Laureolus the Robber, [which was] feigned. For many relate that Domitian, out of excessive cruelty, was accustomed to represent tragic deaths for real on the bodies of wretched people at the theatre; and Tacitus in the Life of Agricola adds: "Nero withdrew his eyes; he ordered crimes but did not watch them. The chief part of our miseries under Domitian was to see and be seen, when our sighs were recorded, when, to mark the pallor of so many men, that savage face and the redness with which he armed himself against shame sufficed."
passages.notes: The quotations from Juvenal and Martial appear to have dropped out after 'aiente' and 'Martiale'.

passages.original: Simili beneficio se honestatam a Dei genitrice glo- riatur Florentia, uti Hieronymus Savanarola testatur, qui ea de re concionem ad Florentinos habuit die 25 Octobris ann. 1495, et inter ejus opera exstat; Epistolae autem textus hic est : Florentia Deo et Do- mino Jesu Christo filio meo et mihi dilecta, tene fidem, insta orationibus, roborare patientia;
passages.english: Florence boasts that it was honoured with a similar favour by the Mother of God, as Girolamo Savonarola testifies, who preached a sermon on the matter to the Florentines on 25 October 1495, which survives among his works. The text of the Letter is this: "Florence, beloved of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ my son and of me, hold to the faith, persist in prayers, be strengthened with patience;

passages.original: forsan quia non illico suum dissipa- bat patrimonium, et eleemosynae quas ille in occulto faciebat, latebant ipsum. Incipit sub num. 53 ejus libri XII. Verbum illud affectu paterno, mutavimus in effante Paterno, nam in antiquis lapidum inscriptionibus effante valde fuit in usu, ut Resendius in epistola ad Ambrosium Moralem affirmat, quae in Hispania illu- strata exstat. Bilbilim antiquam sitam esse, non quidem ad Salonis confluentem ubi nunc Calatayud, sed in vertice montis, ad dimidiam inde leucam, auctores sunt Barrerius et Nonnius in sua Hispania cap.
passages.english: perhaps because he did not at once squander his patrimony, and the alms which he gave in secret were hidden from him. It begins at no. 53 of his book XII. We changed the words 'affectu paterno' (with paternal affection) to 'effante Paterno' (with Paternus speaking), for 'effante' was much in use in ancient stone inscriptions, as Resende affirms in a letter to Ambrosio de Morales, which survives in [the latter's] Hispania illustrata. That ancient Bilbilis was situated not at the confluence of the Salo, where Calatayud now is, but on the summit of a mountain half a league from there, is the view of Barreiros and Nonius in his Hispania, chapter
passages.notes: Paternus is a friend of Martial; 'ipsum' refers to Martial, who did not know of the alms.

passages.original: Duosque Senecas. unicumque Lucanum Facunda loquitur Corduba. Gaudent jocosae Canio suo Gades, Emerita Deciano meo. Te, Liciane, gloriabitur nostra, Nec me tacebit Bilbilis.
passages.english: And eloquent Corduba speaks of the two Senecas and the one and only Lucan. Playful Gades rejoices in its Canius, Emerita in my Decianus. Of you, Licinianus, our [Bilbilis] will boast, nor will Bilbilis be silent about me.
passages.notes: Verse quotation (Martial, Epigrams I.61), given here as running text. 'Liciane' is evidently for 'Liciniane' (Licinianus). The construction 'loquitur' with the accusative is the poet's: Corduba 'speaks of' them.

passages.original: Ponuntur Aquae Quintia- nae a Ptolemaeo in Seburris, Gallicorum Lucensium populis, quo loci nunc Oviedo, aut prope. Moletius et Millius contendunt nunc vocari Aquas Caldas. Multa olim in Hispania exstiterunt oppida ab Aquis denominata. Erant enim et Aquae Sextianae, quas Plinius memorat : ut creditur Lucensis urbs, Lugo hodie. Erant et Aquae Calidae, nunc Orense; rursus Aquae Cellenae, vel Gallinae, ut vocat Antonini Itine- rarium, oppidum non longe ab Orense, versus Tu- dem, hodie los Vanos de Melgazo, vel Pregigueiro in ditione Monasterii S.
passages.english: The Aquae Quintianae are placed by Ptolemy among the Seburri, peoples of the Gallaeci Lucenses, at or near the place where Oviedo now is. Moletius and Millius maintain that it is now called Aquas Caldas. Many towns in Spain were once named from 'Aquae' (waters). For there were also the Aquae Sextianae, which Pliny mentions: as is believed, the city of the Lucenses, today Lugo. There were also the Aquae Calidae, now Orense; again the Aquae Cellenae, or Gallinae, as the Itinerary of Antoninus calls it, a town not far from Orense, towards Tude, today los Baños de Melgaço, or Pregigueiro, in the jurisdiction of the Monastery of St.
passages.notes: 'Vanos' is presumably for 'Baños'. 'Moletius et Millius' not securely identified. The sentence runs on into the following passage ('Mary of Melon').

passages.original: Ambrosius Morales erudite credit Arsam esse quae nunc Azuaga nuncupatur, non longe a Fuente Obejuna, quae Cordubae vicina est; quo loci antiquitatis magnae urbis vestigia non modica reperiuntur. Meminit Arsae Plinius dum de Baeturia agit lib. III.
passages.english: Ambrosio de Morales learnedly believes that Arsa is the place now called Azuaga, not far from Fuente Obejuna, which is near Corduba; in that place no small traces of a great ancient city are found. Pliny mentions Arsa when he treats of Baeturia, in book III.

passages.original: De Simone legimus in Actis Apost. cap. XIII : Erant autem in Ecclesia, quae erat Antiochiae, prophetae et doctores : in quibus Barnabas, et Simon qui vocabatur Niger, et Lucius Cyrenensis, etc. Hilarius, Ambrosius, Beda et Leo, quos Maldonatus refert, asserunt Simonem (et filios consequenter) fuisse gentilem; ipse vero Ju- daeum credit, sed absque fundamento, quod enim Marcus vocet eum fratrem Alexandri et Rufi; quasi notorum hominum, non probat Judaeum fuisse;
passages.english: Of Simon we read in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter XIII: 'Now there were in the church that was at Antioch prophets and teachers, among whom were Barnabas, and Simon who was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene,' etc. Hilary, Ambrose, Bede and Leo, whom Maldonatus cites, assert that Simon (and consequently his sons) was a gentile; he himself, however, believes him a Jew, but without foundation; for the fact that Mark calls him the father of Alexander and Rufus, as of well-known men, does not prove that he was a Jew;
passages.notes: The Latin has 'fratrem' (brother) of Alexander and Rufus; Mark 15:21 calls Simon their father, and the context speaks of his sons, so 'patrem' is probably intended. Translated as 'father'.

passages.original: Io Romano Martyrologio ad diem 26 Martii sic legimus : Syrmii sanctorum martyrum Montani presbyteri, et Maximae, qui ob Christi fidem in flumen demersi sunt. Hieronymus in suo Martyro- logio, quem Equilinus sequitur, lib. III, cap. 233, non in fluvio, sed in mari mersos scribit, idemque Usuardus affirmat : Montanus presbyter et Maxima virgo, ait Hieronymus, in oppido Syrmio passi sunt : qui dum Christum Dominum viva voce confiterentur, ab infidelibus tenti, et vinculis ferreis colligati, ambo in mare mersi sunt, 6 kalend. Aprilis. Usuardus vero, In Syrmio sanctorum martyrum Montani presbyteri et Maximae in mare mersorum.
passages.english: In the Roman Martyrology on the 26th of March we read thus: 'At Syrmium, [the feast] of the holy martyrs Montanus, priest, and Maxima, who for the faith of Christ were drowned in a river.' Jerome in his Martyrology, whom Equilinus follows in book III, chapter 233, writes that they were drowned not in a river but in the sea, and Usuard affirms the same. 'Montanus the priest and Maxima the virgin,' says Jerome, 'suffered in the town of Syrmium: while they were confessing Christ the Lord aloud, they were seized by unbelievers and bound with iron chains, and both were drowned in the sea, on the 6th day before the Kalends of April.' Usuard, however [says]: 'At Syrmium, [the feast] of the holy martyrs Montanus, priest, and Maxima, drowned in the sea.'
passages.notes: 'Io' read as 'In'. 'Equilinus' is Petrus de Natalibus, bishop of Equilio.

passages.original: et quod difficilius erat, a Diocletiano occisos scribit, Utrumque tamen sine auctore, ac proinde in neutro audiendus, quinimmo confundit hunc Mon- tanum socium S. Maximae virginis, cum alio comite S. Irenaei episcopi, et Demetrii diaconi, ac Pollionis lectoris, qui diverso mortis genere sub Diocletiano passi sunt; nam (uti Equilinus scribit lib. IV, cap. 94) Irenaeus et Montanus in flumen praecipitati, De- metrius capite plexus, Pollio flammis exustus est, tametsi quod ad Irenaeum spectat, Romanum Marty- rologium 25 Martii asserat, non quidem suffocatum, sed abscisso capite consummatum fuisse.
passages.english: and, what was more difficult, he writes that they were killed by Diocletian. Yet [he says] both without authority, and therefore is to be heeded in neither; indeed, he confuses this Montanus, the companion of St Maxima the virgin, with another, the companion of St Irenaeus the bishop, Demetrius the deacon, and Pollio the lector, who suffered under Diocletian by different kinds of death; for (as Equilinus writes, book IV, chapter 94) Irenaeus and Montanus were thrown headlong into a river, Demetrius was beheaded, Pollio was burnt in the flames; although, as regards Irenaeus, the Roman Martyrology for 25 March asserts that he was not drowned but was finished off by having his head cut off.

passages.original: Et tamen si Romam, et ultra missi fuissent, haud dubium, quin Hieronymus in eos incideret, de eisque ageret in libro de Script. Ecclesiast. Quod enim quidam respondent, Hiero- nymum eo libro solum egisse de auctoribus quorum opera apud Eusebii bibliothecam exstabant, gratis dicitur, et contra Hieronymi intentum, et Dextri petitionem, ut ex prologo ipsius liquet. Unum tan- dem non sileam, verba illa Dionysii in epistola ad Titum : Sanctus quidem Timotheus, honestissime Tite, nescio an aliquid scripserim de theologicis signis, cujus ipse ignarus abscesserit;
passages.english: And yet, if they had been sent to Rome and beyond, there is no doubt that Jerome would have come upon them and treated of them in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers. For what some reply, that Jerome in that book dealt only with authors whose works were extant in the library of Eusebius, is said without grounds, and against both Jerome's purpose and Dexter's request, as is clear from his prologue. Finally, I will not pass over one thing: that those words of Dionysius in the letter to Titus, 'Holy Timothy, most honourable Titus, I do not know whether I have written anything on the theological symbols, of which he departed ignorant;'
passages.notes: The quotation from Dionysius is garbled; sense of 'cujus ipse ignarus abscesserit' uncertain. The sentence continues into the next passage.

passages.original: VESPASIANO AVGVSTO. PONT. MAX. TRIB. POT. X. IMPER. XX. PP. COSS. IX. IMPERATORI. TITO VESP. CAESAR. AVG. F. COSS. VI. .......... (Deleta fuit Domitiani memoria .......... ex senatusconsulto, teste Suetonio.) CALPETANO RANTIO QVIRINALI. VALERIO FESTOLEG. AVG. PR. PR. etc.
passages.english: TO VESPASIAN AUGUSTUS, PONTIFEX MAXIMUS, WITH TRIBUNICIAN POWER FOR THE 10TH TIME, HAILED IMPERATOR 20 TIMES, FATHER OF HIS COUNTRY, CONSUL 9 TIMES; TO THE IMPERATOR TITUS VESPASIAN CAESAR, SON OF AUGUSTUS, CONSUL 6 TIMES; .......... (The memory of Domitian was erased .......... by decree of the senate, as Suetonius testifies.) CALPETANUS RANTIUS QUIRINALIS VALERIUS FESTUS, LEGATE OF AUGUSTUS WITH PROPRAETORIAN POWER, etc.
passages.notes: Inscription; 'FESTOLEG.' read as 'FESTO LEG.' The case of the final names (dative/ablative) is unclear; possibly the inscription is dated or dedicated under this legate.

passages.original: nem occupavit : et tenuit in mari Rubro classem, et instituit ut peream Indiae urbes devastarentur, ut vi- deas quantum Trojano debeat Roma, quantum suum dilataverit imperium. Memoriam ejusmodi Martialis libro XII, occinit, cum dixit, epigram. 8 : Porro Dacorem regem nonnulli Decebalum, ut Xi- philinus et Eusebius, alii Diurpaneum vocant, ut Orosius lib. VII, cap. 10.
passages.english: [and Babylon] he occupied; and he kept a fleet in the Red Sea, and arranged that the cities of India should be laid waste, so that you may see how much Rome owes to Trajan, how far he extended its empire. Martial sings of a memorial of this kind in book XII, when he said, epigram 8: Further, some call the king of the Dacians Decebalus, as Xiphilinus and Eusebius do, others Diurpaneus, as Orosius, book VII, chapter 10.
passages.notes: 'ut peream' is probably corrupt (perhaps for 'ut per eam', 'through it'). 'Trojano' for 'Trajano', 'Dacorem' for 'Dacorum'. The Martial quotation is missing from the text.

passages.original: Avitus ad Fortunatas insulas ( Canarias ) profectus praedicandi Evangelii gratia, pro Christo martyrio coronatus fuit, quod itidem Primus Cabi- lonensis episcopus in sua Topographia SS. Christi martyrum his verbis dixit : Canaria insula in Oceano Atlantico, huc dilatata est Christi fides; hic Avitus martyr. Forsan ille Avitus quem Martialis saepe al- loquitur lib. I, epigr. 16, lib. IX, in principio, et lib. X, epigr. 96. De duumviro priore A. Cornelio Palma nonnulla diximus. P. Turacus, seu Turanus ille mihi est ad quem Martialis lib. V, epigramma scri- psit 78, cujus principium est : Vide quanta eum colat reverentia, et amicitia, post multa enim subdit :
passages.english: Avitus, having set out to the Fortunate Islands (the Canaries) for the sake of preaching the Gospel, was crowned with martyrdom for Christ, which Primus, bishop of Chalon, likewise stated in his Topography of the Holy Martyrs of Christ in these words: 'Canaria, an island in the Atlantic Ocean; the faith of Christ was spread here; here [lies] Avitus the martyr.' Perhaps this is that Avitus whom Martial often addresses, book I, epigram 16, book IX at the beginning, and book X, epigram 96. Of the first duumvir, A. Cornelius Palma, we have said something. P. Turacus, or Turanus, is to my mind the man to whom Martial wrote epigram 78 of book V, whose beginning is: See with how much reverence and friendship he honours him, for after much he adds:
passages.notes: The Martial quotations are omitted in the text. 'Primus Cabilonensis' not securely identified.

passages.original: Spiritu una cum S. Clemente divina ora- cula gentibus desseminanda acceperat, fideliter omni- bus Hesperiis plagis distribuit. Quis autem nesciat Hispaniam a Graecis Hesperiam dictam, et a Latinis non semel, ut apud Martialem videre esi (ut alios omittam) qui de Corduba loquens lib. IX, epigram. 61, cujus initium, In Tartessiacis, inquit : Addo Breviarii Gothoci Toletani sacrum hymnum, quo ejusdem S. Dionysii Areopagitae asseritur in Hispanias adventus.
passages.english: Spirit, together with St. Clement, had received divine oracles to be disseminated among the nations, he faithfully distributed to all the Hesperian regions. But who does not know that Spain was called Hesperia by the Greeks, and more than once by the Latins too, as can be seen in Martial (to pass over others), who, speaking of Cordoba in book IX, epigram 61, which begins "In Tartessiacis," says: I add the sacred hymn of the Gothic Breviary of Toledo, in which the coming of the same St. Dionysius the Areopagite into Spain is asserted.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence, continuing a quotation from Methodius ("whatever he had received from St. ..."). The quotations of Martial and of the hymn have dropped out of the text; the edition passes directly to the next sentence. "esi" read as "est"; "Gothoci" as "Gothici".

passages.original: Floruerunt olim Hispali Flo- rentii duo, praecipua sanctitate perspicui, sed diverso tempore et mortis genere sublati. Vetustior fuit Rustici Bolani filius, viri consularis Hispani, qui anno Domini 113 consulatum Romanum gessit cum Cal- purnio Pisone, ut Cassiodorus et Onuphrius habent, et iterum an. 118 cum Trajano. Florentius ejus filius, qui integro nomine M. Bolanus Florentius dictus est, ab apostolis ad fidem conversus in Castro Tile, sive Silae vel Asila, in Turditanis Baeticae prope Hispalim, quo loco Asila ponitur a Ptolomaeo et Vil- lanova, in tabula veleris Hispaniae, tandem pro Christo jugulum praebuit die 27 Octobris, ut Roma- num martyrologium, Beda, Usuardus, Ado, et Gale- sinus testantur, et Equilinus lib.
passages.english: There once flourished at Seville two Florentii, conspicuous for outstanding holiness, but taken away at different times and by different kinds of death. The older was the son of Rusticus Bolanus, a Spanish man of consular rank, who held the Roman consulship in the year of the Lord 113 with Calpurnius Piso, as Cassiodorus and Onuphrius have it, and again in the year 118 with Trajan. Florentius his son, who by his full name was called M. Bolanus Florentius, converted to the faith by the apostles in Castrum Tile, or Sila or Asila, among the Turditani of Baetica near Seville (in which place Asila is located by Ptolemy and by Villanova in his map of ancient Spain), at last offered his throat for Christ on 27 October, as the Roman Martyrology, Bede, Usuard, Ado and Galesinus testify, and Equilinus in book
passages.notes: Sentence continues in the following context ("XI, last chapter"). "veleris" read as "veteris".

passages.original: Utriusque praeclaro quidem elogio meminit M. Maximus in Chronico anno 612, dicens : Floret memoria per Hispanius utriusque Florentii His- palensis : prioris, qui dictus est Rusticus (ob patris nomen) ad quem scripsit Plinius secundus, martyris sub Trajano passi : alterius, confessoris, sub Zenone episcopo Hispalensi Agit de Zenone ipse anno 483, asseritique Felicem papam designasse eum legatum a latere in Hispania. De S.
passages.english: M. Maximus mentions both with a distinguished eulogy in his Chronicle under the year 612, saying: "The memory of both Florentii of Seville flourishes throughout Spain: of the former, who was called Rusticus (on account of his father's name), to whom Pliny the Younger wrote, a martyr who suffered under Trajan; of the other, a confessor, under Zeno, bishop of Seville." He himself treats of Zeno under the year 483, and asserts that Pope Felix appointed him legate a latere in Spain. Concerning St.
passages.notes: "Hispanius" read as "Hispanias"; "asseritique" as "asseritque". Final sentence continues in the following context.

passages.original: 5. Fl. Rutilius, etc. Hoc anno agitur de ejus fuga in Hispaniam, anno vero 116 de ejus martyrio. Ejus- dem meminit Tertullianus lib. de Fuga in persecu- tione cap. 5 : Rutilius, inquit, sanctissimus martyr cum totiens fugisset persecutionem de loco in locum : etiam periculum, ut putabat, nummis redemisset, post totam securitatem quam sibi prospexerat, ex inopinato apprehensus, et praesidi oblatus, tormentis dissipatus (credo pro fugae castigatione), dehinc ignibus datus, passionem quam vitarat, misericordiae Dei retulit. Quae fere verba Martyrologium Romanum sibi assumpsit die Aug.
passages.english: 5. Fl. Rutilius, etc. Under this year his flight into Spain is treated, and under the year 116 his martyrdom. Tertullian also mentions him in his book On Flight in Persecution, chapter 5: "Rutilius," he says, "a most holy martyr, after he had so often fled persecution from place to place, and had even bought off the danger, as he thought, with money, after all the security he had provided for himself, was unexpectedly seized and brought before the governor, torn apart by tortures (I believe as punishment for his flight), then given to the flames, and rendered to the mercy of God the suffering he had avoided." The Roman Martyrology adopted almost these very words on August
passages.notes: The date continues in the following context ("2").

passages.original: Sed si tempora quibus hic et ille floruit trutina pendantur exacta, fateamur necesse est Mar- cellum Victorium, cui Quintilianus libros dedit circa annum Domini 90 patrem fuisse hujus cui Statius Sylvam dicat anno. 110, nam de juventute ipsius, lit- teris ac viribus florida, multa Statius canit. Incipit quidem; Laudat Oratoriam ipsius : Laudat ingenium : Et post pauca : Audi de fortitudine : Sed quid de stirpe?
passages.english: But if the times in which this one and that one flourished are weighed on an exact balance, we must admit that Marcellus Victorius, to whom Quintilian dedicated his books around the year of the Lord 90, was the father of this man to whom Statius dedicates a Silva in the year 110; for Statius sings much about his youth, flourishing in letters and in strength. Indeed he begins: He praises his oratory: He praises his talent: And after a little: Hear about his courage: But what about his lineage?
passages.notes: The quotations from Statius introduced by each colon have dropped out of the text.

passages.original: 3. Astae, etc. Ptolomaeus meminit urbis Astensis in Beatica non longe a Nebrissa in Turdetanis popu- lis. Fuit sane Romanis in pretio, qui coloniae Ro- manae privilegiis eam decorarunt, et, ut Plinius auctor est, nuncuparunt Astam regiam. Referi etiam Titus Livius lib. XXXIX, C. Cathinium post fusos Lu- sitanos in agro Astensi, Astam expugnasse, sed cum incautus muros ascendit, ictum, post dies paucos obiisse.
passages.english: 3. Astae, etc. Ptolemy mentions the city of Asta in Baetica, not far from Nebrissa, among the Turdetanian peoples. It was certainly valued by the Romans, who honoured it with the privileges of a Roman colony and, as Pliny attests, named it Asta Regia. Titus Livy also relates in book XXXIX that C. Catinius, after routing the Lusitanians in the territory of Asta, stormed Asta, but, being struck as he incautiously climbed the walls, died a few days later.
passages.notes: "Beatica" read as "Baetica"; "Referi" as "Refert".

passages.original: 130 numero 80, dicens : Macarius et Ru- finus, Justus et Theophilus pridie kalendas Martii martyrio coronantur; cum tamen lib. VI cap. 117 egisset fuse de SS. Justa et Rufina. Usuardus cum Molani additionibus : Eodem die, ait, sanctorum Macarii et Rufini, Justi et Theophili; qui tamen die 19 Julii agit de Justa et Rufina. Vetus Romanum Mar- tyrologium sic : Pridie kal. Martii, natalis sanctorum martyrum Macarii, Rufini, Justi et Theophili. Baro- nius addit Romae, sed de suo, et sine auctore, nam nullus aliorum urbem apposuit, cum tamen si appo- nenda esset, non Romae, sed Hispali in Hispania dici oporteret.
passages.english: 130, number 80, saying: "Macarius and Rufinus, Justus and Theophilus are crowned with martyrdom on the day before the Kalends of March"; although in book VI, chapter 117, he had treated at length of Saints Justa and Rufina. Usuard with Molanus' additions says: "On the same day, of Saints Macarius and Rufinus, Justus and Theophilus"; yet he treats of Justa and Rufina on 19 July. The old Roman Martyrology thus: "On the day before the Kalends of March, the feast of the holy martyrs Macarius, Rufinus, Justus and Theophilus." Baronius adds "at Rome," but on his own account and without authority, for none of the others added the city; and yet, if it were to be added, one ought to say not "at Rome" but "at Seville in Spain."
passages.notes: Begins mid-reference (Equilinus book XI, chapter 130).

passages.original: egit de Ignatio, inter caeteras ejus epistolas harum non meminit; sed ar- gumentum negativum obesse non potest, cum posi- tiva testimonia nobilium auctorum adsunt. Ergone opera Dionysii apposititia sunt, quia Hieronymus eorum non meminit? absit. Quod si Hieronymus siluit, Dexter ejus coaevus loculus est, loculus et Bernardus, qui apocryphis fidem numquam dedisse comperitur : suscipiunt gravissimi viri, Carthusia- nus, Marianus Victorius, Symphorianus Clamperius, Petrus Canisius, AEneas Sylvius, Sixtus Senensis, Franciscus Arias, et innumeri alii, quos longum esset recensere.
passages.english: treated of Ignatius, among his other letters does not mention these; but an argument from silence cannot prevail when the positive testimonies of distinguished authors are present. Are the works of Dionysius then spurious because Jerome does not mention them? Far from it. And if Jerome was silent, Dexter his contemporary spoke, and Bernard spoke, who is never found to have given credence to apocrypha; and they are accepted by most weighty men: the Carthusian, Marianus Victorius, Symphorien Champier, Peter Canisius, Aeneas Sylvius, Sixtus of Siena, Francisco Arias, and countless others whom it would be long to list.
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence ("while Jerome, in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, ..."). "apposititia" read as "supposititia" (spurious); "loculus" as "locutus". "Carthusianus" presumably Denis the Carthusian.

passages.original: Eusebius hoc anno dixit : Hadrianus Judaeos capit secundo contra Roma- nos rebellantes : anno vero 120, dixerat : Ηadrianus Trajani invidens gloriae, de Assyria, Mesopotamia t Armenia, quas ille provincias fecerat, revocavit exer- citus. Obierat quidem Trajanus anno Domini 119, cum imperasset annos 19, mens. 2, dies 15, et prius in Caesarem adoptasset Hadrianum consobrinae suae filium. Eusebius anno 120, sic ait : Hadrianus Italicae in Hispania natus, consobrinae Trajani filius fuit; ut videas errare eos qui Hadriae In Piceno ni- tum fabulantur, et qui Romae ortum dicunt, tametsi nullus sit qui non affirmet ipsum genus suum ex Ita- lica Hispaniae deduxisse.
passages.english: Eusebius said under this year: "Hadrian captures the Jews who were rebelling a second time against the Romans"; but under the year 120 he had said: "Hadrian, envious of Trajan's glory, recalled the armies from Assyria, Mesopotamia and Armenia, which [Trajan] had made provinces." Trajan had indeed died in the year of the Lord 119, having reigned 19 years, 2 months, 15 days, and had earlier adopted as Caesar Hadrian, the son of his cousin. Eusebius under the year 120 says thus: "Hadrian, born at Italica in Spain, was the son of Trajan's cousin"; so that you may see that those err who fable that he was born at Hadria in Picenum, and those who say he was born at Rome, although there is no one who does not affirm that he derived his family from Italica in Spain.
passages.notes: "nitum" read as "natum".

passages.original: 2. Idem Hadr., etc. Sic Eusebius : Hadrianus re- liquias tributorum urbis relaxavit, chartis publice in- censis : plurimos etiam ipsis tribulis liberos praestitit.
passages.english: 2. The same Hadrian, etc. Thus Eusebius: "Hadrian remitted the arrears of the city's taxes, the records being publicly burned; he also made very many free from the taxes themselves."
passages.notes: "tribulis" read as "tributis".

passages.original: 2. Bellum, etc. Eusebius : Bellum contra Sauro - matas gestum. Vide Orosium, libr VII, cap. 13, et ejus illustratorem Marcoduranum in nolis ejus capitis.
passages.english: 2. The war, etc. Eusebius: "A war waged against the Sauromatae." See Orosius, book VII, chapter 13, and his commentator Marcoduranus in his notes on that chapter.
passages.notes: "Sauro - matas" read as Sauromatas; "libr" as libro; "nolis" as notis. Marcoduranus is presumably Franciscus Fabricius Marcoduranus, editor of Orosius.

passages.original: 6. Aquis prope Toletum, etc. Ptolemaeus, in Carpe- taniae suae tabula, prope Toletum ponit Liboram, quam Plinius vocat Eburam, aliis Elbora, et de ea Tit. Livius lib. XL loquens : Quint, Flaccus, ait, prin- cipio veris exercitum in Carpetaniam duxit, et castra locavit ad oppidum Eburam, modico praesidio in urbe posito.
passages.english: 6. At Aquae near Toledo, etc. Ptolemy, in his map of Carpetania, places Libora near Toledo; Pliny calls it Ebura, others Elbora. Titus Livy, speaking of it in book XL, says: "Quintus Flaccus at the beginning of spring led the army into Carpetania and pitched camp at the town of Ebura, having placed a small garrison in the city."
passages.notes: "Aquis" may be the place-name Aquae or simply "at the waters"; the lemma is cut short.

passages.original: 4. Metellini, etc. Diximus alibi Metellinum, vulgo Medellin nuncupari, nomenque a Caecilio Metello consule sumpsisse, uti Ambrosius Morales lib. VIII cap. 18 et lib. IX cap. 32 auctor est, et quod olim Colonia Metellinensis dicebatur. Sancti vero Euse- bii Palatini, et sociorum novem celebratur passio in Romano Martyrologio 5 Martii die, ubi sic dicitur : Eodem die passio sanctorum Eusebii Palatini et alio- rum novem martyrum;
passages.english: 4. Of Metellinum, etc. We have said elsewhere that Metellinum is commonly called Medellín, and that it took its name from the consul Caecilius Metellus, as Ambrosio de Morales states in book VIII, chapter 18 and book IX, chapter 32, and that it was formerly called Colonia Metellinensis. The passion of Saint Eusebius Palatinus and his nine companions is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 5 March, where it is said thus: "On the same day, the passion of the saints Eusebius Palatinus and nine other martyrs;"

passages.original: A. C. 141. — Hoc tempore, etc. Idipsum de Galeno scripsit Hieronymus in Chronico Eusebii, hoc anno, et Isidorus in suo. Agant de ejus gestis medici, quorum princeps est.
passages.english: A.D. 141. — At this time, etc. Jerome wrote this very thing about Galen in the Chronicle of Eusebius, under this year, and Isidore in his own. Let the physicians, of whom he is the chief, deal with his deeds.

passages.original: A. C. 166. — Vologesus, etc. Haec quoque habet idem Eusebius anno 166. Orosius vastasse inquit Armeniam, Cappadociam, Syriamque lib. VII, cap. 17. Contra Vologesum, bellum Parthicum destruc- tum est, de quo multa Dio in Antonino, Misus pri- mum Severianus dux Romanorum militum, gentes cum vita, telo confossus amisit;
passages.english: A.D. 166. — Vologesus, etc. The same Eusebius also has this under the year 166. Orosius says, in book VII, chapter 17, that he laid waste Armenia, Cappadocia and Syria. Against Vologesus the Parthian war was waged, about which Dio says much in [his life of] Antoninus: Severianus, first sent as commander of the Roman soldiers, lost his forces together with his life, pierced by a weapon;
passages.notes: "destructum" (destroyed) seems corrupt; probably "instructum" or "gestum" (waged). "Misus" read as Missus. "gentes" probably for the army/troops he led.

passages.original: A. C. 167. — 1. Seleucia, etc. Adest in promon- torio Syriae Antiochenas Seleucia olim a Seleuco Ni- canore condita, teste Josepho lib. XVIII Antiq. cap. 16, quam S. Paulus peragrasse Lucas narrat Act. XIII, hodie Soldino dicta. Hanc Vologesus Parthorum rex cum cepisset, et circumjacentes provincias depopu- lasset, toti Syriae formidini erat. Verum a Romano exercitu iterum bello capta duce L. Caesare, cum trecentis millibus hominum, quod etiam cum Dextro narrat Eusebius hoc ipso anno : Orosius quadraginta millia capta refert.
passages.english: A.D. 167. — 1. Seleucia, etc. On a promontory of Antiochene Syria stands Seleucia, once founded by Seleucus Nicanor, as Josephus witnesses in book XVIII of the Antiquities, chapter 16, which Luke relates in Acts 13 that Saint Paul passed through; today it is called Soldino. When Vologesus, king of the Parthians, had taken it and ravaged the surrounding provinces, he was a terror to all Syria. But it was taken in war again by the Roman army under the command of Lucius Caesar, with three hundred thousand men, which Eusebius also relates, together with Dexter, in this very year; Orosius reports that forty thousand were captured.
passages.notes: "Antiochenas" read as Antiochenae. "with three hundred thousand men" probably refers to the number captured, contrasted with Orosius' forty thousand.

passages.original: A. C. 170. — 1. Persecutione, etc. Idem Eusebius in Chronico sic ait : Anno Domini 170 persecutione orta in Asia, Polycarpus et Pionius fecere martyrium, quorum scriptae quoque passiones feruntur. Fuit haec a M. Aurelio excitata persecutio, quarta in ordine, si primam sub Nerone, secundam sub Domitiano, et tertiam sub Trajano fuisse dicamus, cum Dex- lero, ad ann.
passages.english: A.D. 170. — 1. A persecution, etc. The same Eusebius in his Chronicle says thus: "In the year of the Lord 170, when a persecution arose in Asia, Polycarp and Pionius suffered martyrdom, and accounts of their passions are also said to have been written." This persecution was stirred up by Marcus Aurelius, the fourth in order, if we say that the first was under Nero, the second under Domitian and the third under Trajan, with Dexter, at the year
passages.notes: "Dexlero" read as Dextero. The sentence continues in the following text (year 86).

passages.original: Cardinalis Ba- ronius in eam sententiam inclinat, ut usque ad an- num 175 non sit assumptus. Aliis placet, assumptum quidem anno 163, occisum autem anno 171; quod sequitur Onuphrius, Morales et Tempesta. Sunt qui ad annum 169 ejus assumptionem referant. Eusebius vero hoc anno 171 putat electum; ait enim in Chro- nico anno 171 : Sother Romanae Ecclesiae episco- patum suscepit annos 14. Inter tantam opinionum varietatem ea dexteritate Dexter usus est, ut solum diceret anno 171 Sotherem rexisse Ecclesiam, in quo plures conveniunt;
passages.english: Cardinal Baronius inclines to the view that he was not raised [to the office] until the year 175. Others hold that he was indeed raised in 163 but killed in 171; this is followed by Onofrio [Panvinio], Morales and Tempesta. There are those who assign his accession to the year 169. Eusebius, however, thinks he was elected in this year 171; for he says in the Chronicle under 171: "Soter took up the episcopate of the Roman Church for 14 years." Amid such variety of opinions Dexter acted with such dexterity that he said only that Soter was governing the Church in 171, on which most agree;
passages.notes: Wordplay on Dexter/dexteritas in the Latin.

passages.original: 2. Dionysius, etc. Eusebius in Chronico hoc anno sic Jiahei, Dionysius episcopus Corinthiorum clarus habetur : agitque de ejus actis et scriptis lib. IV His- tor. cap. 22. Hieronymus vero ejusdem cum laude meminit tum epist. 84 citata, tura etiam lib. de Script. ubi haec leguntur capite 37 : Dionysius Co- rinthiorum Ecclesiae episcopus tantae eloquentia et in- dustriae fuit, ut non solum sua civitatis et provinciae populos, sed et aliarum urbium et provinciarum epi- scopos, epistolis erudiret;
passages.english: 2. Dionysius, etc. Eusebius in the Chronicle under this year says thus: "Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, is held in renown"; and he treats of his deeds and writings in book IV of the History, chapter 22. Jerome also mentions him with praise, both in the letter 84 cited above and in the book On Illustrious Men, where these words are read in chapter 37: "Dionysius, bishop of the Church of the Corinthians, was of such eloquence and industry that he instructed by letters not only the people of his own city and province but also the bishops of other cities and provinces;
passages.notes: "Jiahei" read as habet; "tura" as tum; "eloquentia", "sua" as eloquentiae, suae.

passages.original: 3. Smyrna, etc. Haec quoque ex Chronico Eusebii mutuata sunt, ubi ait hoc ipso anno. Smyrna urbs Asiae terraemotu ruit; ad cujus reparationem decennalis tributorum immunitas data est.
passages.english: 3. Smyrna, etc. This too is borrowed from the Chronicle of Eusebius, where he says under this very year: "Smyrna, a city of Asia, collapsed in an earthquake; for its rebuilding an exemption from taxes for ten years was granted."

passages.original: Ac tan- dem in prologo 5 : Traductis diligentissime omnibus haereticis in quatuor libris, qui sunt tibi ante hunc a nobis editi, et doctrinis illorum manifestatis in hoc li- broV, ex reliquis doctrinis Domini nostri, et ex apo- stolicis Epistolis conabimur ostensiones facere, quem- admodum postulasti a nobis, obedientibus tuo prae- cepto, etc. In quibus obiter contemplari placet, quanti apud Irenaeum Turibus noster habebatur, cujus praecepto obedientiam se praestare profitetur. Commendat quoque eruditionem ejus et sapientiam, id quod in praefatione ad I librum Irenaeus eidem scribit : Ea quae tibi cum dilectione scripta sunt, cum dilectione percipies, et ipse augeas ea penes te, ut ma- gis idoneus, quam nos.
passages.english: And finally, in the prologue to [book] 5: "Having most diligently exposed all the heretics in the four books which we published for you before this one, and having made their doctrines manifest, in this fifth book we shall try to make demonstrations from the remaining teachings of our Lord and from the apostolic Epistles, as you asked of us, in obedience to your command," etc. In these words it is worth observing in passing how highly our Turibus was regarded by Irenaeus, since he declares that he is rendering obedience to his command. He also commends his learning and wisdom, as Irenaeus writes to the same man in the preface to book I: "What has been written to you with love, you will receive with love, and you yourself will enlarge upon it in your own mind, as being more capable than we are."
passages.notes: "libroV" read as "libro V" (fifth book). The addressee is identified by the commentator as "Turibus"; the identification is his own.

passages.original: In tanta prorupisse scelera Commodum scribit Lam- pridius in ejus Vita, ut publico populi clamore ap- pellatus fuerit, Nerone crudelior, et Domitiano im- purior. Sed tandem scelerum suorum meritas luit poenas in domo Vestiliani strangulatus : sic enim scribit Eusebius in Chronico hoc ipso anno : Com- modus, inquit, strangulatur in domo Vestiliani. Deerat haec olausula in Dextro Caesaraugustae excuso, sed error typographi in pagina correctionum ejusdem impressionis notatus est.
passages.english: Lampridius writes in his Life of Commodus that he broke out into such great crimes that he was called by the public outcry of the people "more cruel than Nero and more impure than Domitian." But at last he paid the deserved penalty for his crimes, strangled in the house of Vestilianus; for so Eusebius writes in his Chronicle under this very year: "Commodus," he says, "is strangled in the house of Vestilianus." This clause was missing in the Dexter printed at Zaragoza, but the printer's error was noted on the page of corrections of that same printing.
passages.notes: "olausula" read as "clausula".

passages.original: 5. Severus, etc. AElio Pertinaci Didius Salvius Ju- lianus successit, qui menses fere septem imperii rexit habenas, juxta Orosium lib. VII, cap. 16. His diebus arripuerant simul, sciderant potius Romanum imperium Pescenninus Niger in Syria, et Albinus in Britannia; sed tandem Albinus Severo cessit, qui ob memoriam AElii vocari quoque voluit Pertinax auc- tore Spartiano, uti fornix triumphalis Romae ad ra- dices Capitolii eum nuncupat. Coepit imperare anno 196 ut Eusebius in Chronico auctor est.
passages.english: 5. Severus, etc. Didius Salvius Julianus succeeded Aelius Pertinax, and held the reins of empire for about seven months, according to Orosius, book VII, chapter 16. In these days Pescennius Niger in Syria and Albinus in Britain had at the same time seized, or rather torn apart, the Roman empire; but at last Albinus gave way to Severus, who in memory of Aelius wished also to be called Pertinax, on the authority of Spartianus, just as the triumphal arch at Rome at the foot of the Capitol names him. He began to reign in the year 196, as Eusebius in his Chronicle states.
passages.notes: "Pescenninus" taken as Pescennius.

passages.original: Corruptis- sime in Caesaraugustae excuso Dextro pro voce et Panthaenus, Espannensius legebatur : cum tamen omnino Panthaenus legendum sit, qui Clementis Alexandrini in litterarum sacrarum interpretatione magister fuit. Eusebius in Chronice sic de utroque scribit, anno 197 : Clemens Alexandrinae Ecclesiae pre- sbyter, et Panthaenus stoicus philosophus in disputa- tione dogmatis nostri disertissimi habentur. Praepo- nitur Panthaeno Clemens, discipulus magistro, for- san propter scriptorum majorem evidentiam : alias autem Panthaenus sanctorum Catalogo ascriptus est, die 7 Julii in Martyrologio Romano sub haec verba : Alexandriae natatis S.
passages.english: In the Dexter printed at Zaragoza, most corruptly, "Espannensius" was read in place of the words "and Pantaenus"; yet "Pantaenus" must certainly be read, who was the teacher of Clement of Alexandria in the interpretation of sacred letters. Eusebius in his Chronicle writes thus of both, under the year 197: "Clement, presbyter of the Church of Alexandria, and Pantaenus, the Stoic philosopher, are regarded as most eloquent in the discussion of our doctrine." Clement is placed before Pantaenus, the disciple before the master, perhaps because of the greater prominence of his writings; but Pantaenus, for his part, is enrolled in the Catalogue of the saints, on 7 July in the Roman Martyrology, in these words: "At Alexandria, the feast of St.
passages.notes: "Chronice" read as "Chronico"; "natatis" read as "natalis" (feast day).

passages.original: A. C. 198. — Polycrates, etc. Corrupte impressus Dexter habebat Polycarpus. Eusebius in Chronico hoc anno sic ait : Polycrates, et Bachylus Asianae pro- vinciae episcopi insignes habentur. D. Hieronymus de Script.
