Eccles. cap. 54 : Bachylus, ait : Corinthi epi- scopus, sub eodem quoque Severo principe clarus habi- tus, de Pascha, ex omnium, qui in Achia erant episco- porum persona, plenum eruditionis librum conscripsit.
passages.english: A.D. 198. — Polycrates, etc. The printed Dexter corruptly had "Polycarp". Eusebius in his Chronicle under this year says thus: "Polycrates and Bacchylus, bishops of the province of Asia, are regarded as distinguished." St Jerome, On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 54, says: "Bacchylus, bishop of Corinth, also held in renown under the same emperor Severus, wrote a book full of learning on Easter, in the name of all the bishops who were in Achaea."
passages.notes: "Achia" read as "Achaia". Eusebius makes Bacchylus a bishop of Asia, Jerome of Corinth; the discrepancy is in the source.

passages.original: — Persecutio, etc. Idem habet hoc anno Eusebius in Chronico, ubi inquit : Persecutione in Christianos facta, Leonides Origenis pater gloriosa martyrii morte transfertur. In lib. vero VI Hist. cap. 2 et 3 refert Origenem 17 annorum adolescentem misisse Leonidi patri in carcerem epistolam in haec verba : Obfirma te, Pater, martyrium fortiter sustine, nec aliud quidquam nostra causa molire. Timebat si- quidem ne in gratiam uxoris et filiorum septem, quos relinquebat pauperes et orphanos, mortem per- fidia redimeret.
passages.english: — Persecution, etc. Eusebius has the same under this year in his Chronicle, where he says: "When a persecution was made against the Christians, Leonides, father of Origen, passed over by the glorious death of martyrdom." And in book VI of the History, chapters 2 and 3, he relates that Origen, a youth of seventeen, sent his father Leonides in prison a letter in these words: "Stand firm, Father, endure martyrdom bravely, and do not contrive anything else for our sake." For he feared that, for the sake of his wife and seven sons, whom he was leaving poor and orphaned, he might buy off death by betraying the faith.

passages.original: Iterum de ejus martyrio Eusebius lib. VI, cap. 11, Ni- cephorus lib. V, cap. 2, Hieronymus lib. de Script. in Origene, Suidas et alii. Fuit haec persecutio sub Se- vero quinta inter illas quas Ecclesia ah ethnicis passa est, ut Orosius fatetur lib. VII, cap. 17.
passages.english: Again, on his martyrdom, [see] Eusebius book VI, chapter 11, Nicephorus book V, chapter 2, Jerome in his book On Writers under Origen, the Suda, and others. This persecution under Severus was the fifth among those which the Church suffered from the pagans, as Orosius states in book VII, chapter 17.
passages.notes: "Suidas" is the traditional name for the author of the Suda lexicon.

passages.original: Ale- xandri episcopi, qui de Cappadocia ex propria civitate (id est Caesarea Cappadociae) ubi erat episcopus, san- ctorum locorum desiderio Hierosolymam veniens, cum Narcissus ejusdem urbis episcopus jam senex Ecclesiam regeret, divina revelatione ejus gubernacula suscepit : postmodum vero in persecutione Decii, cum longaevae aelatis veneranda canitie praefulgeret, ductus Caesaream (Palaestinae) et clausus in carcere, ob confessionem Christi martyrium complevit. Ejus res gestas narrat Eusebius lib. VI Hist. cap. 8 et 32, Niceph. lib. V, cap, 9 et 10, et Hieronymus de Scriptoribus Ec- cles. cap. 72, ubi de Epistolis ejus ad Antinoitas, ad Antiochenses, ad Origenem, et pro Origene, etc.
passages.english: of Bishop Alexander, who, coming from Cappadocia, from his own city (that is, Caesarea in Cappadocia), where he was bishop, to Jerusalem out of desire for the holy places, when Narcissus, bishop of that city, already an old man, was governing the Church, by divine revelation took up its government; afterwards, in the persecution of Decius, when he was shining with the venerable white hair of long age, he was led to Caesarea (in Palestine), shut up in prison, and completed his martyrdom for confessing Christ." His deeds are narrated by Eusebius, History book VI, chapters 8 and 32, Nicephorus book V, chapters 9 and 10, and Jerome, On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 72, where [he speaks] of his Letters to the Antinoites, to the Antiochenes, to Origen, and on behalf of Origen, etc.
passages.notes: Begins mid-quotation from the Roman Martyrology ("feast of Blessed Alexander").

passages.original: A. C. 208.—1. Clodio Albino, etc. Consonat hoc anno Eusebius in Chronico, sic inquiens : C. Albino qui se in Gallia Caesarem fecerat apud Lugdunum interfecto, Severus in Britannos bellum transfert, ubi ut receptas provincias ab incursione Barbarica faceret securiores, vallum per 132 millia passuum a mari ad mare duxit.
passages.english: A.D. 208. — 1. Clodius Albinus, etc. Eusebius agrees under this year in his Chronicle, saying thus: "When C. Albinus, who had made himself Caesar in Gaul, was killed at Lyon, Severus transferred the war to the Britons, where, to make the recovered provinces more secure from barbarian incursion, he drew a rampart for 132 miles from sea to sea."

passages.original: A. C. 218. —Antoninus, etc. Sic idem Eusebius anno praesenti : Antoninus tam impatiens libidinis fuit, ut novercam suam Juliam uxorem duxerit. Spartianus ejus scelera referens : Hic tamen, inquit, omnium dirissimus, et (ut uno complectar verbo) parricida, et incestus; patris, ac fratris, ac matris inimicus. Con- sentit Orosius lib. VII, c. 18.
passages.english: A.D. 218. — Antoninus, etc. So the same Eusebius under the present year: "Antoninus was so unable to control his lust that he married his stepmother Julia." Spartianus, relating his crimes, says: "Yet he was the most dreadful of all, and (to sum it up in one word) a parricide and incestuous, an enemy of his father, his brother, and his mother." Orosius agrees, book VII, chapter 18.
passages.notes: Antoninus here is Caracalla.

passages.original: A. C. 219. —1. Antoninus occiditur, etc. Carrae civitas fuit Mesopotamiae trans Edessam, Crassi et Romani exercitus olim inibi caesi, cruore nobilis, cujus meminit Plinius lib. V, c. 24, et Lucanus cum dixit : Assyrias Latio maculavit sanguine Carras : An- tonini etiam Caracallae nece insigniores redditae sunt. Hic enim, ut Rufus consularis scribit, intra Euphratem apud civitatem Edessam periit, cum le- vandae vesicae gratia ex equo descendisset.
passages.english: A.D. 219. — 1. Antoninus is killed, etc. Carrhae was a city of Mesopotamia beyond Edessa, famous for bloodshed, since Crassus and a Roman army were once slaughtered there. Pliny mentions it in book V, chapter 24, and Lucan, when he said: "Carrhae, which stained Assyria with Latin blood." It was made more notable still by the killing of Antoninus Caracalla. For he, as the consular Rufus writes, perished on this side of the Euphrates near the city of Edessa, when he had dismounted from his horse to relieve his bladder.
passages.notes: Lucan's line (Pharsalia 1.105) is usually read as "Assyrias Latio maculavit sanguine Carras," i.e. "[the death of Crassus] stained Assyrian Carrhae with Latin blood"; the translation of the quoted line follows that sense loosely. "Rufus consularis" is presumably Sextus Rufus (Festus).

passages.original: A. C. 220. — 1. Circensibus, etc. Habet ipsissima verba Eusebius seu Hieronymus in Chronico hoc ipso anno. Erant Vulcanalia festa Vulcano dicata, Augusti mense fieri solita, ut ex Columella colligi- tur, lib. XI de Re rustica, cap. 3. Circenses vero ludi, certaminis currulis genus, in honorem consiliorum Dei primum instituti; qua de re videndus est Gellius lib. III, c. 10.
passages.english: A.D. 220. — 1. At the Circensian games, etc. Eusebius, or Jerome, in the Chronicle has these very words in this same year. The Vulcanalia were a festival dedicated to Vulcan, usually held in the month of August, as can be gathered from Columella, On Agriculture, book XI, chapter 3. The Circensian games, a kind of chariot contest, were first instituted in honour of the god of counsels; on this matter Gellius, book III, chapter 10, should be consulted.
passages.notes: "consiliorum Dei" probably refers to Consus, god of counsels, to whom the Consualia (origin of the Circus games) were dedicated.

passages.original: 2. Hippone, etc. Nobilis Hipponensis in Carpetani? urbis mentio habetur apud Livium, lib. XXXIX, in haec verba : Eodem anno in Hispania, praetores C. Calpur- nius et L. Quinctius, cum primo vere ex hibernis co- pias eductas in Beturia junxissent; in Carpetaniam, ubi hostium castra erant, progressi sunt. Haud procul Hippone et Toleto urbibus, inter pabulatores pugna orta est. Exstat quoque memoria ejus in Ptolomaei Geographia, ubi tamen corrupte legitur Hispinon, et corruptius Ispinum, prope Liboram et Toletum.
passages.english: 2. At Hippo, etc. Mention of the noble [city of] Hippo in Carpetania is found in Livy, book XXXIX, in these words: "In the same year in Spain the praetors C. Calpurnius and L. Quinctius, having led their forces out of winter quarters at the beginning of spring and joined them in Baeturia, advanced into Carpetania, where the enemy's camp was. Not far from the cities of Hippo and Toletum a battle arose between foragers." There is also a record of it in Ptolemy's Geography, where however it is read corruptly as Hispinon, and more corruptly as Ispinum, near Libora and Toletum.
passages.notes: "Carpetani?" in the text is a garbled form, evidently for Carpetaniae.

passages.original: De Beryllo autem haec scribit cap. 70 : Beryllus Arabiae Bostrenus episcopus, cum aliquanto tempore gloriose rexisset Ecclesiam, ad extremum lapsus in haeresim, quae Christum ante incarnationem negat; ab Origene correptus scripsit varia opuscula, et maxime epistolas, in quibus Origeni gratias egit, etc. Claruit sub Alexandro Mammeae filio, et Maximino, et Gor- diano, qui ei in imperium successerunt. De eisdem tribus Scriptoribus agit hoc anno Eusebius in Chro- nico, iisdem fere verbis atque Dexter.
passages.english: About Beryllus he writes this in chapter 70: "Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, after he had governed the Church gloriously for some time, at last fell into the heresy which denies [that] Christ [existed] before the incarnation; corrected by Origen, he wrote various short works, and especially letters, in which he thanked Origen," etc. He flourished under Alexander, son of Mammaea, and under Maximinus and Gordian, who succeeded him in the empire. Eusebius treats these same three writers in this year in the Chronicle, in almost the same words as Dexter.

passages.original: Collegia instituit, in quibus Mammenae puellae, et Mammeani pueri in memoriam matris alerentur, ut Lampridius scribit anno Urbis 984; aedificavit etiam Mammeum pontem super Anienem fluvium, qui hodieque Ponte Mammolo vocatur, tertio ab Urbe lapide : de quo loquitur Cicero lib. de claris Oratoribus. Fuisse vero Mammeam Christianam testatur Orosius lib. VII, cap. 18, inquiens : Cujus mater Mammea Christiana Origenem presbyterum audire curavit, quod itidem innuere videtur Hieronymus infra citandus.
passages.english: He founded colleges in which Mammaean girls and Mammaean boys were to be maintained in memory of his mother, as Lampridius writes, in the year of the City 984. He also built the Mammaean bridge over the river Anio, which is still called Ponte Mammolo today, at the third milestone from the City; Cicero speaks of it in his book On Famous Orators. That Mammaea was a Christian is attested by Orosius, book VII, chapter 18, saying: "whose mother Mammaea, a Christian, took care to hear the presbyter Origen"; Jerome, to be cited below, also seems to hint at the same.
passages.notes: The claim that Cicero's Brutus mentions this bridge is anachronistic, as stated by the author; translated as written.

passages.original: A. C. 235. — Origenes, etc. Meminit ejusdem iti- neris Origenis Eusebius hoc anno in Chron. et Hie- ronymus lib. de Script., c. 64 : Cum jam, inquit, mediae esset aetatis Origenes, et propter Ecclesias Achaiae quae pluribus haeresibus vexabantur, sub testi- monio Ecclesiasticae epistolae, Athenas per Palaestinam pergeret, a Theoclisto et Alexandro Caesareae et Hiero- solymorum episcopis presbyter ordinatus, etc.
passages.english: A.D. 235. — Origen, etc. Eusebius mentions this same journey of Origen in this year in the Chronicle, and Jerome in the book On Illustrious Men, chapter 64: "When Origen was already of middle age," he says, "and was travelling through Palestine to Athens on account of the churches of Achaea, which were troubled by many heresies, under the authority of an ecclesiastical letter, he was ordained presbyter by Theoctistus and Alexander, bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem," etc.
passages.notes: "Theoclisto" is read as Theoctistus.

passages.original: A. C. 238. — Maximinus, etc. Quod hic dicitur miles gregarius, Eusebius latinitate donatus a S. Hieronymo, ex corpore militari, exponit, sic enim ait : Maximinus primus ex corpore militari sine Sena- tus auctoritate, ab exercitu imperator electus est. Id vero ex Lampridio et aliis satis constat.
passages.english: A.D. 238. — Maximinus, etc. What is called here "a common soldier" Eusebius, as rendered into Latin by St Jerome, expresses as "from the military body"; for he says thus: "Maximinus was the first from the military body to be chosen emperor by the army without the authority of the Senate." This is well established from Lampridius and others.

passages.original: A. C. 240. — Maximinus a Pupieno, etc. Ita quo- que scribit Eusebius anno praesenti, a quo multa eorum, quae ad imperatorum historiam pertinent, Dexter mutuo accepisse conspicitur. Ducebat Pupie- nus antiquam originem a Gadibus Hispaniae, ut ex vetustioribus notavit Morales ad annum Christi 239.
passages.english: A.D. 240. — Maximinus by Pupienus, etc. Eusebius also writes thus in the present year; Dexter is seen to have borrowed from him many of the things that pertain to the history of the emperors. Pupienus traced his ancient origin from Gades in Spain, as Morales noted from older [authors] at the year of Christ 239.

passages.original: A. C. 241. —Gordianus, etc. Consonant his, quae scribunt Julius Capitolinus, Paulus Orosius lib. VII, cap. 19, et Eutropius item lib. VII. Eusebius quoque in Chronico, cujus sunt illa verba : Gordiano Ro- mam ingresso Pupienus, et Galbinus (Alias Balbinus) qui imperium arripuerant, in palatio occisi sunt.
passages.english: A.D. 241. — Gordian, etc. This agrees with what Julius Capitolinus writes, as do Paulus Orosius, book VII, chapter 19, and Eutropius likewise, book VII. So also Eusebius in the Chronicle, whose words these are: "When Gordian entered Rome, Pupienus and Galbinus (otherwise Balbinus), who had seized the empire, were killed in the palace."

passages.original: A. C. 243. — Gordianus, etc. Id etiam Eusebius testatur hoc ipso anno. Gordianus Saporem Persa- rum regem vicit, Syria expulit, Antiochiam recepit, Carras et Nisibim subegit; qua de re scribunt Oro- sius, Capitolinus et Eutropius superius citati.
passages.english: A.D. 243. — Gordian, etc. Eusebius too attests this in this same year. Gordian defeated Sapor, king of the Persians, drove him out of Syria, recovered Antioch, and subdued Carrhae and Nisibis; on this matter Orosius, Capitolinus and Eutropius, cited above, write.

passages.original: Caeterum natum fuisse hoc anno 253, inde deducitur, quod obiisse constat anno 21 impe- rii Constantii, videlicet Christi 358, ut Hieronymus in Chronico docet; cum Antonius quintum et cente- simum annum ageret; ipso Hieronymo auctore in lib. de Script. Eccles. in Antonio : et Athanasio magno in ejus vita.
passages.english: Moreover, that he was born in this year 253 is deduced from the fact that he is established to have died in the 21st year of the reign of Constantius, that is, [the year] of Christ 358, as Jerome teaches in the Chronicle, when Antony was in his hundred and fifth year, on the authority of Jerome himself in the book On Ecclesiastical Writers, under Antony, and of Athanasius the Great in his Life of him.

passages.original: eamque existimo, quam modo Belil- lam dicimus, cymbalo miraculose saepe pulsato ma- gnorum eventuum portento, celebrem : nam tam Belsinia quam Bellica, non longe a Turiasona a Ptolemaeo collocantur. Plinius Bellicam municipium Caesaraugustanae jurisdictionis asserit. Differt vero Dexter a Ptolomaeo, quod ille in Carpetania, hic ve- ro in Celliberia utramque urbem constituat. Qua in re Dextro assentiendum, utpote Hispano auctori de rebus Hispaniae scribenti.
passages.english: and I think it is the one we now call Belilla, famous for its bell, often miraculously rung as a portent of great events; for both Belsinia and Bellica are placed by Ptolemy not far from Turiasona. Pliny asserts that Bellica was a municipality of the jurisdiction of Caesaraugusta. But Dexter differs from Ptolemy in that the latter places both cities in Carpetania, the former in Celtiberia. In this matter one should agree with Dexter, as a Spanish author writing about the affairs of Spain.
passages.notes: 'Celliberia' read as Celtiberia. 'cymbalo' taken as bell (Belilla is famed for its miraculous bell, the 'campana de Velilla').

passages.original: De pestilentia his diebus in orbem grassante egere Orosius lib. VII, cap. 71, Nyssenus in oratione de Gregorio Thaumaturgo, Eu- sebius lib. VII, cap. 17, et in Chronico anno Domini 255, S. Pontius in Vita S. Cypriani : et ex ethnicis Eutropius in Gallo, et Volusiano. Scripsit ejus occa- sione librum de mortalitate S. Cyprianus, et Diony- sius Alexandrinus litteras de eadem re, quas Euse- bius affert, citato cap.
passages.english: On the plague raging through the world in these days, Orosius has treated in book VII, chapter 71, Gregory of Nyssa in the oration on Gregory Thaumaturgus, Eusebius in book VII, chapter 17, and in the Chronicle at the year of the Lord 255, St Pontius in the Life of St Cyprian; and among the pagans, Eutropius under Gallus and Volusianus. On its occasion St Cyprian wrote the book On Mortality, and Dionysius of Alexandria letters on the same matter, which Eusebius quotes in the chapter cited.
passages.notes: 'cap. 71' for Orosius book VII is probably an error (perhaps ch. 21).

passages.original: Eusebius in Chronico hoc ipso anno pene eisdem verbis : Valerianus, in- quit, in Christianos persecutione commota, statim a Sapore, Persarum rege, capitur, ibique servitute mi- serabili consenescit. Agunt de hoc mirabili Dei judi- cio Trebellius Pollio, Aurelius Victor, Eutropius, et Dionysius Alexandrinus apud Eusebium lib. VII, cap. 9. Quinimmo Constantinus Magnus imperat, in oratione ad sanctum Coetum : Quia in, Valeriane, ait, eamdem crudelitatem in Dei famulos ostendens justum sanctumque Dei judicium ante oculos omnium statui- sti;
passages.english: Eusebius in the Chronicle, in this very year, in almost the same words: "Valerian," he says, "having stirred up a persecution against the Christians, was immediately captured by Shapur, king of the Persians, and there grew old in wretched slavery." Of this wonderful judgement of God Trebellius Pollio, Aurelius Victor, Eutropius, and Dionysius of Alexandria (in Eusebius book VII, chapter 9) treat. Indeed, Constantine the Great, in the Oration to the Holy Assembly, [says]: "You too, Valerian," he says, "showing the same cruelty toward the servants of God, set up the just and holy judgement of God before the eyes of all;
passages.notes: 'imperat' is probably a scanning error (perhaps for 'inquit' or similar); translated as introducing the quotation. 'Quia in' read as 'Tu quoque' / 'Tu etiam'-like sense.

passages.original: Dicta propterca videtur Ce- lerina ab L. Pompeio Celerino, cujus erat abneptis, sic dicto, ut credo, a perdomitis Celerinis. Fuisse vero Pompeiorum stirpem in Hispania illud convin- cit, quod Plinius de Sexto Pompeio narrat, quod nimirum cum Hispaniae citerioris princeps existens horreis suis ventilandis praesideret, correptus dolore podagrae, mersit in triticum sese super genua, leva- tusque siccatis pedibus mirabili modo, eo postea remedio usus est. Primus Pompeiorum qui in Hispa- niam trajecit fuit Q. Pompeius contra Numantinos missus, ab eisque superatus turpem et ignominiosam pacem fecit, ut refert Florus lib.
passages.english: She seems therefore to have been called Celerina after L. Pompeius Celerinus, whose great-great-granddaughter she was, he being so called, as I believe, from the subjugation of the Celerini. That a line of the Pompeii existed in Spain is proved by what Pliny relates of Sextus Pompeius: namely that, while he was a leading man of Hither Spain and was supervising the winnowing in his granaries, being seized by a pain of gout, he plunged himself into the wheat above the knees, and being relieved, his feet dried out in a wonderful way, he afterwards used that remedy. The first of the Pompeii who crossed into Spain was Q. Pompeius, sent against the Numantines, and, defeated by them, he made a base and ignominious peace, as Florus relates in book
passages.notes: 'propterca' read as 'propterea'. The book number of Florus runs into the following context ('II').

passages.original: Rescripsit ad interrogata Calydonio Cyprianus, et tametsi non exstet ipsum rescriptum, meminit tamen ejusdem Cyprianus ipse in epistola 20, in- quiens : Sed et quid mihi Calydonius collega pro in- tegritate fidei suae scripserit, quidve ego scripserim, utrumque ad vos legendum transmisi. Insuper cum Novatus schismaticus insurgeret in Ecclesiam, mis- sus fuit Calydonius ad montes contra ipsum, ut constat ex epist. Cypriani 38 : in epistola vero 39 continetur sententia quam adversus quosdam lapsos tulit, missa ad Herculanum et socios, videlicet : Abs- tinuimus communicatione Felicissimum, et Augendum, item Repostum de extorribus, et Irenem Rutilorum, et Paulam Sarcinatricem, quod ex annotatione mea scire debetis.
passages.english: Cyprian wrote back to Calydonius in answer to his questions, and although the reply itself does not survive, Cyprian himself nevertheless mentions it in letter 20, saying: "But both what my colleague Calydonius wrote to me for the integrity of his faith, and what I wrote, I have sent to you to read." Furthermore, when the schismatic Novatus rose up against the Church, Calydonius was sent to the mountains against him, as is clear from Cyprian's letter 38; and in letter 39 is contained the sentence which he passed against certain lapsed, sent to Herculanus and his companions, namely: "We have excluded from communion Felicissimus and Augendus, also Repostus of the exiles, and Irene of the Rutili, and Paula the seamstress, which you ought to know from my note."
passages.notes: 'ad montes' may be a misreading (Cyprian's letters mention sending agents, not 'mountains'); translated literally.

passages.original: Germani vero orienta- lior natio, prope Asiam facilem in ipsam Asiam, et in Italiam usque Ravennam transitum habebant. De eisdem cladibus lege Eusebium in Chronic. ad ann. 264, qui tamen ad annum 266 subdit : Germa- nis Hispanias tenentibus Tarracon expugnata est. Qua de re Orosius loco citato haec ait : Germani ulterio- res abrasa potiuntur Hispania; et post pauca : Exstant adhuc per diversas provincias in magnarum urbium ruinis parvae et pauperes aedes, signa miseriarum, et nominum indicia servantes; ex quibus nos quoque in Hispania Tarraconem nostram ad consolationem mi· seriae recentis ostendimus. De his iterum Dexter ad annum 424.
passages.english: The Germans, on the other hand, a more easterly nation, near Asia, had an easy passage into Asia itself and into Italy as far as Ravenna. On these same disasters read Eusebius in the Chronicle at the year 264, who nevertheless adds at the year 266: "While the Germans held the Spains, Tarraco was stormed." On this matter Orosius in the place cited says this: "The further Germans, Spain having been scraped bare, take possession of it"; and a little after: "There still exist through various provinces, in the ruins of great cities, small and poor dwellings, preserving signs of the miseries and traces of the names; among which we too in Spain point to our Tarraco, for consolation in recent misery." On these again Dexter at the year 424.

passages.original: A. C. 273. — 1. Quintillius, etc. Eusebius hoc anno sic ait : Quintillius Claudii frater a senatu Augustus appellatus, decimoscptimo Imperii sui die, Aquileiae occiditur. De eodem Trebellius in Claudio.
passages.english: Year of Christ 273. — 1. Quintillus, etc. Eusebius says thus in this year: "Quintillus, brother of Claudius, proclaimed Augustus by the senate, was killed at Aquileia on the seventeenth day of his reign." On the same, Trebellius in [the life of] Claudius.

passages.original: Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus Catechesi 6 auctor est, Manetem, a quo Manichaei dicti, sub Probo im- peratore coepisse impietatem disseminare. Idemque asserit S. Leo papa serm. 2 Pentecostes, et Cassio- dorus in Chronico, et Epiphanius haeresi 66. Dissen- tiunt Beda, qui, libro de sex aetatibus, sub Tacito coe- pisse affirmat, et Zonaras III par. Annal. qui sub Caro : sed vetustioribus assentimur.
passages.english: Cyril of Jerusalem in Catechesis 6 states that Mani, from whom the Manichaeans are named, began to spread his impiety under the emperor Probus. The same is asserted by Pope St Leo in the second sermon on Pentecost, by Cassiodorus in the Chronicle, and by Epiphanius in heresy 66. Dissenting are Bede, who in the book On the Six Ages affirms that he began under Tacitus, and Zonaras in part III of the Annals, [who says] under Carus; but we agree with the older [authorities].

passages.original: o martyr, etc.. unde subditur : Per te omnipotens Conditor ocius, durum quo premi- mur hoc jugum auferat, etc. Vernula enim est dimi- nutivum a verna, quod servum domi nostrae natum significat; uti apud Martialem lib. XIV videri potest, dum de Crepitacillo ait : Vernam vero servum significare testes sunt Plautus in Mil. et Amph., Tibullus lib. II elegia 1, Horatius lib. I Serm., Festus et Coel, cit., et, ut caeteros omittam, Paulus leg.
passages.english: O martyr, etc., whence it continues: "Through you may the almighty Creator swiftly remove this harsh yoke by which we are oppressed," etc. For vernula is a diminutive of verna, which means a slave born in our own house, as can be seen in Martial book XIV, where he says of the Rattle: That verna means a slave is attested by Plautus in the Miles and the Amphitruo, Tibullus book II elegy 1, Horace book I of the Satires, Festus and Caelius cited, and, to omit the rest, Paul in the law
passages.notes: The Martial quotation after 'ait' is missing from the text. 'Coel.' taken as Caelius (Rhodiginus?), uncertain.

passages.original: cum a consueta significatione penes quam perpetuo in hymnis ejus- dem gothici Breviarii accipitur, ad alios sensus dis- trahatur : idem significat quod vernaculus, quae vox nativum vel naturalem denotat; quo pacto vernacu- lam linguam dicimus, et saporem vernaculum, ut Cicero in Bruto, et crimen domesticum, ac vernaculum; Cicer, in Verr. 6, et putationem vernaculam, id est, regioni nostrae consuetam; Plin. lib. XVII qui etiam lib. XIV cap. 2 potissimam nobilitatem dixit, verna- culam Italiae.
passages.english: when it is drawn away to other senses from the customary meaning in which it is always taken in the hymns of the same Gothic Breviary: it means the same as *vernaculus*, a word which denotes native or natural; in which way we speak of a vernacular language, and a vernacular flavour, as Cicero [does] in the Brutus, and a domestic and vernacular crime (Cicero, Verrines 6), and vernacular pruning, that is, customary in our region (Pliny, book XVII), who also in book XIV, chapter 2, called the foremost nobility [of wines] vernacular to Italy.
passages.notes: The sentence begins mid-construction; the subject (the word *vernulus*) is in the preceding context. In the Pliny reference, 'nobility' probably refers to the excellence of wines or vines; this is inferred, not stated in the passage.

passages.original: Adhaerebat igitur tunc tem- poris lateri imperatoris. Deinde anno sequenti, sci- licet 317, Gallicano et Basso coss., orta contentione inter Arium et Alexandrum episcopum Alexandri- num, ad aures imperatoris causa perlata est, quo tempore (auctore Eusebio lib. II de Vita Constant. c. 63) exstincto Licinio imperii competitore, summa totius imperii ad ipsum devoluta, profectionem ad Orientem parabat. Eodemque anno Sardicae existens constitutionem edidit, misitque ad Octavianum eo mitem Hispaniae, Hosio Cordubensi dictante, man- dans, ut quicumque clarissimae dignitatis virginem ra- puerit, vel fines aliquos invaserit, vel in aliqua culpa seu crimine fuerit deprehensus, statim intra Provinciam in qua facinus perpetravit, publicis legibus subjugetur.
passages.english: So at that time he was at the emperor's side. Then in the following year, namely 317, in the consulship of Gallicanus and Bassus, when a dispute had arisen between Arius and Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, the case was brought to the emperor's ears. At that time (according to Eusebius, Life of Constantine book II, chapter 63), Licinius, his rival for the empire, having been eliminated and the supreme power over the whole empire having passed to him, he was preparing a journey to the East. In the same year, while at Sardica, he issued a constitution, at the dictation of Hosius of Córdoba, and sent it to Octavianus, count of Spain, ordering that whoever of senatorial (*clarissimus*) rank abducted a virgin, or seized any lands, or was caught in any fault or crime, should at once be subjected to the public laws within the province in which he committed the deed.
passages.notes: 'eo mitem' is evidently a scanning error for 'comitem' (count). The Latin 'clarissimae dignitatis' could be read with 'virginem', but the following context (on nobles' immunity) shows it refers to the offender.

passages.original: Ne videlicet praetextu suae immunitatis, qua nobiles, nisi ab imperatoribus puniri non poterant, insolen- tes redderentur. Quae constitutio, ut ex ipsa liquet, C. Theod. lib. I de Accus., ad Cordubenses specialius directa fuit, quos nimirum Hosius reformare satage- bat. Ut autem Arii tumultus sedarentur, misit impe- rator eumdem Hosium Alexandriam, qui ejus rei gratia synodum Alexandrinam congregavit, et ut quaestionem de ratione celebrandi Paschatis, iis die- bus in utraque Ecclesia, acriter agitatam decideret.
passages.english: That is, lest under pretext of their immunity, by which nobles could not be punished except by the emperors, they should become insolent. This constitution, as is clear from the text itself (Theodosian Code, Book I, On Accusations), was directed more specially to the people of Córdoba, whom Hosius was striving to reform. And so that the disturbances of Arius might be calmed, the emperor sent the same Hosius to Alexandria, who for that purpose convened the synod of Alexandria, and also to settle the question of the manner of celebrating Easter, then fiercely debated in both Churches.

passages.original: 4° Camerinus Tuccitanus. Tucci nobilis Hispaniae Baeticae urbs, olim Romanorum colonia, et episco- palis sedes fuit, alio nomine Augustagemella dicta, hodie Martos, non longe ab urbe Giennensi, ut probat Ambrosius Morales lib. IX cap. 32. Sedes haec ad Hispalensem metropolim pertinebat, sicut et Corduba.
passages.english: 4. Camerinus of Tucci. Tucci was a noble city of Baetic Spain, once a Roman colony and an episcopal see, called by another name Augusta Gemella, today Martos, not far from the city of Jaén, as Ambrosio de Morales proves in book IX, chapter 32. This see belonged to the metropolitan [see] of Seville, as did Córdoba too.

passages.original: 10. Galerius Maxim, etc. Hoc etiam pluribus verbis apud Eusebium habes citato loco et anno. Eadem refert Orosius citato cap. 25.
passages.english: 10. Galerius Maximianus, etc. You also have this in more words in Eusebius, at the place and year cited. Orosius reports the same things in the cited chapter 25.

passages.original: 13. L. Valerius, etc. Berosus Chaldaeus Babylonia oriundus 300 annis ante Christi Domini nativitatem historiam suam scripsit, teste Josepho lib. I Anti- quit. Jud. et contra Appionem Gramm. quibus locis auctor est, ipsum omnem Chaldaicam deflorasse historiam, et veluti publicae fidei notarium omnem antiquitatem transcripsisse, ac inter alia diluvii ma- gui meminisse, nominasseque Noam et filios ejus.
passages.english: 13. L. Valerius, etc. Berosus the Chaldean, a native of Babylonia, wrote his history 300 years before the birth of Christ the Lord, as Josephus testifies in Jewish Antiquities book I and in Against Apion the Grammarian; in which places he states that he culled the whole of Chaldean history and, like a notary of public trust, transcribed all antiquity, and among other things made mention of the great flood and named Noah and his sons.
passages.notes: 'magui' read as 'magni'.

passages.original: Sane hoc prae- misit, ut sub hac sententia simul complecteretur quotquot in persecutione Diocletiana, in Hispaniis martyrium perpessi sunt, praesertim usque ad an- num 306, quo vehementius persecutio saevit, ut etiam habet Eusebius in Chronico.
passages.english: Indeed he put this first so as to include under this statement at once all those who suffered martyrdom in the Spains in the Diocletianic persecution, especially up to the year 306, in which the persecution raged more violently, as Eusebius also has in his Chronicle.

passages.original: Difficilius nonnullis visum est quod de S. Spiridione asseritur, nimirum episcopum fuisse To- letanum, et egregie Oreti pro Christi nomine pu- gnasse. Nam Spiridion in Cypro episcopus fuit, ut Rufinus lib. I, cap. 5 Sozomenus lib. I cap. 11, So- crates lib. I cap. 8, et ejus acta apud Surium a Tri- phillo ejus discipulo edita manifestant. Caeterum si quis vellet duos Spiridiones asserere, Cyprium alte- rum, alterum Toletanum, non posset falsitatis ma- nifeste redargui.
passages.english: What is asserted of St Spiridion has seemed rather difficult to some, namely that he was bishop of Toledo and fought splendidly at Oretum for the name of Christ. For Spiridion was bishop in Cyprus, as Rufinus book I, chapter 5, Sozomen book I, chapter 11, Socrates book I, chapter 8, and his acts in Surius, published by Triphyllius his disciple, make clear. However, if anyone wished to assert two Spiridions, one Cypriot and the other of Toledo, he could not be plainly convicted of falsehood.

passages.original: 41. Antecedenti, etc. Id refert Eusebius in Chro- nico ad annum Christi 305, ubi de hoc triumpho agit. Consule quae de Narseo et ejus cum Maximiano conflictibus scribit inter alios Orosius lib. VII cap. 25.
passages.english: 41. Antecedenti, etc. Eusebius reports this in the Chronicle at the year of Christ 305, where he deals with this triumph. Consult what Orosius, among others, writes about Narses and his conflicts with Maximian, book VII, chapter 25.
passages.notes: 'Antecedenti' is the lemma quoted from the chronicle; left untranslated.

passages.original: 26 et 29, et Constantinus Magnus in oratione quam habuit ad Patres in Nicaena synodo congregatos, et Acta S. Menae et sociorum, ubi as- seruntur purpuram deposuisse eo dolore conster- nati, quod non potuissent contra Christi fideles praevalere. Eusebius affirmat, Diocletianum Nicome- diae, Maximianum vero Mediolani imperio ac pur- pura se abdicasse. Caeterum semel indicia toto orbe in Christianos persecutio nihilominus perseve- ravit.
passages.english: 26 and 29, and Constantine the Great in the oration he delivered to the Fathers gathered at the synod of Nicaea, and the Acts of St Menas and companions, where they are said to have laid down the purple, overwhelmed by grief that they had not been able to prevail against Christ's faithful. Eusebius states that Diocletian abdicated the empire and the purple at Nicomedia, and Maximian at Milan. However, the persecution, once proclaimed against the Christians throughout the world, nevertheless continued.
passages.notes: Begins mid-citation (Eusebius, Eccl. Hist. VIII, chapters 26 and 29). 'indicia' read as 'indicta' (proclaimed).

passages.original: Isidori reperitur : Domine Jesu Christe, qui sic Virginem matrem hono- rificasti, quousque conceptionis ejus gratia, eam co- ram te suffragatricem incomparabilem invenimus, etc. Invenimus certe eam suffragatricem, dum Dei Ver- bum concepit, non vero dum concepta est. Insuper in idem recidit, si verum est quod ex Paulo Orosio Dextri coaevo referunt Mauricius de Villa probata in Corona, Mariana Serm. 16 et Bernardinus Busti Serm. 8 de Concept. par. 3 scripsisse videlicet in quadam epistola ad sanctam Eustochium Hieronymi discipulam : Coram Deo novi, et in veritate comperi, quod nulla mulier in partu periclitatur, super quam devote Mariae gratia imploratur, et dies conceptionis ejus celebratur : quando nimirum sine pudore conce- pit, ut sine dolore pareret.
passages.english: of Isidore is found: 'Lord Jesus Christ, who so honoured the Virgin Mother that, by the grace of her conception, we find her before you an incomparable intercessor,' etc. We find her an intercessor, certainly, when she conceived the Word of God, not when she was conceived. Moreover, it comes to the same thing, if it is true what Mauricio de Villaprobata in the Corona Mariana, sermon 16, and Bernardino de Busti, sermon 8 On the Conception, part 3, report from Paulus Orosius, a contemporary of Dexter, namely that he wrote in a certain letter to St Eustochium, disciple of Jerome: 'I know before God, and have found in truth, that no woman is endangered in childbirth over whom the grace of Mary is devoutly implored and the day of her conception is celebrated': that is, when she conceived without shame, so that she might give birth without pain.
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence ('in the Breviary of St Isidore'). 'Mariana' taken as part of the title 'Corona Mariana' rather than as the author Mariana.

passages.original: Ut igitur ad Dextrum regrediamur, hoc certum deinceps apud omnes sit, nihil aliud voluisse hoc loco, quam Hispanos ab apostolo suo Jacobo festum Annuntiationis angelicae recepisse. Cui etiam conso- nat, quod apud Augustinum, Rufinum et alios legi- mus, cum apostoli Symbolum ederent per partes, et Petrus praemisisset : Credo in Deum Patrem om- nipotentem, factorem coeli et terroe; et Andreas : Et in Jesum Christum Filium ejus unicum, Dominum nostrum : Jacobum nostrum tertio loco illam parti- culam subjunxisse : Et conceptus est de Spiritu sancto, natus ex Maria Virgine : nimirum innuit, hoc mysterium sibi prae aliis dulcius semper fuisse, unde et in ejus honorem primum templum Caesar- augustae erigi curavit, ut egregie M.
passages.english: To return, then, to Dexter: let this henceforth be certain among all, that in this place he meant nothing other than that the Spaniards received the feast of the angelic Annunciation from their apostle James. With this also agrees what we read in Augustine, Rufinus and others: that when the apostles composed the Creed part by part, and Peter had put first, "I believe in God the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth"; and Andrew, "And in Jesus Christ his only Son, our Lord"; our James in the third place added that clause, "And was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary". By this, surely, he indicates that this mystery was always sweeter to him than others; and hence he also had the first church built in its honour at Zaragoza, as M.
passages.notes: "M." begins the name Maximus, continued in the following context (Marcus Maximus, the hymn's supposed author).

passages.original: Ispali etc. Longe alia urbs haec est a cele- berrima illa Hispali Baeticae provinciae : hujus vero situm Orthelius ignorasse se fatetur in charta ve- teris Hispaniae, sed Dexter illum designat. Sane Plinius Ispalensium populorum Tarraconensis Hi- spaniae meminit lib. III, qui longe positi ab Hispali Baeticae debent esse. De sanctis martyribus inibi passis agit Romanum Martyrologium ad 10 Septembr. his verbis : Item sanctorum martyrum Apellii, Lucoe, et Clementis.
passages.english: "Ispalis" etc. This city is quite different from that most famous Hispalis of the province of Baetica. Ortelius confesses in his map of ancient Spain that he did not know its site, but Dexter indicates it. Pliny, indeed, in Book III mentions the Ispalensian peoples of Tarraconensian Spain, who must have been situated far from Hispalis of Baetica. The Roman Martyrology treats of the holy martyrs who suffered there on 10 September in these words: "Likewise of the holy martyrs Apellius, Luke and Clement."
passages.notes: Hispalis of Baetica is Seville.

passages.original: Galerius vero Illyrici, Groecioe et Orienti. Sane Chlorum de Hispaniis optime meri- tum fuisse sedatio probat persecutionis, sub ejus enim principatu nullus legitur martyrio coronatus : quin potius (ut Eusebius scribit de Vita Constantini lib. I) eos, qui de Palatio suo negarunt se Christia- nos esse, cum essem, domo ejecit; cos vero qui fassi sunt, ut qui Deo fideles erant, fideles sibi repu- tans honoravit.
passages.english: and Galerius over Illyricum, Greece and the East. Indeed, that Chlorus deserved very well of the Spains is proved by the calming of the persecution, for under his rule no one is read of as crowned with martyrdom. Rather (as Eusebius writes in Book I of the Life of Constantine), those of his palace who denied that they were Christians, when they were, he expelled from his house; but those who confessed it he honoured, reckoning that those who were faithful to God would be faithful to himself.
passages.notes: "cum essem" read as "cum essent" ("when they were"); "cos" read as "eos".

passages.original: Errore transcribentium effectum erat, ut haec clausula quae ad annum 310 spectabat, in anno 110 collocaretur, quam et nos necessitate temporum ducti mutavimus. Vixit qui- dem Porphyrius, utpote Plotini discipulus et Ori- genis condiscipulus, Aureliani imperatoris tempori- bus, Eusebius vero et Apollinaris Laudicenus, Con- stantii et Constantini. Meminit Hieronymus, lib. de Script. Eccl., aliquorum ex his qui contra Porphy- rium scripserunt, et de Eusebio ait in catalogo ope- rum ejus : Contra Porphyrium qui eodem tempore scribebat in Sicilia ((ut quidam putant) libri triginta; de quibus ad me viginti tantum pervenerunt. De Apol- linari vero : Exstant ejus adversus Porphyrium, qui inter coetera opera ejus vel maxime probantur. De Methodio sic : Methodius Olympi Lycioe, et postea Tyri episcopus, nitidi, compositique sermonis adversus Porphyrium confecit libros, etc.
passages.english: Through the error of copyists it had come about that this clause, which belonged to the year 310, was placed in the year 110; and we, led by the requirements of chronology, have changed it. Porphyry, indeed, being a disciple of Plotinus and a fellow pupil of Origen, lived in the times of the emperor Aurelian, but Eusebius and Apollinaris of Laodicea in those of Constantius and Constantine. Jerome, in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, mentions some of those who wrote against Porphyry. Of Eusebius he says in the catalogue of his works: "Against Porphyry, who was writing at the same time in Sicily (as some think), thirty books, of which only twenty have reached me." Of Apollinaris: "There are extant his [books] against Porphyry, which among his other works are especially approved." Of Methodius thus: "Methodius, bishop of Olympus in Lycia and afterwards of Tyre, composed books in a polished and well-ordered style against Porphyry," etc.

passages.original: Narrat rem gestam Au- gustinus citato lib., cap. 4, ea occasione, quod Do- natistae, quos olim in capite Hosius exagitaverat, utpote Caeciliani defensor existens, de Hosii con- demnatione gloriabantur. En verba Augustini : Quod enim dicunt de Hosio Cordubensi, flagitandum est ut probent, non solum talem illum fuisse, qualem dicunt (nam hoc falsis conductis testibus probari poterat), sed quod talis fuerit manifestum illis fuisse, quibus eum communicare asserunt : hoc enim nisi probaverint, frustra dicunt se scisse qualis fuerit : quia nescientibus obesse non potuit; a quibus se isti innocentibus sepa- rando, propter istam separationis sacrilegam iniquita- tem, innocentes esse non possunt.
passages.english: Augustine relates the affair in the book cited, chapter 4, on the occasion that the Donatists, whom Hosius had once vigorously harried, being the defender of Caecilian, were boasting of Hosius' condemnation. Here are Augustine's words: "As for what they say about Hosius of Córdoba, they must be required to prove not only that he was such as they say (for this could be proved by false hired witnesses), but that it was manifest that he was such to those with whom they assert he was in communion. For unless they prove this, they say in vain that they knew what he was, since he could not harm those who did not know; and by separating themselves from these innocent men, because of this sacrilegious iniquity of separation, they cannot be innocent."
passages.notes: "in capite" (lit. "at the head") is unclear; rendered loosely as "vigorously".

passages.original: A. C. 312. — Hoc anno, etc. Rem gestam narrat pluribus Eusebius, lib. IX Hist, cap. 8, et de Vita Constantini lib. I, cap. 32, et in Panegyrico post victoriam : at in Chronico hoc ipso anno breviter : Maxentius (ait) juxta pontem Milvium a Constantino superatus occiditur, anno imperii sui sexto.
passages.english: A.D. 312. — "In this year," etc. Eusebius narrates the affair at greater length in Book IX of the History, chapter 8, in Book I of the Life of Constantine, chapter 32, and in the Panegyric after the victory; but in the Chronicle, under this very year, briefly: "Maxentius," he says, "is defeated by Constantine near the Milvian Bridge and killed, in the sixth year of his reign."

passages.original: inde Nicomediam perductam rhe- toricam etiam docuisse; penuria vero discipulorum, ob Graecam videlicet civitatem, ad scribendum se contulisse : atque in ultima senectute magistrum fuisse Crispi Caesaris filii Constantini in Gallia. De eo Eusebius : Fuit (ait) vir omnium suo tempore elo· quentissimus; sed adeo in hac vita pauper, ut plerum. que etiam necessariis indiguerit, nedum deliciis. Haec ille in Chron. Nonnulli eum Africanum crediderunt, sed sine sufficienti fundamento;
passages.english: that, brought thence to Nicomedia, he also taught rhetoric there; but for lack of pupils, because it was a Greek city, he turned to writing; and in extreme old age he was tutor in Gaul to Crispus Caesar, son of Constantine. Of him Eusebius says: "He was the most eloquent man of his time, but so poor in this life that he often lacked even necessities, let alone luxuries." So he in the Chronicle. Some have believed him an African, but without sufficient foundation;

passages.original: A. C. 344. Multoe, etc. Et hoc etiam apud Hieronymum in Chronico leges.
passages.english: A.D. 344. "Many," etc. You will read this too in Jerome's Chronicle.

passages.original: 38, in epistola pro Athanasio, ubi de ejus adversariis loquens : In tantum, inquit, invaluerunt, quoe de Athanasio dicebantur, ut eum ubicumque re· periretur, juberet Constantius imperator occidi; cum quo et Theodulum, et Olympium Proesules Ecclesia- rum Thracensium. Athanasius quoque in epistola ad solitariam vitam agentes. Diodorum, ait, episcopum suis sedibus expulerunt; Olympium item ex AEnis, ac Theodulum ex Trajanopoli, ambos episcopos Thra- cioe, bonos et orthodoxos viros, infensos hoeresi, ca- lumniis impetiverunt; semel quidem cum ad Eusebia- norum calumnias Constantius imperator edictum misit : iterum autem cum illius rei memoria ab Euse- bianis refricata est (Eusebianos vocat Arianos, quod eorum signifer fuisset Eusebius). Habebat autem edictum, ut non solum civitatibus, et Ecclesiis ejice- rentur, sed et capitali poena, ubicumque inventi essent, plecterentur. Idem replicat in Apologia de fuga sua. Inde factum ut Olympius Hosio specialibus amicitiis jungeretur, in concilio praesertim Sardicensi, ubi ejus monitis legem, quam cap.
passages.english: 38, in the letter on behalf of Athanasius, where, speaking of his adversaries, it says: "The things said about Athanasius gained such strength that the emperor Constantius ordered him to be killed wherever he was found; and with him Theodulus and Olympius, prelates of the churches of Thrace." Athanasius too, in the letter to those living the solitary life, says: "They drove the bishop Diodorus from his see; likewise they assailed with calumnies Olympius of Aenus and Theodulus of Trajanopolis, both bishops of Thrace, good and orthodox men, hostile to heresy; once when the emperor Constantius sent an edict in response to the calumnies of the Eusebians, and again when the memory of that affair was revived by the Eusebians" (he calls the Arians Eusebians because Eusebius had been their standard-bearer). "The edict provided that they should not only be expelled from the cities and churches, but punished with capital penalty wherever they were found." He repeats the same in the Apology for his flight. Hence it came about that Olympius was joined to Hosius in special friendship, especially at the Council of Sardica, where on his advice the law which [Hosius] had passed in canon
passages.notes: Begins and ends mid-reference (chapter numbers 38 and 14 fall outside).

passages.original: quod si tu quoque persecutionem moves, etiam nunc ad quidvis potius sustinendum paratus sum, quam ut effundam innocentem sanguinem, et veritatem prodam, teque numquam probo talia scribentem, et istiusmodi minas denuntiantem. Desinas igitur istiusmodi scribere, neque sentias cum Ario, neque audias Orientales, neque Ur- sacio et Valenti fidem habeas; quoe enim illi dicunt, non ob Athanasium, sed ob suam hoeresim dicunt. Mihi crede, qui tibi avus oetate esse possem. Fui ipse in Sar- dicensi concilio, cum tu, tuusque frater beatus Constans, nos omnes eo convocabat; ipseque ultro Athanasii ini- micos provocavi, cum ad Ecclesiam ubi ego morabar advenissent, ut si quid contra eum haberent, ederent;
passages.english: and if you too stir up persecution, even now I am ready to endure anything rather than shed innocent blood and betray the truth; and I never approve of you writing such things and uttering threats of this kind. Stop, therefore, writing such things; do not side with Arius, do not listen to the Easterners, and do not trust Ursacius and Valens; for what they say, they say not on account of Athanasius but on account of their own heresy. Believe me, who in age could be your grandfather. I was myself at the Council of Sardica, when you and your brother, the blessed Constans, called us all together; and I myself of my own accord challenged the enemies of Athanasius, when they had come to the church where I was staying, to bring forward whatever they had against him;
passages.notes: "convocabat" (singular) likely for "convocabatis"/"convocavit"; sense unaffected.

passages.original: Calumniantur igitur eum, sed non ut illi Danielem apud Darium, illibenter talia au- dientem, sed ut Jesabel contra Nabeth, et ut Judoei apud Herodem his verbis agentes. Non solum non sub- scribit contra Athanasium, sed et nos ob Athana- sium condemnat, et hoeresim tali odio prosequitur, ut aliis scribat, melius esse mortem perferre, quam pro- ditores fieri veritatis : ob hoeresim deinde ait dilectum fratrem Athanasium persecutionem sustinere, et Libe- rium Romanorum episcopum, coeterosque alios insidiis tentari.
passages.english: So they slandered him, but not as those men [slandered] Daniel before Darius, who heard such things unwillingly, but as Jezebel [acted] against Naboth, and as the Jews [did] before Herod, pleading in these words: "Not only does he not sign against Athanasius, but he even condemns us on account of Athanasius, and pursues the heresy with such hatred that he writes to others that it is better to endure death than to become betrayers of the truth. Then he says that it is on account of the heresy that our beloved brother Athanasius is suffering persecution, and that Liberius, bishop of the Romans, and all the others are being assailed by plots."
passages.notes: Scanning errors such as 'hoeresim' (haeresim) and split words have been read as intended. 'Herodem' may stand for Pilate in the original source; the text as given reads Herod.

passages.original: Reperitur in diptycha sanctorum Toletano- rum antistitum, quae est in liturgia Missalis S. Isi- dori, immediate praecedens S. Olympium. Et quidem S. Gregorius unus ex illis censetur, de quibus S. Athanasius scripsit ad solitarios : Quis enim cum videret Patrem episcoporum magnum Hosium tot mala pati, et episcopos ex Hispania, et aliis regionibus in exsilium deportari, non animadvertit omnes crimina- tiones contra Athanasium falsas esse?
passages.english: He is found in the diptych of the holy bishops of Toledo that is in the liturgy of the Missal of St Isidore, immediately preceding St Olympius. And indeed St Gregory is reckoned one of those of whom St Athanasius wrote to the solitaries: "For who, seeing the father of bishops, the great Hosius, suffer so many evils, and bishops from Spain and other regions deported into exile, did not perceive that all the accusations against Athanasius were false?"
passages.notes: 'Missal of St Isidore' presumably refers to the Mozarabic (Isidorian) missal.

passages.original: 24 : Simul atque senex ille eorum fidei assentiri abnuebat, plagoe illi erant inflictoe, membraque machinis distorta. Idem habet Theodoretus lib. II, cap. 15. En magni Hosii et nonnullorum Patrum apud Ariminum ca- sus. Cum vero de palinodia ejus certi simus, teste Athanasio, et haec in nulla alia quam Cordubensi synodo recantata ab ipsis fuerit, cogimur Cordu- bensem confiteri, et quod de ea Damasus dixerit : In ipso principio, ab his ipsis, qui in Arimino revocare, aut retractare compellebantur, usque ad hoc causa correcta est, ut confiterentur, circumventione sibi sub- reptum.
passages.english: 24: "As soon as that old man refused to assent to their faith, blows were inflicted on him, and his limbs were wrenched by machines." Theodoret has the same in book II, chapter 15. Here is the fall of the great Hosius and of some Fathers at Ariminum. But since we are certain of his recantation, on the testimony of Athanasius, and these things were recanted by them in no other synod than that of Corduba, we are compelled to acknowledge [a synod] of Corduba, and [to apply to it] what Damasus said of it: "At the very beginning, by those very men who were compelled at Ariminum to revoke or retract, the matter was corrected to this point, that they confessed that they had been taken in by deceit."
passages.notes: The opening '24' continues a reference begun in the preceding context (Socrates, book II, chapter 24). The Damasus quotation is elliptical; the sense of 'revocare, aut retractare' is uncertain.

passages.original: Erat jam tempore Ariminensis circumventionis Hosius centenarius, uti Athanasius ad solitarios dixit : Nec senectutem hominis jam centenarii inhu- manus ille respexit. Porro ex his quos Dexter in Cordubensi concilio adfuisse refert, nonnulli Sardi- censis actis subscripserunt;
passages.english: At the time of the deception at Ariminum Hosius was already a hundred years old, as Athanasius said to the solitaries: "Nor did that inhuman man respect the old age of a man already a hundred years old." Further, of those whom Dexter reports were present at the council of Corduba, some had signed the acts of Sardica;

passages.original: 3. Carthagine, etc. Exstat liber de ira Dei, quem Hieronymus pulcherrimum vocat lib. de Script. Ec- cles. in Lactantio; ejus initium est : Animadverti soepe, Donate, plurimos existimare, non irasci Deum, etc. De Donato vero ipso martyrium passo agit Usuar- dus I Martii : Eodem, inquiens, die S.
passages.english: 3. At Carthage, etc. There survives the book On the Wrath of God, which Jerome calls most beautiful in the book On Ecclesiastical Writers, under Lactantius. Its opening is: "I have often noticed, Donatus, that very many think that God does not become angry," etc. Of this Donatus himself, who suffered martyrdom, Usuard treats on 1 March, saying: "On the same day [the feast of] St
passages.notes: The sentence breaks off; it continues in the following passage.

passages.original: Fuit quidem in Hispania Justus alter Urgelensis episcopus, cujus dies festa in Romano Martyrologio habetur ad 28 Maii, hic vero multo recentior fuit Dextro, ut ne- quiret ad eum respicere. Exstant sancti Ambrosii epistolae duae ad Justum scriptae, altera in lib. I epist. 1, altera vero in lib. VIII epist. 2, quae in ordine est 63. In iis rogatus Ambrosius nonnullas exponit quaestiones ad sacras litteras pertinentes. In priori explicat, quid significet illud didrachmum, cujus dimidium Hebraeus praecipitur offerre pro redem- ptione animae suae. Ejus initium : Ambrosius Justo : Pulchre admones, frater, ut epistolares fabulas, et sermonem absentium ad interpretationem conferamus oraculi coelestis, etc.
passages.english: There was indeed in Spain another Justus, bishop of Urgel, whose feast day is held in the Roman Martyrology on 28 May; but he was much later than Dexter, so that [Dexter] could not have referred to him. There survive two letters of St Ambrose written to Justus, one in book I, letter 1, the other in book VIII, letter 2, which is 63 in the series. In them Ambrose, having been asked, expounds some questions pertaining to the sacred scriptures. In the first he explains what is meant by that didrachm, half of which the Hebrew is commanded to offer for the redemption of his soul. Its opening: "Ambrose to Justus: You do well to urge, brother, that we turn our letter-conversations, and the speech of those absent from one another, to the interpretation of the heavenly oracle," etc.

passages.original: Eusebio Coesariensi episcopo scriptas reperi- mus. Nam Constantinus Augustus, cum Coesaream fuisset ingressus, et diceret memorato antistiti, ut pe- teret aliqua beneficia Coesariensi Ecclesioe profutura : legitur respondisse Eusebium : opibus suis Ecclesiam ditatam, nulla petendi beneficia necessitate compelli : sibi tamen desiderium immobile exstitisse, ut quidquid in Republ. Romana gestum sit erga sanctos Dei, judi- ces judicibus succedentes in universo orbe Romano, sol- licita perscrutatione, monumenta publica discutiendo, perquirerent, et qui Martyrum, a quo Judice, in qua provincia vel civitate, qua die, quave perseverantia pas- sionis suoe obtinuerunt palmam, de ipsis archiviis sub- lata, ipsi Eusebio, regio jussu dirigerent.
passages.english: ... written by St Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea. For when the emperor Constantine Augustus had entered Caesarea and told the said bishop to ask for some benefits that would be of use to the Church of Caesarea, Eusebius is read to have replied that the Church was enriched by its own resources and was compelled by no need to ask for benefits; yet he himself had an unshakable desire that whatever had been done in the Roman state concerning the saints of God should be searched out by the judges succeeding one another throughout the whole Roman world, by careful investigation, examining the public records; and that they should send to Eusebius himself, by royal command, [records] taken from the archives themselves, [showing] which of the martyrs, under which judge, in which province or city, on which day, and with what perseverance in their suffering, obtained the palm.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence, continuing 'quorum passiones a S.' from the preceding context.

passages.original: 1 sic inquit : Astipulatur et liber Martyrologii, qui Beati Hieronymi nomine, ac proefatione attitulatur : quamvis idem Hieronymus illius libri non auctor, sed interpres, Eusebius autem auctor exstitisse narretur. Praefationem intelligo epistolam de qua nunc agimus. Walafridus vero Strabo haec scribit lib. de Reb. Ec- clesiast. cap. 28 : Hieronymus Martyrologium, secutus Eusebium Coesariensem per anni circulum conscripsit; ea occasione ab Episcopis Chromatio, et Heliodoro illud opus rogatus componere, quia Theodosius, reli- giosus imperator, in concilio episcoporum laudavit Gregorium Cordubensem episcopum, quod omni die missas explicans, eorum martyrum quorum natalitia essent, nomina plurima commemoraret.
passages.english: 1 says as follows: "The book of the Martyrology, which bears the name and preface of Blessed Jerome, also agrees, although the same Jerome is said to have been not the author of that book but its translator, while Eusebius was its author." By the preface I understand the letter we are now discussing. Walafrid Strabo, moreover, writes this in the book On Ecclesiastical Matters, chapter 28: "Jerome, following Eusebius of Caesarea, wrote a Martyrology through the circuit of the year, having been asked to compose that work by the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus on this occasion: because Theodosius, the devout emperor, in a council of bishops praised Gregory, bishop of Corduba, because in celebrating masses every day he commemorated very many names of those martyrs whose birthdays [into heaven] fell [on that day]."
passages.notes: The opening '1' continues a reference begun in the preceding context (Bede, Retractations on Acts, chapter 1).

passages.original: Regnavit hic in Francia orientali super Francos, tertius a Phara- mundo, cui successit frater ejus Marcomerus, huic autem filius ipsius Priamus nomine, qui circa an- num Domini 423 legitur habuisse imperium et suc- cessorem Gennebaldum : ut habes apud Trithemium, lib. de Origine Francorum, et alios. Meminit ejus- dem Priami Prosper Tyro in Chron. suo, ad annum 4 Gratiani Augusti, apud Canisium, tom. I Lect. antiqu.
passages.english: He reigned in eastern Francia over the Franks, the third from Pharamond; he was succeeded by his brother Marcomer, and Marcomer by his own son named Priam, who is read to have held power around the year of the Lord 423 and to have had Gennebaud as his successor, as you have it in Trithemius, in the book On the Origin of the Franks, and in others. Prosper Tiro mentions the same Priam in his Chronicle, at the fourth year of Gratian Augustus, in Canisius, volume I of the Ancient Readings.

passages.original: ejus copiam legit Vasaeus, bar- barice admodum, et Gothice, ut sua ferebant tem- pora, scripti. Hinc fit, ut tres Isidori Chronicon scripsisse reperiantur; Cordubensis Senior conti- nuavit Eusebium et Hieronymum, quemadmodum Prosper Aquitanicus, Victor Tunensis, Idatius La- macensis, et Marcellinus Comes fecerunt, a principio imperii Theodosii, usque ad sua quisque tempora. Isidorus Junior Cordubensis a scribendo Chronico abstinuit;
passages.english: ... Vasaeus read a copy of it, written very barbarously and in Gothic fashion, as his times allowed. Hence it comes about that three Isidores are found to have written chronicles. The Elder of Corduba continued Eusebius and Jerome, as Prosper of Aquitaine, Victor of Tunnuna, Idatius of Lamego and Marcellinus Comes did, from the beginning of the reign of Theodosius, each up to his own times. Isidore the Younger of Corduba refrained from writing a chronicle;
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence. 'Tunensis' is read as Tunnunensis (Victor of Tunnuna).

passages.original: Et quid opus est con- jecturis, cum inferius nobis exprimat urbis nomen, in qua natus fuit Vigilantius, nimirum Convennas? haec tamen Ptolomaeo, Plinio, et caeteris auctoribus in Aquitania sita est, vulgo dicta Commenge, seu Commingeois. Audi Hieronymum : Nimirum respon-det suo generi, ut qui de latronum et Convennarum natus est semine (quos Cu. Pompeius edomita Hispa- nia, et ad triumphum redire festinans, de Pyrenoei jugis deposuit, et in unum oppidum congregavit, unde et Convennarum urbs nomen accepit) hucusque latro- cinetur contra Ecclesiam Dei.
passages.english: And what need is there for conjectures, when [Jerome] further on expresses to us the name of the city in which Vigilantius was born, namely Convennae? This, however, according to Ptolemy, Pliny and the other authors, is situated in Aquitania, commonly called Commenge, or Commingeois. Hear Jerome: "Evidently he is true to his stock, as one who was born of the seed of brigands and of the Convennae (whom Gnaeus Pompey, having subdued Spain and hastening to return for his triumph, brought down from the ridges of the Pyrenees and gathered into a single town, from which the city of the Convennae also took its name), so that up to now he plays the brigand against the Church of God."
passages.notes: "Cu. Pompeius" read as Cn. (Gnaeus) Pompeius.

passages.original: Dato igitur semel Oro- sio in ejus disciplinam, non est unde divinemus, eodem ipso, vel sequenti anno ab ubere doctrinae ablactatum, et in Orientem amandatum : quinimmo consentaneum est rationi judicaro, aliquot annos apud Augustinum edisse litterarum studiis va- cando; et tandem in iis provectum ad Hierony- mum contendisse, quo tempore sancti proto martyris reliquiae adinventae sunt. His accedit, quod Orosius nisi post multos annos non rediit in Hispanias, cum tamen subito, responso litterarum quas tulerat ac- cepto, redire deberet, si illarum gratia praecipue, et non ut studiis vacaret, in Africam profectus fuisset.
passages.english: Once Orosius had been given over to his instruction, then, there is no ground for us to guess that he was weaned from the breast of [Augustine's] teaching in that same year or the next and sent off to the East; rather, it is consistent with reason to judge that he spent some years with Augustine, devoting himself to the study of letters, and at length, having advanced in them, made his way to Jerome at the time when the relics of the holy protomartyr were discovered. To this is added the fact that Orosius did not return to Spain until after many years, whereas he ought to have returned at once, on receiving the reply to the letters he had brought, if he had gone to Africa chiefly for their sake and not in order to devote himself to study.
passages.notes: "judicaro" read as judicare; "edisse" apparently for sedisse ("stayed, spent").

passages.original: Caeterum ut de Origenistis aliqud dicamus, re- fert in consultatione sua Orosius, duos Avitos Tar- raconenses, extra patriam actos errores quosdam in eam reduxisse, qui Romam petierat, Victorini; qui Hierosolymam, Origenis : nimirum libros Periar- chon Origenis secum deferebat, et errores, quibus passim scatent, praedicabat et inter alia, Verbum Patris dominum prius successive omnium hierar- charum angelorum ad suam hypostasim naturas assumpsisse, et ultimo tandem humanam. Cum his advenerat in Hispaniam quidam sanctus Basilius Graecus (ut ipse Orosius nuncupat) identidem do- cens, sed quisnam fuerit ignoratur. Omnes tamen scriptis D. Augustini convictos, ab inceptis desti- tisse satis ex eo manifestum lit, quod postmodum ad annum Domini 429 eorumdem cum honore et laude meminit Dexter : et quia memoria ejusmodi errorum in nullo hujus aetatis Hispano concilio facta est.
passages.english: But to say something about the Origenists: Orosius relates in his consultation that two Aviti of Tarragona, driven outside their homeland, brought back into it certain errors — the one who had gone to Rome, those of Victorinus; the one who [had gone] to Jerusalem, those of Origen. He, namely, carried with him Origen's books Peri Archon and preached the errors with which they everywhere teem, and among other things [taught] that the Word of the Father, the Lord, had first taken on successively to his hypostasis the natures of all the hierarchies of angels, and last of all, at length, the human [nature]. With them had come into Spain a certain holy Basil, a Greek (as Orosius himself calls him), teaching the same things, but who he was is unknown. That all of them, however, refuted by the writings of St Augustine, desisted from what they had begun, is sufficiently clear from the fact that afterwards, under the year of the Lord 429, Dexter mentions them with honour and praise, and because no mention of errors of this kind is made in any Spanish council of this period.
passages.notes: "aliqud" read as aliquid; "lit" as fit.

passages.original: quod nimirum utrumque Stilicone consule habitum sit. Non habito delectu dc numero consulatus, cum cer- tum sit primum Stiliconis in annum Domini 400 in- cidisse, secundum in 405. quod Idatius, Marcellinus, Cassiodorus et caeteri testantur. Porro subscriptio- nes 19 episcoporum quae exstant, hujus necessario fuisse id convincit, quod Paternus omnium primus subscribit (nimirum Bracarensis) eo quod praesidis in eo functus officio sit;
passages.english: that both were evidently held when Stilicho was consul, without any distinction being made as to the number of the consulship, since it is certain that Stilicho's first [consulship] fell in the year of the Lord 400 and the second in 405, as Idatius, Marcellinus, Cassiodorus and the rest attest. Further, that the subscriptions of the nineteen bishops which survive must necessarily belong to this [council] is proved by the fact that Paternus (namely, of Braga) subscribes first of all, because he discharged the office of president in it;
passages.notes: The unit begins mid-sentence. "dc" read as de.

passages.original: A. C. 406.— 1. Leporius, etc. Quis is Leporius fue- rit non omnibus constat, nam sunt qui velint hoc tem- pore duos ejus nominis exstitisse : alterum ex familia sancti Augustini, cujus ipse meminit Serm. 50 de Di- versis; alterum, qui Pelagii tabe infectus gratiae Dei contrarius existens, pravum dogma in Galliis dissemi- navit, sed ab Augustino admonitus, palinodiam recan- tavit; de quo Gennadius lib.
passages.english: Year of Christ 406. — 1. Leporius, etc. Who this Leporius was is not agreed by all, for there are some who hold that at this time there were two of that name: one of the household of St Augustine, whom he himself mentions in Sermon 50 On Various [Subjects]; the other, who, infected with the plague of Pelagius and being opposed to the grace of God, spread a perverse doctrine in Gaul, but, admonished by Augustine, recanted with a palinode; concerning whom Gennadius, book
passages.notes: Ends mid-reference (continues "de Viris illustribus, cap. 59").

passages.original: Perperam tamen, nihil etenim horum ex scriptis auctorum constat; sed demus respersum canis ser- monem illum 50 scripsisse Augustinum, quoniam in eo dicit : Ego quidem quem Deo propitio videtis epi- scopum vestrum, juvenis veni ad istam civitatem, etc, non decet hos canos, etc., attamen conversionem et initium monachatus Leporii non refert quasi recen- tem, et iis ipsis diebus factam, sed ante multos an- nos. En verba ipsius : Leporius quidam fuit nobilitate soeculari conspicuus, et proedives, comparandus in plu- ribus Piniano.
passages.english: Wrongly, however, for none of this is established from the writings of the authors; but let us grant that Augustine wrote that Sermon 50 when already sprinkled with grey hairs, since in it he says: "I, whom by God's favour you see as your bishop, came to this city as a young man," etc., "these grey hairs do not befit," etc.; yet he does not report the conversion and the beginning of Leporius's monastic life as something recent and done in those very days, but many years before. Here are his words: "There was a certain Leporius, conspicuous for worldly nobility and very rich, comparable in many respects to Pinianus."

passages.original: Quid vero in causa fuerit, ut Augustinus canoni- cos regulares instituere inciperet, promit ipse lucu- lenter Serm. 1 de communi Vita Clericorum; nimi- rum quia factus episcopus, ut suo muneri pontifi- cali incumberet, et hospites supervenientes huma- niter reciperet, quod eo temporis episcoporum erat, nequibat in monasterio Eremi cum monachis ut prius habitare;
passages.english: What was the reason why Augustine began to institute canons regular he himself sets out clearly in Sermon 1 On the Common Life of Clerics: namely, that having been made bishop, in order to attend to his episcopal duty and receive arriving guests kindly, which at that time was the business of bishops, he could not live as before in the monastery of the Hermitage with the monks;
passages.notes: "Eremi" may be a place-name or simply "of the desert/hermitage".

passages.original: Hoc loco in quibusdam codicibus inse- rebantur ejusmodi verba : Avitus imperator in Hispa- nias trajicit, ibique deposita imperii dignitate magnis itineribus ad Gallias properat. Sed haec aliunde trans- lata sunt; nam Dexter non potuit agnoscere Avitum ad imperium provectum, cum teste Idatio et Prospero tyrone in Chron. assumptus fuerit ann. Domini 455.
passages.english: At this point in certain manuscripts words of this kind used to be inserted: "The emperor Avitus crosses into Spain, and there, having laid down the imperial dignity, hastens by forced marches to Gaul." But these have been carried over from elsewhere; for Dexter could not have known of Avitus raised to the empire, since, as Idatius and Prosper Tiro in his Chronicle attest, he was elevated in the year of the Lord 455.

passages.original: Multa de eo diximus ad annos Domini 388 et 406; ejusque festa dies in Usuardi martyrologio, quod Galesinus in suo sequi- tur, satis celebris astruitur 24 Aprilis. Exstat liber de Fide in tomis Bibliothecae Vet. Patrum : cujus etiam Hieronymus meminit lib. de Script. Eccles. Porro Augustam cui dedicatus est, non solum Pla- cidiam, sed simul Gallam Placidiam vocatam, quod nonnemo abnuit, expresse docet cum Dextro, Pau- lus Diaconus lib. XIII. de gestis Longobardorum, et tamquam rem certam ac notissimam narrat Petrus in Catalogo lib.
passages.english: We have said much about him under the years of the Lord 388 and 406; and his feast day is set down as quite well known on 24 April in the martyrology of Usuard, which Galesinus follows in his own. There survives a book On the Faith in the volumes of the Library of the Old Fathers, which Jerome also mentions in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers. Moreover, that the Augusta to whom it is dedicated was called not only Placidia but also Galla Placidia, which someone denies, is expressly taught, together with Dexter, by Paul the Deacon in book XIII On the Deeds of the Lombards, and Peter in the Catalogue, book
passages.notes: Ends mid-reference. The subject "him" is unnamed here; context suggests Gregory of Elvira.

passages.original: Solvit Stilico morte pro- pria proditionis poenas, Barbari vero insolentiores effecti imperii provincias invadunt; et anno se- quenti agente Constante Constantini tyranni filio contra Didymum et Verinianum, ut Prosper in Chronico affirmat, Alani, Wandali, et Suevi Hispa- nias ingressi sunt, videlicet aera Caesaris 447, Christi vero anno 409, uti Idatius et caeteri notant, Hono- rio VIII et Theodosio Arcadii filio III, coss.
passages.english: Stilicho paid the penalty for his treason by his own death, but the barbarians, grown more insolent, invaded the provinces of the empire; and in the following year, while Constans, son of the usurper Constantine, was acting against Didymus and Verinianus, as Prosper affirms in his Chronicle, the Alans, Vandals and Suevi entered Spain, namely in the Era of Caesar 447, but in the year of Christ 409, as Idatius and the rest note, Honorius for the eighth time and Theodosius son of Arcadius for the third time being consuls.

passages.original: Asturii Ovetum translatum est, in Hispaniarum captivitate sub duro Sarracenorum jugo, ibique honorifice conditum in Sacello sancto, vulgo Camera sancta nuncupato requiescit in lignea arca; quae anno Domini 1572, die 25 Julii, aperta coelestium aromatum fragrantiam dedit, ut refert Ambrosius Morales lib. XIII Hist. cap. 38, habetque titulum Sancti Serrani, ejus nimirum qui vocabatur Asturius Serranus. Celebrat ejus festum Ecclesia Ovetensis 8 die Martii sub nomine Sancti Serrani episcopi, et confessoris, ut in kalendario sanctorum Hispanorum Matrili impresso anno 1614 inveni.
passages.english: [After many years the body of St.] Asturius was translated to Oviedo, during the captivity of the Spains under the harsh yoke of the Saracens, and there, honourably laid to rest in the holy chapel commonly called the Cámara Santa, it rests in a wooden chest; this, when opened in the year of the Lord 1572, on 25 July, gave off a fragrance of heavenly spices, as Ambrosio de Morales reports in book XIII of his History, chapter 38, and it bears the title of Saint Serranus, that is, of the one who was called Asturius Serranus. The Church of Oviedo celebrates his feast on 8 March under the name of Saint Serranus, bishop and confessor, as I found in the calendar of the saints of Spain printed at Madrid in the year 1614.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the subject 'corpus S.' (the body of St.) comes from the preceding context and is supplied in brackets. 'Matrili' taken as Madrid.

passages.original: 2. Celebris, etc. Hic fuit ille magnus Olympius, quem Augustinus doctorem praeclarum Ecclesiae, ac sanctum appellat, dum ejus librum citat. Consule quae de Olympio ejus nominis primo scripsimus ad ann. Domini 356, de eo siquidem agitur in prae- senti.
passages.english: 2. Celebrated, etc. This was that great Olympius whom Augustine calls an illustrious doctor of the Church, and a saint, when he cites his book. Consult what we wrote about Olympius, the first of that name, at the year of the Lord 356, since it is he who is dealt with in the present [passage].
passages.notes: 'Celebris, etc.' is a lemma quoting the text being commented on.

passages.original: ut non sit sensus, quod fuerit episcopus Tarraconensis, quia non fuit nisi Caldaquensis; sed quod Paulus Tarra- conensis natione, fuit episcopus Caldaquensis : cui Bonifacius in episcopatu successit. Scripsit ad Pau- lum hunc Augustinus epist. 216, ex qua constat dis- cipulum ipsius fuisse, nam ait : Tibi enim maxime debeo, quia in Christo Jesu per Evangelium ego te genui. Dure tamen eum objurgat, quod Caldaquen- sem seu Cataquensem Ecclesiam absque necessitate debitis oneraverat : Cum enim tu magis magisque implicare te non cesses, ut etiam rebus quibus renun- tiasti, te post renuntiationem inserueris (professus igitur sub Augustini magisterio regularia vota fue- rat), et in ea professione virere dicaris, cui frugalitas Ecclesioe tace sufficere non possit, ut quid quoeris com- munionem meam, etc.
passages.english: so that the sense is not that he was bishop of Tarragona, since he was only [bishop] of Caldaqua, but that Paul, a Tarraconensian by birth, was bishop of Caldaqua, and Boniface succeeded him in the episcopate. Augustine wrote to this Paul in letter 216, from which it is clear that he was his disciple, for he says: "For I owe most to you, because in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel." Yet he rebukes him harshly for having burdened the Church of Caldaqua or Cataqua with debts without necessity: "For since you do not cease to entangle yourself more and more, so that you have even involved yourself, after your renunciation, in the affairs which you renounced" (he had therefore professed the regular vows under Augustine's direction), "and you are said to live in such a style that the frugality of so great a Church cannot suffice for it, why do you seek my communion?" etc.
passages.notes: 'virere' (to flourish) is likely a scanning error for 'vivere' (to live); translated as 'live'. 'Ecclesioe tace' read as 'Ecclesiae tantae' (of so great a Church); the text is garbled here. 'Caldaquensis/Cataquensis' refers to the see of Cataqua (Cataquas) in Numidia.

passages.original: VI scripsit, Placidia, soror im- peratoris (Honorii), apud Alaricum manebat, vicem illa quidem obsidis quodammodo implens, ita tamen ut omni honore cultuque regali frueretur. Minime ergo vis illi illata est, sed ipsamet pro bono pacis sponte se nuptiis Ataulphi obtulit : Ob hoc enim (ait Orosius lib. VII, cap. 40) abstinere a bello, ob hoc in- hiare paci Ataulphus nitebatur; proecipue Placidioe uxoris suoe, feminoe sane ingenio acerrimoe religionis satis probatoe, ad omnia bonarum ordinationum opera, persuasu et consilio, temperatus. In ea etiam caetera a Daniele annotata signa verificantur. Non enim ste- tit semen ejus; omnes siquidem ab Ataulpho suscepti filii cum eo pariter occisi sunt, ut jam diximus.
passages.english: [As Zosimus wrote in book] VI, Placidia, the sister of the emperor (Honorius), was staying with Alaric, in a way filling the role of a hostage, yet in such a manner that she enjoyed every royal honour and attention. So no force at all was used against her; rather, she herself, for the sake of peace, freely offered herself in marriage to Ataulf. "For this reason," says Orosius, book VII, chapter 40, "Ataulf strove to refrain from war, for this reason to long for peace, being moderated toward all works of good government chiefly by the persuasion and counsel of his wife Placidia, a woman indeed of the keenest intelligence and of well-proven religion." In her the other signs noted by Daniel are also verified. For his seed did not endure, since all the sons begotten by Ataulf were killed together with him, as we have already said.
